school-senior-biology.title: Senior Biology (Class 11–12)
school-senior-biology.description: Pathshala Senior biology: cells and genetics, human physiology, reproduction and reproductive health, biotechnology and ecology — explained clearly with diagrams-in-words, worked genetics problems and real stories.

courses.title: Cells, inheritance & molecular genetics
courses.summary: How cells are built and divide, how traits are inherited (Mendel and beyond), and how DNA is copied, read and translated into proteins.
outcomes: Learners can describe organelles and compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
Learners can explain mitosis and meiosis and why meiosis creates variation
Learners can solve monohybrid, dihybrid, blood-group and sex-linked crosses
Learners can explain replication, transcription, the genetic code and translation

scenes.text: Anaya, 15, in Thiruvananthapuram, scrapes the inside of her cheek with a clean toothpick and looks at it under her school microscope.
Next to it is a slide of onion peel. The onion cells look like neat bricks with thick walls; her cheek cells look like irregular flat pebbles.
'Why the difference?' she asks Mrs Thomas. 'Because plants and animals solved the problem of living differently,' her teacher replies.

steps.title: Cell theory
steps.body:
- All living organisms are made of cells (Schleiden and Schwann).
- New cells arise only from pre-existing cells (Virchow: *omnis cellula e cellula*).
- The cell is the basic unit of structure and function.

**Prokaryotes** (bacteria): no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles, DNA in a nucleoid, 70S ribosomes, often plasmids. **Eukaryotes** (plants, animals, fungi, protists): true nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm.

steps.title: The organelles and their jobs
steps.body:
- **Plasma membrane**: fluid mosaic model—a lipid bilayer with proteins; selectively permeable.
- **Nucleus**: DNA in chromatin; nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA.
- **Ribosomes**: protein synthesis.
- **Endoplasmic reticulum**: rough ER (with ribosomes) makes proteins for export; smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies.
- **Golgi apparatus**: modifies, packages and dispatches proteins; forms lysosomes.
- **Lysosomes**: digestive enzymes ('suicide bags').
- **Mitochondria**: aerobic respiration, ATP ('powerhouse'); have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes.
- **Chloroplasts** (plants): photosynthesis; also have their own DNA.
- **Vacuole**: large central vacuole in plant cells keeps them turgid.
- **Cell wall** (plants: cellulose; fungi: chitin).

steps.title: Plant vs animal cells
steps.body:
Anaya's onion cells: cell wall ✔, large central vacuole ✔, plastids (chloroplasts in green tissue; onion bulb cells lack them) and a regular shape.

Her cheek cells: no cell wall, small vacuoles if any, centrioles present, irregular shape.

Both have a nucleus, membrane, mitochondria, ER, Golgi and ribosomes.

steps.title: Why mitochondria have their own DNA
steps.body: The **endosymbiotic theory** proposes that mitochondria and chloroplasts descended from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral cell. Evidence: double membranes, their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and division by fission. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited mainly from the mother.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying prokaryotes have no ribosomes (they have 70S ribosomes).
- Saying all plant cells contain chloroplasts (root and onion-bulb cells don't).
- Mixing up 'cell membrane' and 'cell wall'—every cell has a membrane; only some have a wall.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A cell secretes large amounts of digestive enzyme protein. Which two organelles would you expect to be especially well developed?

Answer: rough ER (to make the protein) and the Golgi apparatus (to package and secrete it).

activity.prompt: Match each organelle with its main job.

quiz.q: Ribosomes in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells are
quiz.why: Eukaryotic ribosomes in the cytoplasm are 80S (60S + 40S subunits). Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S.

quiz.q: Which organelle is called the 'suicide bag'?
quiz.why: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that can digest the cell if they burst, so they are called 'suicide bags'.

quiz.q: Which statement fits prokaryotes?
options: DNA in a nucleoid, no membrane-bound organelles
quiz.why: Prokaryotes like bacteria have their DNA in a nucleoid, with no nuclear envelope and no membrane-bound organelles. Their cell wall is not made of cellulose.

quiz.q: The fluid mosaic model describes the
quiz.why: The fluid mosaic model describes the plasma membrane as a lipid bilayer with proteins that can move laterally within it.

quiz.q: Evidence that mitochondria were once bacteria
options: They are found only in plants
They have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes
quiz.why: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, like bacteria, which is key evidence for the endosymbiotic theory.

scenes.text: Kabir scrapes his knee playing football in Jalandhar. Within a week, new skin has covered the wound.
At dinner he looks at his two sisters: same parents, yet they look so different from each other.
Two kinds of cell division explain both: mitosis repairs and grows; meiosis makes unique gametes.

steps.title: The cell cycle
steps.body:
Interphase (most of the time): **G₁** (growth), **S** (DNA replication), **G₂** (preparation). Then the **M phase** (mitosis + cytokinesis). Some cells leave the cycle and rest in **G₀** (e.g., many nerve cells).

Checks at each stage stop damaged cells from dividing; failure of these controls can contribute to cancer.

steps.title: Mitosis (equational division)
steps.body:
- **Prophase**: chromatin condenses into chromosomes (two sister chromatids each); nuclear envelope breaks down; spindle forms.
- **Metaphase**: chromosomes line up on the equatorial (metaphase) plate—best stage to count chromosomes.
- **Anaphase**: centromeres split; sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
- **Telophase**: nuclear envelopes re-form; chromosomes decondense.
- **Cytokinesis**: animal cells by a cleavage furrow; plant cells by a cell plate.

Result: 2 genetically identical diploid cells (2n → 2n). Used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

steps.title: Meiosis (reductional division)
steps.body:
One DNA replication, two divisions, four haploid cells (2n → n).
- **Prophase I**: homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis); **crossing over** at pachytene exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids; chiasmata are visible at diplotene.
- **Metaphase I/Anaphase I**: homologous pairs separate (independent assortment of each pair).
- **Meiosis II**: like mitosis—sister chromatids separate.

Variation comes from crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation. Humans: 2n = 46, gametes n = 23.

steps.title: Counting variation
steps.body: With 23 chromosome pairs, independent assortment alone can produce 2²³ ≈ 8.4 million different chromosome combinations in a person's gametes—before crossing over adds even more. That is why Kabir's sisters differ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking DNA replicates in prophase (it replicates in the S phase).
- Confusing sister chromatids (identical copies) with homologous chromosomes (one from each parent).
- Saying meiosis II halves the chromosome number—meiosis I does that.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A cell has 16 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will each cell have after (a) mitosis, (b) meiosis?

Answer: (a) 16; (b) 8.

activity.prompt: Put the stages of mitosis in order.
items: Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator

quiz.q: DNA replication occurs in
quiz.why: DNA replication occurs in the S (synthesis) phase of interphase.

quiz.q: Crossing over takes place during
quiz.why: Crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes takes place during pachytene of prophase I.

quiz.q: Mitosis produces
quiz.why: Mitosis is an equational division that produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells.

quiz.q: Best stage to count chromosomes
quiz.why: Metaphase is the best stage for counting and studying chromosomes, since they are most condensed and aligned on the equator.

quiz.q: Human gametes contain
quiz.why: Human gametes are haploid, so they contain 23 chromosomes (n = 23). Body cells have 46.

lessons.title: Mendel and the rules of inheritance

scenes.text: Rohan, 17, in Indore, fails a colour-vision test for a pilot's medical. He is red–green colour blind. His parents both see colours normally.
His grandmother remembers that her own father was colour blind. 'But nobody else in between!' she says.
Rohan's biology teacher, Mr Saxena, draws a pedigree—and Mendel's rules plus X-linkage explain everything.

steps.title: Mendel's laws
steps.body:
Mendel worked on garden peas with clear contrasting traits.
- **Law of dominance**: in a heterozygote (Tt) one allele (T) masks the other (t).
- **Law of segregation**: the two alleles separate during gamete formation; each gamete gets one.
- **Law of independent assortment**: alleles of different genes (on different chromosomes) assort independently.

Monohybrid cross Tt × Tt: genotypes 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt; phenotypes 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
Dihybrid cross RrYy × RrYy: phenotypes 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Test cross (with the recessive homozygote) reveals an unknown genotype: Tt × tt → 1 : 1.

steps.title: Beyond simple dominance
steps.body:
- **Incomplete dominance**: snapdragon red × white → pink F₁; F₂ 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
- **Codominance**: ABO blood groups. Alleles Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant, i is recessive. 6 genotypes, 4 phenotypes (A, B, AB, O).
- **Multiple alleles**: more than two alleles in the population (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i).
- **Polygenic traits**: skin colour, height—many genes, continuous variation.
- **Linkage**: genes close together on one chromosome tend to be inherited together; crossing over separates them.

steps.title: Sex determination and sex-linked traits
steps.body:
Humans: females XX, males XY; the father's sperm (X or Y) determines the child's sex.

**X-linked recessive** traits (red–green colour blindness, haemophilia) appear far more often in males, who have only one X. A carrier mother (XᶜX) passes the allele to half her sons (affected) and half her daughters (carriers).

steps.title: Rohan's pedigree solved
steps.body:
Great-grandfather XᶜY → his daughter (Rohan's grandmother) must be a carrier XᶜX → Rohan's mother received Xᶜ from her: carrier XᶜX, with normal vision → Rohan (son) received Xᶜ from his mother and Y from his father ⇒ XᶜY, colour blind.

For his parents' future children: sons 50% affected, daughters 0% affected but 50% carriers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that a son's X always comes from his mother.
- Writing 3:1 for a test cross (it is 1:1).
- Treating blood group O as dominant.
- Ratios are probabilities for each child, not guarantees for a family of four.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Parents with blood groups A (Iᴬi) and B (Iᴮi). What blood groups can their children have?

Answer: AB, A, B and O, each with probability ¼.

a.text: Rohan's cousin Meera is a known carrier of colour blindness (XᶜX). She asks: if she marries a man with normal vision, what are the chances for her children?

choices.label: All sons will be colour blind
choices.feedback: Each son has a 50% chance, not 100%.

choices.label: Each son has a 50% chance; daughters won't be affected but half may be carriers
choices.feedback: Correct—a classic X-linked recessive cross.

b.text: Redraw the Punnett square: XᶜX × XY. What do the sons get?

choices.label: Half XᶜY, half XY
choices.feedback: Yes—each son has a 50% chance.

c.text: Meera worries. What is the most helpful next step?

choices.label: Talk to a genetic counsellor or doctor for personalised advice
choices.feedback: Good: professionals can explain risks and options calmly.

choices.label: Believe a forum post that says 'it skips generations, so you're safe'
choices.feedback: Myth: inheritance follows probabilities, not 'skipping' rules.

e.text: The forum is wrong. What now?

choices.label: Ask a doctor or genetic counsellor
choices.feedback: Right.

d.text: Meera understands her risks. Colour blindness is common and usually mild—many careers are open, though a few (like some pilot roles) have colour-vision standards.

quiz.q: F₂ phenotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross with complete dominance
quiz.why: In a monohybrid cross with complete dominance, the F₂ phenotypic ratio is 3 : 1, three dominant to one recessive.

quiz.q: A test cross of a heterozygote gives
quiz.why: A test cross of a heterozygote (Tt × tt) gives a 1 : 1 ratio of dominant to recessive offspring.

quiz.q: ABO blood groups show
quiz.why: ABO blood groups show multiple alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i) and codominance, since Iᴬ and Iᴮ are both expressed in AB.

quiz.q: Haemophilia is more common in males because
options: they have only one X chromosome
quiz.why: Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele on it is expressed. Females need two copies.

quiz.q: Pink snapdragons crossed together give red : pink : white =
quiz.why: Crossing two pink snapdragons shows incomplete dominance and gives red : pink : white in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio.

story.title: The DNA that solved a mystery

scenes.text: Forensic scientist Dr Priya Nair in Hyderabad receives a tiny blood spot from a crime scene—far too little DNA to analyse directly.
Her lab copies the DNA millions of times, then compares repeating patterns between samples.
To understand how, intern Arjun must first understand how DNA stores, copies and reads information.

steps.title: DNA structure
steps.body:
- Double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953, using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins).
- Two antiparallel strands (5'→3' and 3'→5') of nucleotides: sugar (deoxyribose), phosphate, base.
- Base pairing: **A=T (2 hydrogen bonds), G≡C (3 hydrogen bonds)** ⇒ Chargaff's rule A = T, G = C.
- Purines A, G; pyrimidines C, T (U in RNA).
- Human genome: about 3 billion base pairs, roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes.

steps.title: Replication
steps.body:
**Semi-conservative** (proven by Meselson and Stahl using ¹⁵N): each new DNA has one old and one new strand.
- Helicase unwinds; DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the **5'→3'** direction.
- **Leading strand**: continuous; **lagging strand**: discontinuous Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase.
- Primers (RNA) start each new strand.

steps.title: Central dogma: transcription and translation
steps.body:
DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein.
- **Transcription**: RNA polymerase reads the template strand; in eukaryotes the primary transcript is processed (introns removed by splicing, 5' cap, poly-A tail).
- **Genetic code**: triplet codons; 64 codons = 61 for amino acids + 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA). **AUG** = start (methionine). The code is nearly universal, degenerate (several codons per amino acid) and non-overlapping.
- **Translation** at ribosomes: tRNA anticodons pair with mRNA codons, bringing amino acids that are joined by peptide bonds.

steps.title: Gene regulation: the lac operon
steps.body: In E. coli, the lac operon's genes (for using lactose) are switched OFF when a repressor binds the operator. When lactose is present, it (as allolactose) inactivates the repressor ⇒ the genes are transcribed. This is an **inducible** system.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
A DNA molecule has 30% adenine. Find the other bases.
- T = A = 30%
- G + C = 40% ⇒ G = C = 20%.

Template DNA strand 3'-TAC GGA TTC-5' → mRNA 5'-AUG CCU AAG-3' → Met–Pro–Lys.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing T in mRNA (RNA uses U).
- Forgetting strands are antiparallel when writing complementary sequences.
- Thinking every codon codes for an amino acid (3 are stop codons).

activity.prompt: Complete the molecular biology facts.
activity.text: Adenine pairs with ___ in DNA. The start codon is ___. Replication is described as semi-___.

quiz.q: If a DNA sample has 20% cytosine, its adenine content is
quiz.why: By Chargaff's rule, C = G = 20%, so A + T = 100 − 40 = 60%. A = T, so A = 30%.

quiz.q: Okazaki fragments are formed on the
quiz.why: Okazaki fragments are short DNA pieces formed on the lagging strand, which is made discontinuously.

quiz.q: Number of stop codons
quiz.why: There are three stop codons: UAA, UAG and UGA.

quiz.q: The experiment proving semi-conservative replication
quiz.why: The Meselson–Stahl experiment, using heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N), proved that DNA replication is semi-conservative.

quiz.q: In the lac operon, lactose acts as an
quiz.why: In the lac operon, lactose acts as an inducer. It binds the repressor and inactivates it, so the genes are switched on.

questions.q: The powerhouse of the cell
questions.why: The mitochondrion is the powerhouse of the cell, the site of aerobic respiration and ATP production.

questions.q: Number of chromosomes in a human body cell
questions.why: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes (2n = 46).

questions.q: The base found in RNA but not DNA
questions.why: Uracil is found in RNA and replaces thymine, which is found in DNA.

questions.q: Plant cytokinesis occurs by
questions.why: Plant cytokinesis occurs by cell plate formation, because the rigid cell wall prevents furrowing.

questions.q: Dihybrid F₂ phenotypic ratio
questions.why: The F₂ phenotypic ratio of a dihybrid cross is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, from independent assortment of two genes.

questions.q: A man with blood group AB marries a woman with group O. Children may be
questions.why: An AB man (IᴬIᴮ) and an O woman (ii) can have children with IᴬI (A) or Iᴮi (B) only, so A or B only.

questions.q: mRNA sequence for the DNA template 3'-TAC-5'
questions.why: The DNA template 3'-TAC-5' gives an mRNA that is complementary and antiparallel, with U in place of T: 5'-AUG-3'.

questions.q: A colour-blind man marries a woman who is not a carrier. Their daughters will be
questions.why: A colour-blind man (XᶜY) and a non-carrier woman (XX) have daughters that each get his Xᶜ and her X, so all are carriers.

questions.q: A cell at G₂ has 20 pg of DNA. DNA content of each cell after meiosis II
questions.why: A G₂ cell has 4C DNA (20 pg). After meiosis II each gamete has 1C, a quarter, so 5 pg.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: Chiasmata become visible in diplotene. Synapsis is in zygotene, crossing over in pachytene and terminalisation in diakinesis.

questions.q: A dsDNA segment of 100 base pairs has 30 adenines. Total hydrogen bonds
questions.why: Total base pairs = 100 with 30 A–T pairs and 70 G–C pairs. Hydrogen bonds = 30 × 2 + 70 × 3 = 60 + 210 = 270.

questions.q: Two genes are 10 map units apart. In a test cross of the dihybrid in coupling (AB/ab), the percentage of recombinant offspring is about
questions.why: Genes 10 map units apart show 10% recombination in a test cross, because 1 map unit = 1% recombination frequency.

questions.q: How many different gametes can an individual of genotype AaBbCc produce (independent assortment)?
questions.why: With 3 heterozygous gene pairs and independent assortment, the number of gamete types = 2³ = 8.

courses.title: Human physiology
courses.summary: Digestion, breathing and circulation, excretion, and neural and hormonal control — how your body keeps you alive every second, with numbers and health connections.
outcomes: Learners can trace digestion and absorption and name key enzymes
Learners can explain gas exchange, transport and the cardiac cycle
Learners can describe nephron function and its regulation
Learners can explain nerve impulses and the roles of major hormones

story.title: The journey of a masala dosa

scenes.text: At a Chennai café, Siddharth bites into a masala dosa: rice-and-lentil batter, potato filling, a little ghee.
Over the next hours, that meal is broken into glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol—small enough to enter his blood.
Let's follow it from mouth to colon.

steps.title: Mouth and stomach
steps.body:
- **Mouth**: chewing; **salivary amylase** begins digesting starch to maltose (about 30% of starch is digested here).
- **Oesophagus**: peristalsis moves food down.
- **Stomach**: HCl (acidic pH, kills microbes, activates pepsinogen to **pepsin**), which breaks proteins into peptides. Mucus protects the stomach lining.

steps.title: Small intestine: the main event
steps.body:
- **Bile** (from the liver, stored in the gall bladder) emulsifies fats—it contains no digestive enzymes.
- **Pancreatic juice**: trypsin (proteins), pancreatic amylase (starch), lipase (fats), nucleases.
- **Intestinal juice** (succus entericus): maltase, lactase, sucrase, dipeptidases complete digestion.
- **Absorption**: villi and microvilli give a huge surface area. Glucose and amino acids enter blood capillaries; fatty acids and glycerol form micelles, are reassembled into chylomicrons and enter the lacteals (lymph).

steps.title: Large intestine
steps.body:
Absorbs water and salts; gut bacteria make some vitamins (e.g., vitamin K). Undigested matter forms faeces.

The liver also stores glycogen, makes bile and detoxifies substances.

steps.title: Health connections
steps.body:
- Lactose intolerance: low lactase in adulthood—milk sugar is fermented by gut bacteria, causing bloating.
- Jaundice: yellowing from bilirubin build-up, often due to liver problems.
- Dehydration from diarrhoea is dangerous—oral rehydration solution (ORS) saves lives. See a doctor if diarrhoea is severe, bloody, or lasts more than a couple of days, or if there are signs of dehydration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying bile digests fats (it only emulsifies them).
- Saying digestion of proteins starts in the mouth (it starts in the stomach).
- Saying fats are absorbed directly into blood capillaries (they enter lacteals first).

activity.prompt: Where does each enzyme or secretion mainly act?

quiz.q: Salivary amylase digests
quiz.why: Salivary amylase digests starch into maltose in the mouth.

quiz.q: Bile is produced by the
quiz.why: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

quiz.q: Fatty acids are absorbed into
quiz.why: Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into lacteals (lymph vessels of the villi) as chylomicrons, not directly into blood capillaries.

quiz.q: Pepsin is activated by
quiz.why: Pepsinogen is activated to pepsin by hydrochloric acid in the stomach.

quiz.q: Main site of water absorption from undigested residue
quiz.why: The large intestine (colon) absorbs most of the water from the undigested residue.

scenes.text: Sunita, 17, runs her first half-marathon in Mumbai. By kilometre 15 her heart is racing and she is breathing hard.
Her watch shows a heart rate of 170 beats per minute; at rest it is about 70.
Her lungs and heart are cooperating to deliver oxygen and remove carbon dioxide—let's see how.

steps.title: Breathing mechanics and gas exchange
steps.body:
- **Inspiration**: diaphragm contracts (flattens), external intercostals lift the ribs ⇒ chest volume ↑, pressure ↓, air flows in.
- **Expiration** at rest is mostly passive.
- Tidal volume ≈ 500 mL; vital capacity ≈ 3.5–4.5 L.
- Gas exchange in the **alveoli** by diffusion: O₂ from alveoli (high pO₂) into blood; CO₂ out.

steps.title: Transport of gases
steps.body:
- About **97% of O₂** is carried by haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin; about 3% dissolved in plasma.
- **CO₂**: about 70% as bicarbonate (via carbonic anhydrase in RBCs), 20–25% as carbaminohaemoglobin, about 7% dissolved.
- The oxygen dissociation curve is sigmoid. High CO₂, high H⁺ (low pH) and high temperature in working muscles shift it right—haemoglobin releases more O₂ exactly where Sunita needs it (the Bohr effect).

steps.title: The heart and circulation
steps.body:
- Four chambers; **double circulation**: pulmonary (right ventricle → lungs → left atrium) and systemic (left ventricle → body → right atrium).
- The **SA node** is the pacemaker; impulses pass to the AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres.
- Cardiac cycle at about 72 beats/min lasts about 0.8 s. Heart sounds: 'lub' (AV valves close), 'dub' (semilunar valves close).
- **Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate** ≈ 70 mL × 72 ≈ 5 L/min at rest.
- Normal adult blood pressure is around 120/80 mmHg (systolic/diastolic). Persistently high readings (hypertension) need medical attention.

steps.title: Sunita's numbers
steps.body: Rest: 70 mL × 70 beats/min ≈ 4.9 L/min. During the race, with stroke volume rising to about 110 mL and heart rate 170: 110 × 170 ≈ 18.7 L/min—nearly four times more blood delivered every minute.

steps.title: Common mistakes and health note
steps.body:
- Saying arteries always carry oxygenated blood (the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood).
- Saying most CO₂ travels bound to haemoglobin (most travels as bicarbonate).
- Chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness during exercise is a medical emergency—stop and call 112.

activity.prompt: A person's stroke volume is 80 mL and heart rate is 75 beats/min. What is the cardiac output in litres per minute?

quiz.q: Most oxygen in blood is carried
quiz.why: About 97% of oxygen in blood is carried as oxyhaemoglobin. Only about 3% is dissolved in plasma.

quiz.q: The pacemaker of the heart
quiz.why: The SA (sinoatrial) node is the pacemaker, because it initiates each heartbeat.

quiz.q: The 'dub' sound is due to closure of the
quiz.why: The second heart sound, 'dub', is due to the closure of the semilunar valves at the start of ventricular relaxation. The first, 'lub', is the AV valves.

quiz.q: During inspiration the diaphragm
quiz.why: During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens, which enlarges the chest cavity so air flows in.

quiz.q: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood?
quiz.why: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. The pulmonary vein and aorta carry oxygenated blood.

scenes.text: Every Tuesday and Friday, Ayaan accompanies his grandfather in Bhopal to a dialysis centre. A machine cleans his blood for four hours.
'My kidneys used to do this all day without me noticing,' his grandfather says.
Ayaan decides to learn exactly what a healthy kidney does—and why it is so hard to replace.

steps.title: The nephron
steps.body:
Each kidney has about a million **nephrons**.
- **Glomerulus + Bowman's capsule**: ultrafiltration under pressure. Filtrate = plasma minus proteins and cells.
- **Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)**: reabsorbs nearly all glucose and amino acids and most water and salts.
- **Loop of Henle**: creates a concentration gradient in the medulla (countercurrent mechanism).
- **Distal tubule and collecting duct**: fine-tune water and salts under hormonal control.

steps.title: The numbers
steps.body: Glomerular filtration rate ≈ 125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day. About 99% is reabsorbed, leaving roughly 1.5 L of urine per day. Humans excrete nitrogen mainly as **urea** (ureotelic), made in the liver by the ornithine (urea) cycle.

steps.title: Regulation
steps.body:
- **ADH (vasopressin)** from the posterior pituitary makes the collecting duct more permeable to water ⇒ concentrated urine. Low ADH (e.g., in diabetes insipidus) ⇒ large volumes of dilute urine.
- **Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone**: low blood pressure ⇒ renin ⇒ angiotensin II (vasoconstriction) and aldosterone (Na⁺ and water reabsorption).
- **ANF** from the heart opposes this, lowering blood pressure.

steps.title: When kidneys fail
steps.body: Kidney failure lets urea and other wastes build up. **Haemodialysis** filters blood through a semi-permeable membrane against dialysis fluid. A kidney transplant from a matched donor is the long-term option. Diabetes and uncontrolled high blood pressure are major causes of kidney damage, so regular check-ups matter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying proteins are filtered normally (they aren't; protein in urine can signal kidney damage).
- Thinking ADH increases urine volume (it decreases it).
- Confusing the PCT (bulk reabsorption) with the collecting duct (fine-tuning).

statements.s: About 180 litres of filtrate are formed per day, but only about 1.5 litres of urine.
statements.why: About 99% is reabsorbed.

statements.s: ADH makes urine more dilute.
statements.why: ADH increases water reabsorption, making urine concentrated.

statements.s: Glucose is normally reabsorbed in the PCT.
statements.why: Glucose in urine suggests blood glucose exceeds the reabsorption limit (e.g., uncontrolled diabetes).

statements.s: Humans excrete nitrogen mainly as ammonia.
statements.why: Humans are ureotelic: mostly urea.

statements.s: Dialysis removes urea by diffusion across a membrane.
statements.why: Wastes diffuse into dialysis fluid.

quiz.q: Ultrafiltration occurs in the
quiz.why: Ultrafiltration occurs in the glomerulus, where high pressure in the capillaries forces fluid into Bowman's capsule.

quiz.q: Main nitrogenous waste in humans
quiz.why: Urea is the main nitrogenous waste in humans. It is made in the liver through the urea cycle.

quiz.q: Aldosterone increases reabsorption of
quiz.why: Aldosterone acts on the distal parts of the nephron and increases reabsorption of Na⁺ (and so water).

quiz.q: Normal GFR in adults is about
quiz.why: The normal glomerular filtration rate is about 125 mL/min, roughly 180 litres a day.

quiz.q: The countercurrent mechanism mainly involves the
options: loop of Henle and vasa recta
quiz.why: The countercurrent mechanism involves the loop of Henle and the vasa recta, and builds the concentration gradient in the medulla.

lessons.title: Nerves and hormones: the body's control systems

scenes.text: As the board exam paper lands on her desk in Kolkata, Riya's palms sweat and her heart pounds.
Her nerves fired in milliseconds; adrenaline from her adrenal glands keeps her alert for minutes.
Fast wiring and slow chemical messages—two control systems working together.

steps.title: The nerve impulse
steps.body:
- **Resting potential** ≈ −70 mV (inside negative), maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) and K⁺ leak.
- **Action potential**: a stimulus opens Na⁺ channels ⇒ Na⁺ rushes in ⇒ depolarisation; then K⁺ flows out ⇒ repolarisation.
- Myelinated fibres conduct faster by **saltatory conduction** (jumping node to node).
- **Synapse**: an impulse releases neurotransmitters (e.g., acetylcholine) that bind receptors on the next cell.

steps.title: Brain and reflexes
steps.body:
- **Cerebrum**: thinking, memory, voluntary actions, senses. **Cerebellum**: balance and coordination. **Medulla**: breathing, heart rate, swallowing. **Hypothalamus**: temperature, hunger, thirst; controls the pituitary.
- **Reflex arc**: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (interneuron) → motor neuron → effector. Pulling your hand from a hot pan happens before you feel pain.

steps.title: Major hormones
steps.body:
- **Pituitary**: GH (growth), TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH, prolactin; posterior lobe releases ADH and oxytocin.
- **Thyroid**: thyroxine (metabolic rate; iodine needed—deficiency causes goitre).
- **Pancreas (islets)**: insulin from β-cells lowers blood glucose; glucagon from α-cells raises it.
- **Adrenal**: adrenaline/noradrenaline ('fight or flight'), cortisol (stress), aldosterone (salt balance).
- **Gonads**: testosterone; oestrogen and progesterone.

steps.title: Diabetes mellitus
steps.body:
- **Type 1**: the immune system destroys β-cells; insulin injections are needed.
- **Type 2**: the body resists insulin; strongly linked to lifestyle and genetics; managed with diet, exercise and medicines.
Symptoms like excessive thirst, frequent urination and unexplained weight loss need a doctor's evaluation.

steps.title: Calming the exam-hall surge
steps.body: Slow breathing (for example, in for 4 seconds, out for 6) activates the parasympathetic system and calms the adrenaline response. If exam anxiety feels overwhelming, see the Mann (wellbeing) courses or call Tele-MANAS at 14416.

cards.front: Hormone that increases water reabsorption in kidneys
Part of the brain for balance

quiz.q: Depolarisation of a neuron is caused by
quiz.why: Depolarisation of a neuron happens when Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ enters the cell.

quiz.q: Saltatory conduction occurs in
quiz.why: Saltatory conduction occurs in myelinated fibres, where the impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier, which makes it faster.

quiz.q: Glucagon
quiz.why: Glucagon, from the α-cells of the pancreas, raises blood glucose by promoting glycogen breakdown in the liver.

quiz.q: Breathing rate is controlled by the
quiz.why: The respiratory centre in the medulla (with the pons) controls breathing rate.

quiz.q: The 'master gland' that is itself controlled by the hypothalamus
quiz.why: The pituitary is the 'master gland', but it is itself controlled by hormones from the hypothalamus.

questions.q: Enzyme in saliva
questions.why: Salivary amylase is the enzyme in saliva. It begins starch digestion in the mouth.

questions.q: Number of chambers in the human heart
questions.why: The human heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles.

questions.q: The functional unit of the kidney
questions.why: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, and each kidney has about a million of them.

questions.q: Insulin is secreted by
questions.why: Insulin is secreted by the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. α-cells secrete glucagon.

questions.q: Cardiac output with stroke volume 70 mL and heart rate 72/min
questions.why: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 70 × 72 ≈ 5040 mL/min, which is about 5 L/min.

questions.q: Most CO₂ is transported as
questions.why: About 70% of CO₂ is transported as bicarbonate ions in plasma. About 20–25% is carbaminohaemoglobin and the rest is dissolved.

questions.q: A person produces large volumes of dilute urine and feels very thirsty, with normal blood sugar. A likely hormone problem
questions.why: Large volumes of dilute urine with thirst and normal blood sugar suggest a lack of ADH, as in diabetes insipidus. Without ADH, too little water is reabsorbed.

questions.q: A rightward shift of the oxygen dissociation curve is caused by
options: high CO₂, low pH and high temperature
questions.why: A rightward shift of the oxygen dissociation curve (Bohr effect) is caused by high CO₂, low pH and high temperature, so haemoglobin releases more oxygen to active tissues.

questions.q: If GFR is 125 mL/min and urine flow 1 mL/min, the percentage of filtrate reabsorbed is about
questions.why: Reabsorbed = (125 − 1)/125 × 100 = 99.2% of the filtrate.

questions.q: During the absolute refractory period, a neuron
questions.why: During the absolute refractory period, Na⁺ channels are inactivated, so the neuron cannot fire another action potential, however strong the stimulus.

questions.q: Which sequence of the conducting system of the heart is correct?
options: Bundle of His → SA node → AV node → Purkinje fibres
SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
SA node → Purkinje fibres → AV node → bundle of His
AV node → SA node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
questions.why: The conduction pathway of the heart is SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres.

questions.q: Chylomicrons are formed in intestinal cells from
questions.why: In intestinal cells, fats are reassembled and coated with proteins to form chylomicrons, which then enter the lacteals.

courses.title: Human reproduction & reproductive health
courses.summary: A calm, scientific, non-explicit course on the reproductive systems, puberty, the menstrual cycle, fertilisation and pregnancy, contraception, STIs, consent and Indian law — the Class 12 syllabus plus the questions teens rarely ask aloud.
outcomes: Learners can describe male and female reproductive anatomy and gametogenesis using correct terms
Learners can explain the menstrual cycle, fertilisation, implantation and pregnancy
Learners can understand puberty changes such as periods and nightfall as normal and healthy
Learners can describe contraception methods and STI prevention factually and know where to get help
Learners can explain consent and India's age-of-consent law under POCSO
courses.guardianNote: This course covers the Class 12 biology topics of human reproduction and reproductive health: anatomy using correct terms, the menstrual cycle, nightfall (nocturnal emission), fertilisation and pregnancy, contraception, sexually transmitted infections, consent and India's POCSO law. It follows UNESCO's International Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education (2018) and WHO guidance for this age group. It is medically accurate, respectful and non-explicit: no images of bodies, no erotic content. It encourages teens to talk to trusted adults and doctors.

story.title: The biology class that nobody giggled in

scenes.text: In a Class 12 classroom in Pune, Dr Kulkarni begins the reproduction chapter. A few students giggle; one hides behind a book.
'I'm a doctor,' she says calmly. 'These are organs, like the heart or kidneys. Using correct names is how we stay healthy and safe.'
By the end of the period, the giggles have turned into good questions.

steps.title: Male reproductive system
steps.body:
- **Testes** (in the scrotum, kept about 2–2.5 °C below body temperature) make sperm in the **seminiferous tubules**; **Leydig cells** make testosterone; **Sertoli cells** nourish developing sperm.
- Sperm mature and are stored in the **epididymis**, travel through the **vas deferens**, and mix with fluids from the **seminal vesicles**, **prostate** and **bulbourethral glands** to form semen.
- The **urethra** carries urine or semen (never both at once) out through the penis.

steps.title: Female reproductive system
steps.body:
- **Ovaries** contain follicles with oocytes and make oestrogen and progesterone.
- **Fallopian tubes (oviducts)**: the fimbriae catch the released ovum; fertilisation usually happens in the **ampulla**.
- **Uterus**: a muscular organ whose inner lining (**endometrium**) thickens each cycle; a pregnancy develops here.
- **Cervix** connects the uterus to the **vagina** (the birth canal).
- **Mammary glands** produce milk after childbirth.

steps.title: Gametogenesis
steps.body:
- **Spermatogenesis** (from puberty, continuous): spermatogonium (2n) → primary spermatocyte → meiosis I → 2 secondary spermatocytes (n) → meiosis II → 4 spermatids → spermiogenesis → 4 sperm.
- **Oogenesis** begins before birth: primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I until puberty. Each cycle, usually one completes meiosis I, producing a secondary oocyte and a small polar body. Meiosis II completes only if a sperm enters. One ovum per oogonium (plus polar bodies).
- Hormones: GnRH (hypothalamus) → FSH and LH (pituitary) → gonads.

steps.title: Variation is normal
steps.body: Bodies differ in size, shape and timing of puberty. Puberty usually begins between about 8 and 13 in girls and 9 and 14 in boys. Comparing yourself with friends or with online images is not a good guide—a doctor is.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying fertilisation happens in the uterus (it usually happens in the ampulla of the fallopian tube).
- Thinking sperm are made in the epididymis (they mature there; they are made in the seminiferous tubules).
- Saying one oogonium gives four ova (it gives one ovum and polar bodies).

items.back: In the seminiferous tubules of the testes

items.front: Why are the testes outside the abdomen?
items.back: Sperm production needs a temperature about 2–2.5 °C lower than core body temperature
In the ampulla of the fallopian tube

items.front: How many ova does one primary oocyte produce?

quiz.q: Testosterone is secreted by
quiz.why: Testosterone is secreted by the Leydig (interstitial) cells of the testes. Sertoli cells nourish developing sperm.

quiz.q: The endometrium is the
quiz.why: The endometrium is the inner lining of the uterus. It thickens each cycle and sheds during menstruation if there is no pregnancy.

quiz.q: Spermatogenesis produces from one primary spermatocyte
quiz.why: One primary spermatocyte undergoes two meiotic divisions to give four spermatids, which become four sperm.

quiz.q: Meiosis II of the secondary oocyte is completed
quiz.why: The secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II and completes meiosis II only after a sperm enters.

quiz.q: Hormones FSH and LH are released by the
quiz.why: FSH and LH are released by the anterior pituitary, under the control of GnRH from the hypothalamus.

scenes.text: Aisha, 16, in Delhi, uses a period-tracking app. Her cycle is sometimes 26 days, sometimes 32. She worries something is wrong.
Her aunt, a gynaecologist, explains that some variation is normal, especially in the first few years after periods begin.
Then she explains what the hormones are doing each week—and how a pregnancy begins.

steps.title: The menstrual cycle (average 28 days)
steps.body:
- **Menstrual phase** (about days 1–5): the endometrium sheds with blood because progesterone has fallen.
- **Follicular / proliferative phase**: FSH helps a follicle grow; it secretes oestrogen, which rebuilds the endometrium.
- **Ovulation** (around day 14 in a 28-day cycle): an **LH surge** releases the secondary oocyte.
- **Luteal / secretory phase**: the empty follicle becomes the **corpus luteum**, which secretes progesterone to keep the endometrium ready. No pregnancy ⇒ corpus luteum degenerates ⇒ progesterone falls ⇒ next period.

Cycles of roughly 21–35 days are commonly considered within the normal range for adults; teens can be more irregular.

steps.title: Fertilisation and implantation
steps.body:
- A sperm reaches the ovum in the ampulla; enzymes from the **acrosome** help it penetrate; only one sperm fertilises the ovum.
- The zygote divides (cleavage) as it moves down the tube → morula → **blastocyst**, which **implants** in the endometrium about a week after fertilisation.
- The embryo's outer cells (trophoblast) help form the **placenta**, which exchanges nutrients, gases and wastes with the mother's blood (the two bloods do not mix directly) and makes hormones such as **hCG** (detected by pregnancy tests), oestrogen and progesterone.

steps.title: Pregnancy and birth
steps.body:
Human pregnancy lasts about 9 months (about 40 weeks counted from the first day of the last period). The heart forms early; by the end of the first trimester major organs are formed. Birth (parturition) is driven by signals from the fully developed fetus and placenta, uterine contractions and the hormone **oxytocin**. After birth, **prolactin** stimulates milk production; colostrum (the first milk) carries antibodies.

In India, determining the sex of a fetus for selection is illegal under the PCPNDT Act.

steps.title: Period care basics
steps.body:
- Use pads, tampons, menstrual cups or period underwear—change them regularly (pads typically every 4–8 hours depending on flow).
- Mild cramps are common; warm compresses, gentle movement and common pain relievers recommended by a doctor or pharmacist can help.
- See a doctor if periods are extremely painful, very heavy (soaking a pad every hour or two), last more than about 7 days, have not started by age 15, or stop for several months.

steps.title: Myths to drop
steps.body:
- Periods are not 'impure' or 'dirty'—menstrual blood is a normal body fluid.
- You can bathe, exercise, study, cook and play during your period.
- An irregular cycle does not mean you can't get pregnant; ovulation can happen at unexpected times.

activity.prompt: Put the events from ovulation to implantation in order.
items: The secondary oocyte enters the fallopian tube
A sperm fertilises it in the ampulla
The zygote divides (cleavage) to form a morula
The blastocyst implants in the endometrium

quiz.q: Ovulation is triggered mainly by a surge of
quiz.why: Ovulation is triggered mainly by a mid-cycle surge of LH.

quiz.q: The corpus luteum mainly secretes
quiz.why: The corpus luteum mainly secretes progesterone, which maintains the endometrium for a possible pregnancy.

quiz.q: Pregnancy tests detect
quiz.why: Pregnancy tests detect hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin), which the placenta produces after implantation.

quiz.q: Menstruation occurs because
options: progesterone falls when the corpus luteum degenerates
quiz.why: If there is no pregnancy, the corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone falls, so the endometrium is shed as menstruation.

quiz.q: The hormone that strongly drives uterine contractions during birth
quiz.why: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary strongly drives uterine contractions during childbirth.

lessons.title: Puberty questions people don't ask aloud

scenes.text: Aman, 14, wakes up with damp, sticky shorts after a dream. He is embarrassed and thinks something is wrong with him.
Across town, his cousin Simran, 12, notices blood on her underwear at school and is scared.
Both message the same school counsellor, Ms Banerjee. Her answers are calm, simple and true: these are normal signs of a healthy, growing body.

steps.title: Nightfall (nocturnal emission)
steps.body:
During puberty, the testes start producing sperm and the body makes semen. Sometimes semen is released during sleep—often with a dream. This is called **nightfall** or a **wet dream**.
- It is **completely normal** and common; it is not an illness and does not weaken you.
- It does not 'waste' anything—sperm are made continuously.
- Some boys have it often, some rarely, some never. All are normal.
- Just wash, change clothes and carry on. There is nothing to be ashamed of.

steps.title: First period (menarche)
steps.body:
A first period usually comes between about 10 and 15 years of age. It may be spotting or light bleeding and often irregular for the first year or two.
- Tell a trusted adult (parent, older sister, teacher, school nurse); keep a pad in your bag.
- Use a pad or other product; change it regularly; wash your hands.
- Bleeding during a period is normal; losing about 30–80 mL over the whole period is typical (it often looks like more).

steps.title: Other normal changes
steps.body:
- Growth spurts, body hair, acne, sweat and body odour.
- Voice deepening in boys; breast development in girls (one side may grow faster for a while).
- New feelings of attraction and strong emotions.
- Masturbation is common and is not harmful to health; it is a private matter and a personal choice.

When in doubt, ask a doctor, a school counsellor or a trusted adult—not anonymous internet sources.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body:
- A family doctor, gynaecologist or adolescent health clinic.
- Under India's adolescent health programme (Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram), many government health facilities run adolescent-friendly clinics.
- Feeling anxious or low: Tele-MANAS 14416.
- If someone touches you in a way that is not okay, or you are unsafe: Childline 1098 or 112.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body:
- No signs of puberty by about 14 (girls) or 15 (boys), or no period by 15.
- Very painful or very heavy periods, or bleeding between periods.
- Pain, swelling or a lump in the testes (testicular pain that is sudden and severe is an emergency).
- Pain or burning when passing urine, or unusual discharge.

activity.prompt: Questions teens often wonder about but don't ask

items.q: Is nightfall a sign of weakness or disease?
items.a: No. It is a normal part of puberty. It does not cause weakness, hair loss, poor eyesight or any illness. Those are myths.

items.q: I got my period but it stopped for two months. Am I sick?
items.a: Irregular periods are very common in the first year or two. If it continues for several months, or you have other worries, see a doctor.

items.q: Can I swim, play sport or visit a friend during my period?
items.a: Yes. With a suitable product you can do all your normal activities.

items.q: My friends say a 'real man' must have a certain size. Is that true?
items.a: No. Bodies vary widely, and size has nothing to do with health, masculinity or worth. Online pictures are often misleading.

items.q: Is it normal to have crushes or new feelings?
items.a: Yes. Attraction and strong emotions are normal in puberty. You decide how to act on feelings, and you always have the right to say no—and the duty to respect others' no.

items.q: Who can I talk to if I'm embarrassed to ask my parents?
items.a: A school counsellor, school nurse, doctor, older sibling or another trusted adult. You can also call Tele-MANAS (14416) if you feel anxious or upset.

quiz.q: Nightfall (nocturnal emission) in teenage boys is
quiz.why: Nocturnal emission is a normal and common part of puberty in boys. It is not a disease or a sign of weakness.

quiz.q: The first menstrual period is called
quiz.why: The first menstrual period is called menarche, which usually occurs between about 10 and 15 years.

quiz.q: Irregular periods in the first year after menarche are
quiz.why: Irregular periods in the first year after menarche are common, since the hormonal cycle takes time to settle. A doctor can be consulted if there is worry.

quiz.q: A sudden, severe pain in a testis should be
options: treated as an emergency—see a doctor immediately
treated with ice for a week
quiz.why: A sudden, severe pain in a testis may be testicular torsion, a medical emergency. See a doctor immediately.

quiz.q: A good source for questions about puberty
quiz.why: A doctor or school counsellor gives accurate, trusted information about puberty. Rumours and anonymous forums can be wrong.

lessons.title: Reproductive health: contraception, STIs, consent and the law

scenes.text: In a hostel in Bengaluru, first-year students Varun and Kiran overhear seniors confidently sharing 'facts' about sex and infections. Half of it sounds wrong.
Kiran remembers her Class 12 biology chapter on reproductive health and a talk by a doctor from the district hospital.
She sorts myth from fact—and remembers that consent and the law matter as much as biology.

steps.title: Contraception (birth control) methods
steps.body:
- **Barrier**: condoms (male and female)—the only common method that also reduces the risk of STIs, including HIV; diaphragms and cervical caps.
- **Hormonal**: oral contraceptive pills (daily), injectables and implants—prevent ovulation and thicken cervical mucus.
- **IUDs** (intrauterine devices) such as copper-T, placed by a health worker; long-acting.
- **Emergency contraception**: pills taken as soon as possible, within 72 hours (some up to 120 hours), after unprotected intercourse—not for regular use.
- **Surgical (permanent)**: vasectomy (men), tubectomy (women).
- 'Natural' methods (calendar, withdrawal) have high failure rates.

Choosing a method is a medical decision best made with a doctor.

steps.title: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)
steps.body:
Examples: gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydia, genital herpes, genital warts (HPV), trichomoniasis, hepatitis B and HIV.
- Many STIs have **no symptoms** at first—testing is the only way to know.
- Possible signs: unusual discharge, sores, itching, pain when passing urine.
- Prevention: abstinence, consistent condom use, mutual monogamy with a tested partner, **vaccines** for HPV and hepatitis B, never sharing needles.
- Most bacterial STIs are curable with prompt treatment; viral ones (HIV, herpes) are treatable and manageable. HIV is **not** spread by hugging, sharing food, toilets or mosquito bites.
- In India, free HIV testing and counselling is offered at government ICTCs (Integrated Counselling and Testing Centres).

steps.title: Consent and the law in India
steps.body:
- **Consent** means a clear, freely given, informed and enthusiastic 'yes' that can be withdrawn at any time. Silence, pressure, threats, intoxication or being asleep are **not** consent.
- Under the **POCSO Act, 2012**, anyone below 18 is a child, and the **age of consent is 18**. Sexual acts with a person under 18 are offences, regardless of 'agreement'.
- Sharing or forwarding sexual images of anyone under 18 is a serious crime, even if they are your own or a friend's.
- If you or a friend faces abuse or pressure: tell a trusted adult, call **1098** (Childline) or **112**.

This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Infertility and help
steps.body: Some couples cannot conceive after trying for a year. Causes can involve either partner. Assisted reproductive technologies include IVF (fertilisation in the lab and embryo transfer), ICSI (a sperm injected into an ovum) and IUI (sperm placed into the uterus). Adoption is another loving path to parenthood.

steps.title: Myths to drop
steps.body:
- 'You can't get pregnant the first time.' False.
- 'You can tell if someone has an STI by looking.' False—many have no symptoms.
- 'Two condoms are safer than one.' False—friction makes them more likely to tear.
- 'Emergency pills are an abortion.' False—they mainly delay or prevent ovulation.
In India, termination of pregnancy is governed by the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act (amended 2021) and must be done by registered medical practitioners.

a.text: In the hostel, a senior says: 'Condoms are useless and only girls get STIs.' Kiran wants to respond. What does she say?

choices.label: Nothing—arguing is awkward
choices.feedback: Staying silent is understandable, but the myth may harm someone.

choices.label: Calmly share the facts: condoms reduce STI and pregnancy risk, and anyone can get an STI
choices.feedback: Accurate and kind—facts protect friends.

b.text: Later, Varun quietly asks Kiran if the senior was right. What now?

choices.label: Explain the facts and suggest asking a doctor
choices.feedback: Good recovery.

c.text: Varun admits he has had pain while passing urine and is too embarrassed to see anyone. What should he do?

choices.label: See a doctor or visit a government clinic or ICTC for confidential testing
choices.feedback: Right—early testing and treatment protect his health and others'.

choices.label: Buy random antibiotics from a shop without a prescription
choices.feedback: Self-medication can hide symptoms and cause antibiotic resistance.

e.text: The pharmacist refuses and suggests a doctor. Varun reconsiders.

choices.label: Book a confidential doctor's appointment
choices.feedback: Wise choice.

d.text: Varun gets tested and treated. Kiran reminds him: if anyone ever feels pressured into anything sexual, that is not consent—talk to someone you trust, or call 112.

quiz.q: Which contraceptive also reduces the risk of STIs?
quiz.why: A condom is a barrier method that reduces the risk of STIs by blocking exchange of body fluids. The other methods do not.

quiz.q: Under the POCSO Act, the age of consent in India is
quiz.why: Under POCSO, a child is anyone below 18, and any sexual act with a person under 18 is an offence. So the age of consent is 18.

quiz.q: Many STIs are
quiz.why: Many STIs often cause no symptoms at first, so testing is needed to know for sure.

quiz.q: Emergency contraception should be taken
options: as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse
quiz.why: Emergency contraception should be taken as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse, since it works best the sooner it is taken. It is not for regular use.

quiz.q: HIV can spread through
quiz.why: HIV spreads through contact with infected blood, such as shared needles, as well as sexual contact and from mother to child. It does not spread by mosquitoes, hugging or sharing food.

questions.q: Fertilisation in humans usually takes place in the
questions.why: Fertilisation in humans usually takes place in the ampulla of the fallopian tube, where the ovum meets the sperm.

questions.q: Nightfall in adolescent boys is
questions.why: Nightfall in adolescent boys is a normal part of puberty and is not harmful.

questions.q: The hormone detected by pregnancy test kits
questions.why: Pregnancy test kits detect hCG, which is made by the developing placenta (trophoblast).

questions.q: Which method is permanent?
questions.why: Vasectomy is a surgical method that is generally considered permanent. Condoms, pills and Copper-T are reversible.

questions.q: Sertoli cells
questions.why: Sertoli cells nourish and support developing sperm in the seminiferous tubules.

questions.q: In a 28-day cycle, ovulation typically occurs around
questions.why: In a 28-day cycle, ovulation typically occurs around day 14, after the mid-cycle LH surge.

questions.q: Which statement about consent is correct?
options: Consent once given can't be withdrawn
Consent must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time
questions.why: Consent must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time. Silence or pressure is not consent.

questions.q: Number of sperm from 10 primary spermatocytes and ova from 10 primary oocytes
questions.why: Each primary spermatocyte gives 4 sperm, so 10 give 40. Each primary oocyte gives 1 ovum, so 10 give 10.

questions.q: If the corpus luteum is maintained, the hormone responsible early in pregnancy is
questions.why: Early in pregnancy, hCG from the trophoblast maintains the corpus luteum, so progesterone keeps being made.

questions.q: Which STI can be prevented by a vaccine?
questions.why: Hepatitis B can be prevented by a vaccine, and a vaccine for HPV also exists. Gonorrhoea, syphilis and chlamydia have no vaccine.

questions.q: The stage at which the human embryo implants
questions.why: The human embryo implants at the blastocyst stage, about a week after fertilisation.

questions.q: A primary oocyte is arrested at which stage until puberty?
questions.why: A primary oocyte starts meiosis in fetal life and is arrested at prophase I (diplotene) until puberty.

questions.q: ICSI differs from conventional IVF in that
options: a single sperm is injected directly into the ovum
questions.why: In ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection), a single sperm is injected directly into the ovum. Conventional IVF mixes many sperm with eggs in a dish.

courses.title: Biotechnology & ecology
courses.summary: Tools of genetic engineering (restriction enzymes, vectors, PCR), real applications in medicine and farming, energy flow in ecosystems, and how to protect biodiversity.
outcomes: Learners can explain the steps of recombinant DNA technology and PCR
Learners can describe applications such as Bt crops, recombinant insulin and gene therapy, and their ethics
Learners can explain energy flow, the 10% law and ecological pyramids
Learners can describe biodiversity, threats to it and conservation strategies

scenes.text: In a biotech start-up lab in Pune, researcher Shreya wants bacteria to make a human protein.
She needs molecular 'scissors', 'glue', a 'delivery vehicle' and a way to copy DNA millions of times.
Her new intern, Daniel from Nairobi, asks her to explain each tool before they start.

steps.title: Restriction enzymes and ligase
steps.body:
- **Restriction endonucleases** cut DNA at specific sequences, usually **palindromes**. EcoRI (from E. coli) recognises 5'-GAATTC-3' and cuts between G and A, leaving **sticky ends**.
- Cutting a gene and a vector with the same enzyme gives matching sticky ends.
- **DNA ligase** joins them, making **recombinant DNA**.

steps.title: Vectors and hosts
steps.body:
- **Plasmids** (small circular DNA in bacteria) such as pBR322 have an **origin of replication (ori)**, **selectable markers** (e.g., antibiotic-resistance genes) and **cloning sites**.
- Insertional inactivation: inserting a gene into a marker gene (e.g., one making a coloured product) lets scientists tell recombinant from non-recombinant colonies (blue–white screening).
- Plants: *Agrobacterium tumefaciens* Ti plasmid (disarmed) delivers genes into plant cells.
- DNA enters bacteria made 'competent' (e.g., calcium treatment and heat shock), or by electroporation, microinjection or a gene gun.

steps.title: PCR: copying DNA
steps.body:
The **polymerase chain reaction** repeats three steps:
1. **Denaturation** (about 94 °C): strands separate.
2. **Annealing** (lower temperature, about 50–60 °C): primers bind.
3. **Extension** (about 72 °C): **Taq polymerase** (heat-stable, from *Thermus aquaticus*) builds new strands.

Each cycle roughly doubles the DNA: after n cycles, up to 2ⁿ copies. 30 cycles ⇒ about a billion copies—enough for forensic analysis from a tiny sample.

steps.title: Gel electrophoresis
steps.body: DNA is negatively charged, so in an agarose gel it moves toward the **positive electrode (anode)**. Smaller fragments move farther. Bands are seen after staining (e.g., ethidium bromide under UV) and can be cut out (elution).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying DNA moves toward the cathode (it moves to the anode).
- Thinking restriction enzymes cut randomly (they cut at specific sites).
- Forgetting why Taq polymerase is used (it survives the 94 °C step).

activity.prompt: Order the steps of making a recombinant bacterium.
items: Isolate the DNA containing the gene of interest
Cut the gene and the plasmid with the same restriction enzyme
Introduce the recombinant plasmid into competent bacteria
Select transformed cells using marker genes
Grow the bacteria and extract the protein product

quiz.q: EcoRI recognises
quiz.why: EcoRI recognises the palindromic sequence GAATTC and cuts between G and A.

quiz.q: DNA ligase
quiz.why: DNA ligase joins DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds, so it is like a molecular glue.

quiz.q: Taq polymerase is used in PCR because it
quiz.why: Taq polymerase is used in PCR because it is heat-stable, as it comes from the heat-loving bacterium Thermus aquaticus.

quiz.q: In gel electrophoresis, DNA moves toward the
quiz.why: DNA is negatively charged, so in gel electrophoresis it moves toward the anode (positive electrode).

quiz.q: After 10 PCR cycles starting from one DNA molecule, the maximum number of copies is about
quiz.why: PCR doubles the DNA each cycle, so after 10 cycles there are 2¹⁰ = 1024 copies.

lessons.title: Biotechnology in medicine and farming

story.title: Cotton, insulin and a careful debate

scenes.text: In Vidarbha, farmer Ramrao grows Bt cotton, which resists bollworm attack. His neighbour worries about seed costs and pest resistance.
His daughter Pallavi, a nursing student, injects her diabetic father with recombinant human insulin made by microbes.
At a village meeting, they debate: biotechnology brings real benefits and real questions.

steps.title: Agriculture
steps.body:
- **Bt cotton**: genes (cry genes) from the soil bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis* make a protein that is activated in the alkaline gut of certain insect larvae (e.g., bollworms) and kills them. It reduces insecticide use, but pests can evolve resistance, so refuge crops and integrated pest management matter.
- **RNA interference (RNAi)**: used to make tobacco plants resistant to a root nematode by silencing a nematode gene.
- **Golden rice**: engineered to produce β-carotene (a vitamin A precursor).
- In India, the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) assesses GM organisms for release.

steps.title: Medicine
steps.body:
- **Recombinant human insulin**: genes for the A and B chains are expressed in E. coli; the chains are combined into insulin—safer and more plentiful than animal insulin.
- **Gene therapy**: correcting a defective gene. An early clinical case (1990) treated ADA deficiency, an immune disorder.
- **Molecular diagnosis**: PCR and ELISA detect pathogens early (e.g., HIV, SARS-CoV-2).
- **Transgenic animals**: used to study disease and to make proteins (e.g., in milk).

steps.title: Ethics and biopiracy
steps.body: Questions include safety testing, effects on ecosystems, farmers' rights and access, and labelling. **Biopiracy** is the use of bio-resources or traditional knowledge without permission or fair benefit-sharing—India has contested patents on products derived from turmeric, neem and basmati rice varieties. Good science goes with transparent regulation.

steps.title: Thinking it through
steps.body: Ramrao's choice: Bt cotton cuts bollworm damage and spray costs; risks include non-target pests (Bt does not kill all pests), resistance, and seed prices. A balanced decision uses evidence from local trials, extension officers' advice and good pest management—not slogans on either side.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Bt toxin is harmful to all organisms (it is activated in the alkaline gut of specific insect groups).
- Saying recombinant insulin comes from pigs (that was older animal insulin).
- Thinking gene therapy is routine for all genetic diseases (it is available for only some conditions).

activity.prompt: Match each application with what it does.
pairs: Makes a protein toxic to bollworm larvae
Silences a nematode gene to protect roots
Supplies a working gene to immune cells
Detects antigens or antibodies for diagnosis

quiz.q: Bt toxin genes come from
quiz.why: Bt toxin genes come from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis.

quiz.q: The Bt protein becomes toxic in the insect gut because
quiz.why: The Bt protein is an inactive protoxin that becomes active in the alkaline pH of the insect gut.

quiz.q: Recombinant human insulin is commonly produced in
quiz.why: Recombinant human insulin is commonly produced in E. coli, which expresses the genes for the A and B chains.

quiz.q: Biopiracy means
options: using bio-resources or traditional knowledge without permission or fair benefit-sharing
quiz.why: Biopiracy is using bio-resources or traditional knowledge without permission or fair benefit-sharing with the people concerned.

quiz.q: In India, GM organisms for release are assessed by
quiz.why: In India, the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) assesses GM organisms before release.

sources: NCERT Biology Class 12 (Biotechnology and its Applications)

scenes.text: Forest guard Biswajit in the Sundarbans explains to visiting students why there are so few tigers compared with deer.
'Each step up the food chain, most energy is lost as heat,' he says. 'A tiger needs a vast forest of plants, insects, fish and deer below it.'
The students sketch an energy pyramid on the boat.

steps.title: Ecosystem components
steps.body:
- **Producers** (green plants, phytoplankton) fix solar energy by photosynthesis.
- **Consumers**: primary (herbivores), secondary and tertiary (carnivores).
- **Decomposers** (bacteria, fungi) recycle nutrients.
- **Productivity**: Gross primary productivity (GPP) − respiration losses (R) = **Net primary productivity (NPP)**, the energy available to consumers.

steps.title: The 10% law
steps.body:
On average, only about **10%** of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next (Lindeman); the rest is used in respiration and lost as heat, or not eaten.

Example: plants fix 10 000 J ⇒ herbivores get about 1000 J ⇒ primary carnivores about 100 J ⇒ top carnivores about 10 J. That is why food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels and why top predators are few.

steps.title: Ecological pyramids
steps.body:
- **Pyramid of energy**: always upright.
- **Pyramid of numbers**: can be inverted (one tree supporting many insects).
- **Pyramid of biomass**: usually upright on land; can be **inverted in the sea** (a small standing biomass of fast-reproducing phytoplankton supports a larger biomass of zooplankton and fish).

Food webs are more realistic than simple chains; detritus food chains (starting from dead matter) carry much of the energy in forests.

steps.title: Succession and nutrient cycles
steps.body: **Ecological succession**: bare rock → lichens → mosses → herbs → shrubs → trees (climax community). Carbon and phosphorus cycle through living things and the environment; burning fossil fuels and deforestation add CO₂ to the air faster than it is removed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a pyramid of energy can be inverted (it can't).
- Thinking energy is recycled like nutrients (energy flows one way; nutrients cycle).
- Forgetting decomposers when describing an ecosystem.

activity.label: Trophic level (with 10 000 J fixed by producers and the 10% law)

bands.text: Level 4 — top carnivores (tigers): about 10 J. Few individuals can be supported.
Level 5 — only about 1 J: why food chains rarely go longer.

quiz.q: The pyramid that is always upright
quiz.why: The pyramid of energy is always upright, because energy decreases at each trophic level.

quiz.q: NPP equals
quiz.why: Net primary productivity = gross primary productivity − respiratory losses (NPP = GPP − R).

quiz.q: If producers fix 20 000 J, energy at the secondary consumer level is about
quiz.why: Energy passes on at about 10% per level. From producers to the secondary consumer is two steps: 20,000 × 0.1 × 0.1 = 200 J.

quiz.q: An inverted pyramid of biomass is typical of
quiz.why: An inverted pyramid of biomass occurs in oceans, since phytoplankton have a small standing biomass because they reproduce and are eaten quickly.

quiz.q: Pioneer species on bare rock are usually
quiz.why: Lichens are the pioneer species on bare rock. They begin soil formation by breaking down the rock.

scenes.text: In the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, Banteilang walks his visiting friend Elena from Spain through a sacred grove no one is allowed to cut.
The grove shelters orchids, rare frogs and birds that have vanished from the surrounding farmland.
Elena asks: why does such a small patch matter so much?

steps.title: Levels and patterns of biodiversity
steps.body:
- **Genetic diversity** (variation within a species—thousands of rice varieties in India), **species diversity** and **ecological (ecosystem) diversity**.
- Diversity generally increases towards the tropics.
- **Species–area relationship**: more area ⇒ more species (log S = log C + Z log A).
- India is one of the world's megadiverse countries, with about 2.4% of the world's land area and a much larger share of its recorded species.

steps.title: Threats: the 'evil quartet'
steps.body:
1. **Habitat loss and fragmentation** (the biggest cause).
2. **Over-exploitation** (overfishing, poaching).
3. **Invasive alien species** (e.g., water hyacinth choking Indian lakes; the Nile perch in Lake Victoria linked to the loss of many native cichlid fish).
4. **Co-extinctions** (a plant and its specific pollinator can disappear together).
Climate change and pollution add further pressure.

steps.title: Conservation strategies
steps.body:
- **In situ** (on site): biodiversity hotspots, national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and **sacred groves**. India has parts of three global hotspots: the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and the Himalaya.
- **Ex situ** (off site): zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, cryopreservation of gametes, tissue culture.
- International efforts include the Convention on Biological Diversity (opened at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro).

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Biodiversity provides ecosystem services—pollination, clean water, flood control, soil formation, climate regulation—plus food, medicines and cultural value. Banteilang's grove protects a local water source and a seed bank of wild species.

steps.title: What you can do
steps.body: Avoid single-use plastics, plant native species, never buy products from wildlife (ivory, turtle shell, wild birds), support community conservation, and report wildlife crime to forest authorities.

activity.prompt: Is each strategy in situ or ex situ conservation?

quiz.q: The greatest cause of biodiversity loss
quiz.why: Habitat loss and fragmentation is the greatest cause of biodiversity loss.

quiz.q: Which is ex situ conservation?
quiz.why: A seed bank conserves species outside their natural habitat, so it is ex situ. Sacred groves, national parks and biosphere reserves are in situ.

quiz.q: Species diversity generally
quiz.why: Species diversity generally increases from the poles toward the tropics, showing a latitudinal gradient.

quiz.q: Water hyacinth in Indian lakes is an example of
quiz.why: Water hyacinth, introduced and spreading aggressively in Indian lakes, is an invasive alien species.

quiz.q: A hotspot found in India
quiz.why: The Western Ghats and Sri Lanka is a biodiversity hotspot found in India. The Amazon basin, Cape region and Madagascar are elsewhere.

questions.q: The enzyme that joins DNA fragments
questions.why: DNA ligase joins DNA fragments. A restriction enzyme cuts DNA and helicase unwinds it.

questions.q: Organisms that make their own food
questions.why: Producers, like green plants, make their own food by photosynthesis.

questions.q: Plasmids are
questions.why: Plasmids are small circular DNA molecules in bacteria, and they are commonly used as cloning vectors.

questions.q: A zoo is an example of
questions.why: A zoo conserves animals outside their natural habitat, so it is ex situ conservation.

questions.q: The temperature for DNA denaturation in PCR is about
questions.why: In PCR, denaturation of DNA happens at about 94 °C, where high heat separates the strands.

questions.q: Pyramid of numbers in a single tree ecosystem is
questions.why: One tree supports many insects, so the pyramid of numbers in a tree ecosystem is inverted (spindle-shaped).

questions.q: Ti plasmid is obtained from
questions.why: The Ti plasmid is obtained from Agrobacterium tumefaciens and is used to transfer genes into plants.

questions.q: If a tertiary consumer receives 5 J, the producers fixed about
questions.why: Energy increases tenfold each step going down: 5 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 5000 J. The tertiary consumer is three steps from the producer.

questions.q: Insertional inactivation helps to
questions.why: In insertional inactivation, the inserted DNA disrupts a marker gene, so recombinant colonies can be told from non-recombinant ones.

questions.q: In the species–area relationship log S = log C + Z log A, Z is the
questions.why: In log S = log C + Z log A, Z is the regression coefficient, the slope of the line on a log–log graph. C is the intercept.

questions.q: A DNA fragment of 500 bp and one of 2000 bp are run on a gel. The 500 bp fragment
questions.why: Smaller fragments move faster through the gel, so the 500 bp fragment moves farther toward the anode than the 2000 bp fragment.

questions.q: Recombinant insulin production required
options: expressing the A and B chain genes and combining the chains
questions.why: Recombinant insulin was made by expressing the genes for the A and B chains separately, then combining the chains with disulfide bonds.

questions.q: Which describes co-extinction?
options: A host-specific parasite dies out when its host goes extinct
A species is introduced to a new island
questions.why: Co-extinction is when a host-specific parasite or partner dies out when its host species goes extinct.

school-senior-chemistry.title: Senior Chemistry (Class 11–12)
school-senior-chemistry.description: Pathshala Senior chemistry: physical, organic and inorganic chemistry explained from first principles, with numericals, mechanisms, lab tests and exam practice.

courses.title: Physical chemistry essentials
courses.summary: Mole concept, thermodynamics, equilibrium and pH, electrochemistry and kinetics — the quantitative heart of Class 11–12 chemistry, with worked numericals throughout.
outcomes: Learners can solve stoichiometry, limiting-reagent and concentration problems
Learners can predict spontaneity with ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
Learners can apply K, Le Chatelier's principle, pH and buffers
Learners can use the Nernst equation, Faraday's laws and first-order kinetics

scenes.text: Ishaan helps at his family's dhaba in Amritsar. The recipe says 2 cups atta to 1 cup water. With 10 cups of atta but only 3 cups of water, he can make only a limited batch.
In the school lab the next day, his teacher Mr Gill says, 'That's a limiting reagent. Chemistry counts particles the same way—in moles.'
Ishaan learns that one mole is just a chemist's 'dozen': 6.022 × 10²³ particles.

steps.title: The mole and molar mass
steps.body:
- **1 mole** = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number N_A).
- **Molar mass** (g/mol) = numerical value of molecular mass in u. H₂O: 2(1) + 16 = 18 g/mol.
- moles n = mass/molar mass = particles/N_A = gas volume/22.4 L (at 0 °C and 1 atm; at 0 °C and 1 bar the molar volume is about 22.7 L).
- Mass % of an element = (mass of element in 1 mol / molar mass) × 100.

steps.title: Limiting reagent
steps.body:
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. React 10 g H₂ with 64 g O₂.
- n(H₂) = 10/2 = 5 mol; n(O₂) = 64/32 = 2 mol.
- 5 mol H₂ would need 2.5 mol O₂—only 2 are available ⇒ **O₂ is limiting**.
- Water formed = 2 × 2 = 4 mol = 72 g. H₂ left = 5 − 4 = 1 mol = 2 g.

Check mass: 10 + 64 = 74 g = 72 + 2 ✔.

steps.title: Empirical and molecular formula
steps.body:
A compound: C 40.0%, H 6.7%, O 53.3%; molar mass 180 g/mol.
- Moles in 100 g: C 40/12 = 3.33; H 6.7/1 = 6.7; O 53.3/16 = 3.33
- Divide by the smallest: C 1, H 2, O 1 ⇒ empirical formula **CH₂O** (mass 30)
- n = 180/30 = 6 ⇒ molecular formula **C₆H₁₂O₆** (glucose).

steps.title: Concentration terms
steps.body:
- **Molarity** M = moles of solute / litres of solution (changes with temperature).
- **Molality** m = moles of solute / kg of solvent (temperature independent).
- **Mole fraction** x = nᵢ / n_total.
- Dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using mass ratios instead of mole ratios with the balanced equation.
- Forgetting to balance the equation first.
- Mixing millilitres and litres in molarity.
- Dividing by total solution mass in molality (it's kg of solvent).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
How many molecules are in 9 g of water?

Answer: 9/18 = 0.5 mol ⇒ 0.5 × 6.022 × 10²³ ≈ 3.01 × 10²³ molecules.

activity.prompt: 4 g of NaOH (molar mass 40 g/mol) is dissolved to make 250 mL of solution. What is the molarity?

quiz.q: Number of moles in 44 g of CO₂
quiz.why: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 44 ÷ 44 = 1 mol for CO₂.

quiz.q: Which concentration term is independent of temperature?
quiz.why: Molality (moles per kg of solvent) uses mass, which does not change with temperature, while molarity, normality and % w/v use volume.

quiz.q: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. 28 g N₂ and 3 g H₂ react. Limiting reagent
quiz.why: 28 g N₂ is 1 mol and needs 3 mol H₂. But 3 g H₂ is only 1.5 mol, so H₂ runs out first and is the limiting reagent.

quiz.q: Empirical formula of a compound with molecular formula C₆H₆
quiz.why: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. C₆H₆ has a 1 : 1 ratio, so CH.

quiz.q: Volume of 2 mol of an ideal gas at 0 °C and 1 atm
quiz.why: One mole of an ideal gas at STP occupies 22.4 L, so 2 mol occupy 2 × 22.4 = 44.8 L.

lessons.title: Chemical thermodynamics: enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs energy

story.title: Why ice melts in Mumbai but water freezes in Leh

scenes.text: Tanvi leaves an ice cube on a plate in Mumbai: it melts in minutes. Her cousin Tsering in Leh, on a −10 °C winter morning, sees water freeze in a bucket outdoors.
Melting absorbs heat (endothermic), yet it happens by itself in Mumbai. So 'spontaneous' can't just mean 'releases heat'.
Their chemistry tutor introduces Gibbs energy: a balance of enthalpy and entropy that depends on temperature.

steps.title: Enthalpy and Hess's law
steps.body:
- ΔH < 0: exothermic; ΔH > 0: endothermic. For gas reactions ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT.
- **Hess's law**: ΔH is a state function, so it is the same whatever route you take.

Example: C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ; CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283.0 kJ. Subtract: **C + ½O₂ → CO, ΔH = −110.5 kJ**—a reaction hard to measure directly.

ΔH_reaction = Σ ΔH_f(products) − Σ ΔH_f(reactants), or ≈ Σ bond enthalpies broken − Σ bond enthalpies formed.

steps.title: Entropy and the second law
steps.body:
