Entropy S measures the dispersal of energy and matter (how many ways the system can be arranged). Solid < liquid < gas. Reactions producing more gas molecules usually have ΔS > 0.

For a reversible process ΔS = q_rev/T. For a spontaneous process, ΔS_total (system + surroundings) > 0.

steps.title: Gibbs energy decides
steps.body:
**ΔG = ΔH − TΔS** (constant T, P). ΔG < 0 spontaneous; ΔG = 0 equilibrium; ΔG > 0 non-spontaneous.
- ΔH −, ΔS +: spontaneous at all T
- ΔH +, ΔS −: never spontaneous
- ΔH −, ΔS −: spontaneous at low T (freezing in Leh)
- ΔH +, ΔS +: spontaneous at high T (melting in Mumbai)

Link to equilibrium: **ΔG° = −RT ln K = −2.303RT log K**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
A reaction has ΔH = +40 kJ/mol and ΔS = +100 J/(mol·K). Above what temperature is it spontaneous?

ΔG = 0 at T = ΔH/ΔS = 40 000/100 = **400 K**. Above 400 K, TΔS > ΔH ⇒ ΔG < 0.

Units trap: ΔH in kJ, ΔS in J—convert before dividing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking spontaneous means fast. Diamond → graphite is spontaneous but immeasurably slow; kinetics decides speed.
- Forgetting to multiply ΔH_f by stoichiometric coefficients.
- ΔH_f of elements in their standard state is zero (O₂ gas, graphite), but not of O₃ or diamond.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
For a reaction ΔG° = −5.7 kJ/mol at 298 K. Estimate K (2.303RT ≈ 5.7 kJ/mol at 298 K).

Answer: log K = 5.7/5.7 = 1 ⇒ K = 10.

activity.label: Temperature for a reaction with ΔH = +40 kJ/mol, ΔS = +100 J/(mol·K)

bands.text: ΔG > 0: TΔS is smaller than ΔH, so the reaction is non-spontaneous.
Near 400 K, ΔG ≈ 0: reactants and products are near equilibrium (K ≈ 1).
ΔG < 0: the entropy term wins and the reaction is spontaneous (like ice melting above 0 °C).

quiz.q: For a spontaneous process at constant T and P
quiz.why: A process is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure if the Gibbs energy decreases, so ΔG < 0.

quiz.q: Standard enthalpy of formation is zero for
quiz.why: The standard enthalpy of formation is zero for an element in its standard (most stable) state. O₂(g) is that for oxygen, while O₃, diamond and water are not.

quiz.q: ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0. The reaction is spontaneous
quiz.why: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0, the −TΔS term is positive, and it grows with T. So ΔG is negative only at low T, where ΔH dominates.

quiz.q: If ΔG° = 0, the equilibrium constant K is
quiz.why: ΔG° = −RT ln K. If ΔG° = 0, then ln K = 0, so K = 1.

quiz.q: Which has the highest entropy?
quiz.why: Entropy is highest for steam, since gas particles are the most dispersed and disordered. Ice has the lowest.

story.title: The fertiliser plant and the antacid

scenes.text: Gurpreet, a chemical engineer at a fertiliser plant in Punjab, explains to visiting students how ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen.
One student, Ayesha, has acidity after spicy food. An antacid helps. 'Both are equilibrium problems,' says Gurpreet.
Push a system and it pushes back—Le Chatelier's principle. And pH is just a log scale of H⁺.

steps.title: Equilibrium constants
steps.body:
For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: **K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b)**, with pure solids and liquids omitted.
- **K_p = K_c(RT)^Δn**, Δn = moles of gaseous products − gaseous reactants.
- Reaction quotient Q: if Q < K, the reaction goes forward; Q > K backward; Q = K at equilibrium.
- Reverse reaction: K' = 1/K; multiply the equation by n: K' = Kⁿ.

steps.title: Le Chatelier's principle
steps.body:
A system at equilibrium shifts to counteract a change.

Haber process N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH ≈ −92 kJ:
- Add N₂ or remove NH₃ ⇒ shifts right.
- Increase pressure ⇒ shifts to fewer gas moles (right).
- Increase temperature ⇒ shifts in the endothermic direction (left), and K decreases.
- Catalyst (iron) ⇒ no shift; equilibrium is reached faster.

Industry compromises: high pressure and a moderate temperature with a catalyst for a good rate and acceptable yield.

steps.title: Acids, bases and pH
steps.body:
- pH = −log[H⁺]; at 25 °C, K_w = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴, so pH + pOH = 14.
- Strong acid 0.01 M HCl: pH = 2.
- Weak acid (K_a, concentration c, small ionisation): [H⁺] ≈ √(K_a c).
- **Buffer** (weak acid + its salt): **pH = pK_a + log([A⁻]/[HA])** (Henderson–Hasselbalch). Blood stays near pH 7.4 because of buffers.
- Solubility product: for AgCl, K_sp = s². A common ion lowers solubility.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) 0.1 M acetic acid, K_a = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵: [H⁺] = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 1.34 × 10⁻³ M ⇒ pH ≈ 2.87.

2) Buffer of 0.1 M acetic acid + 0.1 M sodium acetate: pH = pK_a = 4.74. Doubling the acetate: pH = 4.74 + log 2 ≈ 5.04.

3) Antacid Mg(OH)₂ neutralises excess HCl: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O. (Frequent or persistent acidity needs a doctor's advice.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including solids (CaCO₃) or water (as solvent) in K.
- Thinking a catalyst changes K or the equilibrium yield.
- Forgetting that K changes only with temperature.
- pH of 10⁻⁸ M HCl is not 8—water's own H⁺ matters; it's slightly below 7.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
For PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂ (all gases), what is Δn and how is K_p related to K_c?

Answer: Δn = 2 − 1 = 1 ⇒ K_p = K_c(RT).

activity.prompt: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH < 0), where does each change shift the equilibrium?

quiz.q: pH of 0.001 M NaOH at 25 °C
quiz.why: For 0.001 M NaOH, [OH⁻] = 10⁻³, so pOH = 3 and pH = 14 − 3 = 11.

quiz.q: A catalyst
quiz.why: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster. It does not change ΔG°, K or the position of equilibrium.

quiz.q: For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K_p and K_c are related by
quiz.why: K_p = K_c(RT)^Δn. For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, Δn = 2 − 2 = 0, so K_p = K_c.

quiz.q: A buffer with [salt]/[acid] = 10 and pK_a = 4.74 has pH
quiz.why: Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKₐ + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.74 + log 10 = 4.74 + 1 = 5.74.

quiz.q: Solubility of AgCl in 0.1 M NaCl compared with pure water is
quiz.why: Chloride from 0.1 M NaCl is a common ion for AgCl, so by Le Chatelier's principle its solubility is lower than in pure water.

scenes.text: Engineer Neha Rao inspects a steel bridge near the sea in Visakhapatnam. Rust spots appear wherever the paint has chipped.
Her son Aditya asks how his phone battery stores energy. 'Rust and batteries are cousins,' she says, 'both are redox reactions with electrons flowing.'
Standard electrode potentials tell which metal gives up electrons more easily.

steps.title: Galvanic cells
steps.body:
- Oxidation at the **anode** (−), reduction at the **cathode** (+) in a galvanic cell. Electrons flow anode → cathode through the wire; a salt bridge completes the circuit.
- E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode (both as reduction potentials).
- Daniell cell: Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu. E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V ⇒ E°_cell = 1.10 V.
- More negative E° ⇒ stronger reducing agent (gives electrons).

steps.title: Nernst equation and Gibbs energy
steps.body:
At 298 K: **E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q**.
- **ΔG° = −nFE°** (F ≈ 96 500 C/mol); a positive E° means spontaneous.
- At equilibrium E = 0 ⇒ log K = nE°/0.0591.

Example: Daniell cell with [Zn²⁺] = 0.1 M, [Cu²⁺] = 1 M: Q = 0.1 ⇒ E = 1.10 − (0.0591/2)(−1) ≈ 1.13 V. ΔG° = −2 × 96 500 × 1.10 ≈ −212 kJ/mol.

steps.title: Electrolysis and Faraday's laws
steps.body:
Mass deposited m = (M/nF) × Q, with Q = It.

Example: 2 A for 965 s through CuSO₄: Q = 1930 C = 0.02 mol e⁻ ⇒ 0.01 mol Cu = 0.635 g.

Conductance: molar conductivity Λ_m = κ × 1000/M (κ in S/cm, M in mol/L). For strong electrolytes Λ_m rises slightly on dilution; for weak electrolytes it rises sharply (more ionisation). Kohlrausch's law gives Λ°_m of weak electrolytes from ionic contributions.

steps.title: Corrosion and protection
steps.body: Rusting is electrochemical: iron is oxidised (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) at one spot and O₂ is reduced at another, with moisture as the electrolyte; dissolved salt speeds it up (sea air!). Protection: paint or other barriers, **galvanising** (a zinc coating corrodes first—sacrificial protection), and cathodic protection with Mg or Zn blocks on pipelines and ships.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying E° by stoichiometric coefficients—E° is intensive; never multiply it.
- Mixing up electrode signs between galvanic and electrolytic cells: in electrolysis the anode is + (but still the site of oxidation).
- Forgetting n (electrons transferred) in Nernst and Faraday calculations.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Can copper displace zinc from ZnSO₄ solution?

Answer: No. For Cu + Zn²⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Zn, E° = −0.76 − 0.34 = −1.10 V (non-spontaneous).

activity.prompt: Fill in the key facts.
activity.text: Oxidation always happens at the ___. The Faraday constant is about ___ C/mol. Galvanised iron is coated with ___.

quiz.q: E°_cell for Zn | Zn²⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag, given E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V
quiz.why: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. Silver is reduced at the cathode and zinc is oxidised at the anode.

quiz.q: A cell reaction is spontaneous when
quiz.why: ΔG° = −nFE°. A cell reaction is spontaneous when E° is positive, which makes ΔG° negative.

quiz.q: Charge needed to deposit 1 mol of Al from Al³⁺
quiz.why: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al needs 3 electrons per atom, so 1 mol needs 3 faradays (3 F).

quiz.q: Molar conductivity of acetic acid on dilution
quiz.why: On dilution, a weak electrolyte like acetic acid ionises more, so the number of ions per mole rises sharply and molar conductivity increases sharply.

quiz.q: Zinc protects iron even when the coating is scratched because
options: zinc has a more negative E° and corrodes preferentially
quiz.why: Zinc has a more negative E° than iron, so it corrodes in preference to iron even where the coating is scratched. This is sacrificial protection.

scenes.text: On a hot July day in Patna, Ravi's milk turns sour by noon; in winter the same milk lasts much longer.
His pharmacist aunt explains that medicines have expiry dates partly because the drug slowly decomposes at a predictable rate.
Kinetics tells how fast reactions go, and how temperature and concentration change that speed.

steps.title: Rate and rate law
steps.body:
Rate = −d[R]/dt = +d[P]/dt (divided by coefficients). **Rate law**: rate = k[A]^x[B]^y, where x + y = **order** — found by experiment, not from the balanced equation.
- Molecularity: the number of species colliding in an elementary step (1, 2, rarely 3).
- Units of k: zero order mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; first order s⁻¹; second order L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

steps.title: Integrated rate laws
steps.body:
- **Zero order**: [A] = [A]₀ − kt; t½ = [A]₀/2k.
- **First order**: k = (2.303/t) log([A]₀/[A]); **t½ = 0.693/k**, independent of starting concentration. Radioactive decay is first order.
- Time for 99.9% completion of a first-order reaction ≈ 10 half-lives.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
A first-order reaction has k = 0.0693 min⁻¹. t½ = 0.693/0.0693 = 10 min. Starting with 0.8 M: after 30 min (3 half-lives), [A] = 0.1 M.

Time to fall from 0.8 M to 0.08 M: t = (2.303/0.0693) × log 10 ≈ 33.2 min.

steps.title: Temperature and catalysts
steps.body:
**Arrhenius equation**: k = A e^(−E_a/RT); log(k₂/k₁) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂). A rough rule: for many reactions near room temperature, a 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate.

A catalyst provides a lower-E_a pathway, speeding up both forward and reverse reactions; it does not change ΔG or K. Enzymes are biological catalysts—refrigeration slows spoilage because at lower T fewer molecules have energy ≥ E_a and microbial enzymes work more slowly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the order off the balanced equation.
- Using t½ = 0.693/k for zero-order reactions.
- Mixing natural log and log₁₀ (the 2.303 factor).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Doubling [A] quadruples the rate. What is the order with respect to A?

Answer: 2ˣ = 4 ⇒ x = 2 (second order).

statements.s: The order of a reaction can always be found from its balanced equation.
statements.why: Order is experimental; only for elementary steps does it match coefficients.

statements.s: The half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on initial concentration.
A catalyst changes the equilibrium constant.
statements.why: It speeds both directions equally; K is unchanged.

statements.s: The unit of a first-order rate constant is s⁻¹.
statements.why: Rate (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹) divided by concentration (mol L⁻¹).

statements.s: Order can be fractional or zero.
statements.why: Order is experimental and can be 0, ½, 3/2 and so on.

quiz.q: For a first-order reaction t½ = 20 min. Fraction left after 60 min
quiz.why: 60 min is 3 half-lives (60 ÷ 20). The fraction left is (1/2)³ = 1/8.

quiz.q: Unit of k for a zero-order reaction
quiz.why: For a zero-order reaction, rate = k, so k has the units of rate: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

quiz.q: Rate = k[A][B]². Overall order
quiz.why: The overall order is the sum of the powers: 1 + 2 = 3.

quiz.q: Activation energy is lowered by
quiz.why: A catalyst provides an alternative path with a lower activation energy. Raising temperature increases the fraction of molecules with enough energy but does not lower Eₐ.

quiz.q: k = 2.303 × 10⁻² s⁻¹ (first order). Time for 90% completion

questions.q: Avogadro's number is
questions.why: Avogadro's number is 6.022 × 10²³, the number of particles in one mole.

questions.q: pH of pure water at 25 °C
questions.why: In pure water at 25 °C, [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ M, so pH = 7.

questions.q: Mass of 0.5 mol of CaCO₃ (M = 100 g/mol)
questions.why: Mass = moles × molar mass = 0.5 × 100 = 50 g.

questions.q: Oxidation occurs at the
questions.why: Oxidation always occurs at the anode, and reduction at the cathode, in both galvanic and electrolytic cells.

questions.q: For an exothermic equilibrium, raising temperature
questions.why: For an exothermic equilibrium, raising the temperature shifts it toward the reactants (endothermic direction), so K decreases.

questions.q: ΔH = −10 kJ/mol, ΔS = −50 J/(mol·K). The reaction is spontaneous below
questions.why: Spontaneous when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0: −10,000 + 50T < 0, so T < 200 K.

questions.q: Volume of 0.2 M H₂SO₄ needed to neutralise 20 mL of 0.4 M NaOH
questions.why: NaOH moles = 0.4 × 20 = 8 mmol. H₂SO₄ is diprotic, so 4 mmol is needed: 4 ÷ 0.2 = 20 mL.

questions.q: A first-order reaction is 75% complete in 60 min. Its half-life
questions.why: 75% complete means 25% is left, which is (1/2)², two half-lives. So 60 min = 2 × t½ and t½ = 30 min.

questions.q: pH of 0.01 M acetic acid (K_a = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵)
questions.why: For a weak acid, [H⁺] = √(Kₐ × C) = √(10⁻⁵ × 10⁻²) = √10⁻⁷ = 10⁻³·⁵. So pH = 3.5.

questions.q: E°_cell = 0.0591 V for a 1-electron reaction at 298 K. K equals
For 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄, K_c = 4 at some T. K_c for N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is
questions.why: The reverse reaction has the reciprocal equilibrium constant: K = 1/4 = 0.25.

questions.q: Rate becomes 4 times when T rises from 300 K to 320 K. E_a is about (R = 8.314 J/mol·K, log 4 = 0.602)
The solubility of Mg(OH)₂ is s mol/L. K_sp equals
questions.why: For Mg(OH)₂ ⇌ Mg²⁺ + 2OH⁻, [Mg²⁺] = s and [OH⁻] = 2s. So K_sp = s × (2s)² = 4s³.

questions.q: A current of 9.65 A flows for 100 s through molten NaCl. Moles of Cl₂ formed at the anode
questions.why: Q = It = 9.65 × 100 = 965 C = 0.01 F. Since 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻, 1 mol Cl₂ needs 2 F, so 0.01 F gives 0.005 mol.

courses.title: Organic chemistry: mechanisms & tests
courses.summary: Electronic effects, intermediates, naming and isomerism, SN1/SN2/E1/E2 and addition mechanisms, and functional-group tests — so organic reactions are reasoned, not memorised.
outcomes: Learners can explain reactivity using inductive, resonance and hyperconjugation effects
Learners can name compounds by IUPAC rules and identify isomers
Learners can predict SN1/SN2/elimination/addition products
Learners can identify functional groups using standard lab tests

lessons.title: General organic chemistry: electrons decide everything

scenes.text: In Kannauj, India's perfume town, Rukhsana's family distils rose attar. Her niece Sana, in Class 11, wonders why some molecules simply smell sweet while others react violently.
A visiting chemist, Dr Ortiz from Madrid, says: 'Organic chemistry is electron bookkeeping. Know where electrons are pushed or pulled, and you can predict reactions.'
He draws curly arrows—each one a moving pair of electrons.

steps.title: Hybridisation and shape
steps.body:
- sp³ (4 σ bonds): tetrahedral, 109.5° — alkanes.
- sp² (3 σ + 1 π): trigonal planar, 120° — alkenes, carbonyls, benzene.
- sp (2 σ + 2 π): linear, 180° — alkynes, nitriles.

More s-character ⇒ more electronegative carbon: sp > sp² > sp³. That's why the H of ethyne is weakly acidic.

steps.title: Electronic effects
steps.body:
- **Inductive (I)**: permanent pull through σ bonds. −I: NO₂, CN, COOH, halogens. +I: alkyl groups. It fades quickly with distance.
- **Resonance (R/M)**: delocalisation of π or lone-pair electrons. +R: −OH, −NH₂, −OR (donate to the ring). −R: −NO₂, −CHO, −COOH.
- **Hyperconjugation**: σ(C–H) electrons next to a carbocation or alkene delocalise; more α-H ⇒ more stabilisation.
- **Electromeric effect**: temporary, only in the presence of a reagent.

steps.title: Reactive intermediates
steps.body:
- **Carbocations** (sp², planar, electron-deficient): stability 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺; benzylic and allylic cations are resonance-stabilised. Rearrangements (hydride/methyl shifts) give more stable cations.
- **Carbanions** (electron-rich): stability CH₃⁻ > 1° > 2° > 3° (alkyl groups destabilise).
- **Free radicals**: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃•.
- Nucleophiles are electron-rich (OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃); electrophiles are electron-poor (H⁺, NO₂⁺, carbocations).

steps.title: Worked example: acidity
steps.body:
Arrange CH₃COOH, ClCH₂COOH, Cl₂CHCOOH and CCl₃COOH by acid strength.

More −I chlorines stabilise the carboxylate anion ⇒ stronger acid: **CCl₃COOH > Cl₂CHCOOH > ClCH₂COOH > CH₃COOH**.

Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because phenoxide is resonance-stabilised; p-nitrophenol is more acidic than phenol (−R of NO₂).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking resonance structures are real molecules flipping back and forth—the real molecule is a single hybrid.
- Moving atoms instead of electrons when drawing resonance structures.
- Confusing carbocation and carbanion stability orders (they are opposite).
- Forgetting halogens are −I but +R on benzene.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Which is more stable: CH₃CH₂⁺ (ethyl cation) or CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺ (allyl cation)?

Answer: the allyl cation—its positive charge is delocalised over two carbons by resonance, while the ethyl cation has only weak hyperconjugation.

activity.prompt: Order these carbocations from MOST stable to LEAST stable.

quiz.q: Hybridisation of carbon in ethyne
quiz.why: Carbon in ethyne (HC≡CH) forms two σ bonds and two π bonds and is sp-hybridised, giving a linear molecule.

quiz.q: Which group shows a +R effect on benzene?
quiz.why: The –OH group shows a +R (resonance donating) effect, because the lone pair on oxygen donates into the benzene ring. –NO₂, –CHO and –CN withdraw electrons.

quiz.q: Most stable free radical
quiz.why: A tertiary free radical is the most stable, because of hyperconjugation and the inductive effect from more alkyl groups, as for carbocations.

quiz.q: Strongest acid
quiz.why: Fluorine has the strongest −I effect, so it stabilises the carboxylate ion most and FCH₂COOH is the strongest acid.

quiz.q: A nucleophile is
quiz.why: A nucleophile is electron-rich and donates an electron pair to an electron-deficient centre.

scenes.text: A lab assistant in Bengaluru, Karan, finds a bottle labelled only 'C₄H₁₀O'. 'That could be four alcohols and three ethers!' says senior chemist Dr Mehra.
She asks Karan to name each possible structure correctly, because a wrong label can be dangerous.
Then she holds up her hands: 'Some molecules are mirror images, like these—and the body can tell them apart.'

steps.title: IUPAC naming steps
steps.body:
1. Find the longest chain containing the principal functional group.
2. Number it to give the principal group the lowest locant; then multiple bonds; then substituents.
3. Name substituents alphabetically (ignore di-, tri- when alphabetising).
4. Suffix by priority: carboxylic acid > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene/alkyne.

Examples: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ = 2-methylbutane; CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ = butan-2-ol; CH₃COCH₃ = propan-2-one; CH₃CH=CHCHO = but-2-enal.

steps.title: Structural isomerism
steps.body:
Same molecular formula, different connectivity:
- **Chain**: butane vs 2-methylpropane (C₄H₁₀ has 2 isomers; C₅H₁₂ has 3).
- **Position**: propan-1-ol vs propan-2-ol.
- **Functional**: ethanol vs methoxymethane (C₂H₆O).
- **Metamerism**: ethoxyethane vs 1-methoxypropane.
- **Tautomerism**: keto ⇌ enol forms.

steps.title: Stereoisomerism
steps.body:
- **Geometrical (cis/trans, E/Z)**: needs restricted rotation (C=C or a ring) and two different groups on each carbon. But-2-ene has cis and trans forms; but-1-ene does not.
- **Optical**: a chiral carbon (4 different groups) gives non-superimposable mirror images (**enantiomers**) that rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions. A racemic mixture (1:1) shows no net rotation.
- Maximum stereoisomers = 2ⁿ for n chiral centres; fewer if a **meso** form exists (tartaric acid: 3 stereoisomers).

steps.title: Worked example: C₄H₁₀O
steps.body:
Alcohols: butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol (chiral—2 enantiomers), 2-methylpropan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Ethers: 1-methoxypropane, 2-methoxypropane, ethoxyethane.

So there are 7 structural isomers; counting the two enantiomers of butan-2-ol separately gives 8 isomers in total.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing the longest chain even when it skips the functional group.
- Alphabetising 'dimethyl' under d.
- Claiming cis/trans for CH₂=CHR (one carbon carries two identical H atoms).
- Assuming every molecule with chiral carbons is optically active (meso compounds are not).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Name: CH₃–CH(Cl)–CH₂–COOH.

Answer: 3-chlorobutanoic acid (the COOH carbon is C-1).

activity.prompt: Match each structure with its IUPAC name.

quiz.q: Number of structural isomers of C₅H₁₂
quiz.why: C₅H₁₂ has three structural isomers: pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.

quiz.q: Which shows geometrical isomerism?
quiz.why: But-2-ene (CH₃CH=CHCH₃) shows geometrical isomerism, since each carbon of the double bond has two different groups. In ethene, propene and but-1-ene one carbon has two identical groups.

quiz.q: Ethanol and methoxymethane are
quiz.why: Ethanol (alcohol) and methoxymethane (ether) have the same formula C₂H₆O but different functional groups, so they are functional isomers.

quiz.q: A racemic mixture is
options: optically inactive due to external compensation
quiz.why: A racemic mixture has equal amounts of two enantiomers, whose rotations cancel, so it is optically inactive by external compensation.

quiz.q: Highest-priority suffix among these
quiz.why: Among these, the –COOH group has the highest priority, so the compound takes the suffix '-oic acid'.

story.title: Making a medicine step by step

scenes.text: At a pharma unit in Hyderabad, process chemist Anjali must convert an alkyl bromide into an alcohol—but the batch keeps giving an alkene instead.
Her mentor Mr Thomas asks: 'Hot alcoholic KOH or warm aqueous KOH? Primary or tertiary bromide?' Conditions decide the mechanism.
They sketch SN1, SN2, E1 and E2 on the whiteboard.

steps.title: SN2 and SN1
steps.body:
**SN2**: one step; the nucleophile attacks from the back as the leaving group departs. Rate = k[RX][Nu]. **Inversion** of configuration (Walden inversion). Fastest for CH₃X > 1° > 2°; not for 3° (steric hindrance). Favoured by strong nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents (acetone, DMSO).

**SN1**: two steps; slow ionisation to a carbocation, then nucleophile attack. Rate = k[RX]. Mostly **racemisation** (planar cation). Fastest for 3° (and benzylic/allylic). Favoured by polar protic solvents (water, alcohols). Watch for rearrangements.

Leaving-group ability: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻.

steps.title: Elimination (E1, E2)
steps.body:
Strong base, heat, alcoholic KOH ⇒ elimination to alkenes.
- **E2**: one step; needs the H and the leaving group anti-periplanar.
- **E1**: via a carbocation (3° substrates).
- **Saytzeff (Zaitsev) rule**: the more substituted alkene is the major product. 2-bromobutane + alc. KOH → but-2-ene (major) + but-1-ene.

Rule of thumb: aqueous KOH → substitution (alcohol); alcoholic KOH with heat → elimination (alkene).

steps.title: Electrophilic addition and aromatic substitution
steps.body:
- HX adds by **Markovnikov's rule**: H goes to the carbon with more H atoms, via the more stable carbocation. Propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane.
- **Peroxide (Kharasch) effect**: with HBr only, in the presence of peroxide, radical addition gives the anti-Markovnikov product (1-bromopropane).
- Bromine water is decolourised by alkenes: a test for unsaturation.
- Benzene prefers electrophilic **substitution** (keeping aromaticity): nitration (conc. HNO₃ + H₂SO₄ generates NO₂⁺), halogenation (with FeBr₃), Friedel–Crafts reactions.

steps.title: Worked example: predict products
steps.body:
1) CH₃CH₂Br + aqueous KOH → CH₃CH₂OH (SN2).
2) (CH₃)₃CBr + water → (CH₃)₃COH (SN1).
3) (CH₃)₃CBr + alcoholic KOH, heat → (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ (elimination).
4) CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr (peroxide) → CH₃CH₂CH₂Br.

Anjali's problem: she had used alcoholic KOH with heat—switching to aqueous base fixed it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Proposing SN2 at a tertiary carbon.
- Applying the peroxide effect to HCl or HI (it works only for HBr).
- Forgetting carbocation rearrangement in SN1/E1 and HX additions.
- Drawing curly arrows from nuclei or from H⁺—arrows start at electron pairs.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
3-methylbut-1-ene + HCl gives mainly 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, not 2-chloro-3-methylbutane. Why?

Answer: the initial 2° carbocation undergoes a hydride shift to the more stable 3° carbocation.

activity.prompt: Does each feature belong to SN1 or SN2?

items.text: Best for methyl and primary halides

quiz.q: Which reacts fastest by SN2?
quiz.why: SN2 is fastest with the least hindered substrate. CH₃Br is a methyl halide, which the nucleophile attacks easily.

quiz.q: Propene + HBr (no peroxide) gives mainly
quiz.why: Propene adds HBr by Markovnikov's rule, with H going to the carbon with more hydrogens, to give 2-bromopropane via the more stable secondary carbocation.

quiz.q: Major product of 2-bromobutane with alcoholic KOH
quiz.why: Alcoholic KOH causes elimination. By Saytzeff's rule the more substituted alkene, but-2-ene, is the major product.

quiz.q: Electrophile in the nitration of benzene
quiz.why: In nitration, the nitronium ion NO₂⁺ is the electrophile, formed when H₂SO₄ protonates HNO₃.

quiz.q: Best leaving group
quiz.why: I⁻ is the best leaving group, since it is the weakest base and the largest, most polarisable halide ion.

scenes.text: For her Class 12 practical exam in Bhopal, Pooja receives an unlabelled liquid. It could be an aldehyde, a ketone, an alcohol or a carboxylic acid.
She has Tollens' reagent, Fehling's solution, NaHCO₃, iodine with NaOH, and 2,4-DNP.
Organic chemistry turns into a detective story: each test rules out suspects.

steps.title: Alcohols and phenols
steps.body:
- Oxidation: 1° alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; 2° → ketone; 3° resists oxidation. PCC stops a 1° alcohol at the aldehyde.
- **Lucas test** (conc. HCl + ZnCl₂): 3° turbid at once, 2° within about 5 minutes, 1° not at room temperature.
- Phenol: weakly acidic (dissolves in NaOH, not in NaHCO₃); gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl₃; bromine water gives white 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

steps.title: Aldehydes and ketones
steps.body:
- Both give an orange/yellow precipitate with **2,4-DNP** (carbonyl test).
- **Tollens'** silver mirror: aldehydes (not ketones). **Fehling's** red Cu₂O: aliphatic aldehydes (benzaldehyde does not respond).
- **Iodoform test** (I₂/NaOH, yellow CHI₃): CH₃CO– compounds and CH₃CH(OH)– alcohols (ethanol, acetone, acetaldehyde, propan-2-ol).
- **Aldol condensation**: aldehyde/ketone with α-H + dilute NaOH → β-hydroxy carbonyl → (heat) α,β-unsaturated carbonyl.
- **Cannizzaro**: aldehydes without α-H (HCHO, C₆H₅CHO) + conc. NaOH → alcohol + carboxylate salt.

steps.title: Acids and amines
steps.body:
- Carboxylic acids liberate CO₂ with NaHCO₃ (brisk effervescence)—phenols usually do not.
- Amines are basic. In water, for methyl amines: (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃; aniline is much weaker (its lone pair is delocalised into the ring).
- **Carbylamine test** (CHCl₃ + alc. KOH): only 1° amines give a foul-smelling isocyanide.
- **Hinsberg's reagent** (C₆H₅SO₂Cl) distinguishes 1°, 2° and 3° amines.
- Aniline + NaNO₂/HCl at 0–5 °C → benzenediazonium chloride (used for dyes).

steps.title: Worked example: Pooja's deduction
steps.body:
Results: 2,4-DNP positive (carbonyl). Tollens' negative (not an aldehyde). Iodoform positive (methyl ketone). NaHCO₃ negative (not an acid). Molecular formula C₃H₆O.

Conclusion: **propan-2-one (acetone)**. Propanal would have given a silver mirror.

steps.title: Common mistakes and safety
steps.body:
- Saying all aldehydes give Fehling's test (aromatic ones generally don't).
- Forgetting that ethanol gives a positive iodoform test (it is oxidised to CH₃CHO first).
- Lab safety: use a fume hood for chloroform and isocyanides; Tollens' reagent must be freshly prepared and never stored (it can form explosive residues). Always wear goggles.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Which aldehyde gives the Cannizzaro reaction but not aldol: CH₃CHO or C₆H₅CHO?

Answer: C₆H₅CHO (it has no α-hydrogen).

a.text: Pooja's unknown has formula C₃H₆O. Which test first?

choices.label: 2,4-DNP
choices.feedback: Good start: it checks for any carbonyl group.

choices.label: NaHCO₃
choices.feedback: C₃H₆O can't be a carboxylic acid (that needs two O atoms). A wasted test.

x.text: NaHCO₃: no fizz, as expected. Now?

choices.label: 2,4-DNP
choices.feedback: Back on track.

b.text: An orange precipitate forms: a carbonyl. Aldehyde or ketone?

choices.label: Tollens' reagent
choices.feedback: Right—Tollens' separates aldehydes from ketones.

choices.label: Lucas test
choices.feedback: Lucas is for alcohols; it won't help here.

y.text: The Lucas test tells you nothing useful. Try again?

choices.label: Tollens' reagent
choices.feedback: Better choice.

c.text: No silver mirror. It's a ketone. Which ketone has formula C₃H₆O?

choices.label: Propan-2-one
choices.feedback: Correct—and the iodoform test will confirm a CH₃CO– group.

choices.label: Propanal
choices.feedback: Propanal is an aldehyde and would have given a silver mirror.

e.text: Re-check: propanal would give a silver mirror. Your choice?

choices.label: Propan-2-one
choices.feedback: Yes.

d.text: A yellow iodoform precipitate confirms it: acetone. Systematic tests beat guessing.

quiz.q: Which gives a positive iodoform test?
quiz.why: The iodoform test needs CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)– groups. Ethanol is oxidised to acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) and gives it. Methanol and propan-1-ol do not.

quiz.q: A silver mirror with Tollens' reagent indicates
quiz.why: A silver mirror with Tollens' reagent shows an aldehyde, since aldehydes reduce Ag⁺ to silver. Ketones do not.

quiz.q: The Cannizzaro reaction is given by
quiz.why: The Cannizzaro reaction is given by aldehydes with no α-hydrogen. HCHO has none, while the others have α-H.

quiz.q: The carbylamine test is positive for
quiz.why: The carbylamine test is positive only for primary amines, which give foul-smelling isocyanides with CHCl₃ and KOH.

quiz.q: Which liberates CO₂ with NaHCO₃?
quiz.why: Acetic acid is a stronger acid than carbonic acid, so it liberates CO₂ from NaHCO₃. Phenol, ethanol and acetone do not.

questions.q: Hybridisation of carbon in benzene
questions.why: Each carbon in benzene is sp² hybridised, giving a planar ring with 120° angles.

questions.q: Functional group in propanone
questions.why: Propanone (CH₃COCH₃) has a C=O group between two carbons, which is a ketone.

questions.q: Bromine water is decolourised by
questions.why: Ethene has a C=C double bond and decolourises bromine water by addition. Alkanes and benzene (without catalyst) do not.

questions.q: Correct IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂OH
questions.why: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂OH has a 3-carbon main chain with –OH on C-1 and a methyl on C-2. So it is 2-methylpropan-1-ol.

questions.q: Which can show optical isomerism?
questions.why: Butan-2-ol has a chiral carbon (C-2) with four different groups: H, OH, CH₃ and C₂H₅. So it shows optical isomerism.

questions.q: The Lucas test gives immediate turbidity with a
questions.why: In the Lucas test, tertiary alcohols react immediately and give turbidity, as they react by SN1 through a stable tertiary carbocation.

questions.q: Order of basicity in water
questions.why: In water, (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > NH₃ because of alkyl group inductive and solvation effects. Aniline is weaker than NH₃.

questions.q: Acetaldehyde with dilute NaOH gives
questions.why: Acetaldehyde has α-hydrogen, so with dilute NaOH it undergoes the aldol reaction to give 3-hydroxybutanal.

questions.q: SN1 reaction of optically active 2-bromobutane in water mainly gives
questions.why: SN1 goes through a planar carbocation that is attacked from both faces, so the optically active substrate gives a largely racemised product.

questions.q: Most acidic
questions.why: p-Nitrophenol is the most acidic here, because the −R and −I effects of the NO₂ group stabilise the phenoxide ion.

questions.q: 3,3-Dimethylbut-1-ene + HCl. Major product
questions.why: HCl adds to give a secondary carbocation, which undergoes a methyl shift to a more stable tertiary carbocation. Chloride attacks it to give 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane.

questions.q: Number of stereoisomers of tartaric acid, HOOC–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–COOH
questions.why: Tartaric acid has two chiral carbons that are identical, so it has two enantiomers (d and l) and one meso form, which is 3 stereoisomers.

questions.q: Which pair can be distinguished by Fehling's solution?
questions.why: Fehling's solution is reduced by aliphatic aldehydes like ethanal (red Cu₂O precipitate) but not by aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde.

courses.title: Inorganic chemistry: bonding to blocks
courses.summary: Periodic trends with their exceptions, VSEPR and molecular orbital theory, coordination compounds with crystal field theory, and essentials of the s, p, d and f blocks.
outcomes: Learners can explain and order periodic properties including exceptions
Learners can predict shapes, hybridisation, polarity and bond order
Learners can name complexes and predict magnetism and isomerism
Learners can recall key s, p and d-block reactions and redox stoichiometry

lessons.title: Periodic trends that explain the table

story.title: The arrangement that predicted the future

scenes.text: History buff Kabir reads that Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements not yet discovered, such as 'eka-silicon'.
When germanium was found, its properties matched the prediction closely. Kabir wants to understand the patterns behind such predictions.
His teacher, Ms D'Souza in Goa, says: 'Effective nuclear charge and shells explain nearly every trend.'

steps.title: The driver: nuclear charge vs shells
steps.body:
Across a period, protons increase while electrons enter the same shell ⇒ effective nuclear charge rises ⇒ electrons are pulled closer. Down a group, new shells are added ⇒ size increases.

Modern periodic law: properties are periodic functions of **atomic number**.

steps.title: The trends
steps.body:
- **Atomic radius**: decreases across a period, increases down a group. Cations are smaller than their parent atoms; anions are larger. Isoelectronic ions (O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺): more protons ⇒ smaller.
- **Ionisation enthalpy**: generally increases across, decreases down. Exceptions: Be > B and Mg > Al (s vs p electron), N > O (stable half-filled p³).
- **Electron gain enthalpy**: becomes more negative across; Cl is more negative than F (F is small, so electron repulsion is high). Noble gases: positive.
- **Electronegativity**: F highest (about 4.0 on the Pauling scale), increases across, decreases down.
- **Metallic character**: decreases across, increases down.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) Size order of Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, F⁻, O²⁻ (all with 10 electrons): O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺.

2) First ionisation enthalpy: B < Be < C < O < N (note the two exceptions).

3) Oxides: Na₂O basic, Al₂O₃ amphoteric, SO₃ acidic—acidity of oxides rises across a period.

steps.title: Diagonal relationship and inert pair
steps.body:
- Li resembles Mg; Be resembles Al; B resembles Si (similar charge/size ratio).
- Heavier p-block elements (Tl, Pb, Bi) prefer the lower oxidation state (+1, +2, +3) because of the **inert pair effect**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying F has the most negative electron gain enthalpy (it's Cl).
- Forgetting ionisation exceptions in ordering questions.
- Comparing sizes of ions without checking whether they are isoelectronic.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Which has the higher second ionisation enthalpy: Na or Mg?

Answer: Na. Na⁺ already has a stable noble-gas configuration; removing another electron means breaking into an inner shell.

statements.s: Fluorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy.
statements.why: Chlorine does; fluorine's small size causes electron–electron repulsion.

statements.s: Nitrogen has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than oxygen.
statements.why: The half-filled 2p³ configuration is extra stable.

statements.s: Atomic radius increases down a group.
statements.why: New shells are added.

statements.s: Mg²⁺ is larger than Na⁺.
statements.why: They are isoelectronic; Mg²⁺ has more protons, so it is smaller.

statements.s: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric.
statements.why: It reacts with both acids and bases.

quiz.q: Most electronegative element
quiz.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, with a Pauling value of about 4.0.

quiz.q: Largest among these isoelectronic ions
quiz.why: In isoelectronic ions (10 electrons), the one with the fewest protons is largest, as it has the least nuclear pull. O²⁻ has 8 protons, so it is largest.

quiz.q: Which has the higher first ionisation enthalpy?
quiz.why: Be has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than B, because Be's 2s electron is held more tightly than B's 2p electron, which is shielded by the 2s electrons.

quiz.q: A diagonal relationship exists between
quiz.why: A diagonal relationship exists between Li and Mg, as well as Be and Al, and B and Si.

quiz.q: Acidic character of oxides across a period
quiz.why: Across a period, non-metallic character increases, so the oxides go from basic to amphoteric to acidic. The acidic character increases.

lessons.title: Chemical bonding: shapes and molecular orbitals

story.title: Why oxygen sticks to a magnet

scenes.text: Srija in Kolkata watches a science video: liquid oxygen poured between the poles of a strong magnet clings there!
Her Lewis structure for O₂ shows all electrons paired. That would make it non-magnetic. Something is missing.
Molecular orbital theory fixes it—and VSEPR theory explains why water is bent.

steps.title: VSEPR: counting electron pairs
steps.body:
Count bond pairs and lone pairs on the central atom; pairs repel and spread out; lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair repulsion.
- 2 pairs: linear (BeCl₂, CO₂)
- 3: trigonal planar (BF₃)
- 4: tetrahedral CH₄ 109.5°; NH₃ pyramidal ~107°; H₂O bent ~104.5°
- 5: trigonal bipyramidal PCl₅; SF₄ see-saw; ClF₃ T-shaped; XeF₂ linear
- 6: octahedral SF₆; BrF₅ square pyramidal; XeF₄ square planar

steps.title: Hybridisation and polarity
steps.body:
Steric number 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 ⇒ sp, sp², sp³, sp³d, sp³d².

Dipole moment is a vector: CO₂, BF₃ and CCl₄ are non-polar (symmetrical) although their bonds are polar; H₂O and NH₃ are polar. NF₃ has a smaller dipole moment than NH₃ because the lone-pair moment opposes the N–F bond moments.

Hydrogen bonding (H attached to F, O or N) explains water's high boiling point and why ice floats.

steps.title: Molecular orbital theory
steps.body:
Bond order = ½(N_b − N_a). Unpaired electrons ⇒ paramagnetic.
- For O₂ and F₂: σ2s, σ*2s, σ2p_z, (π2p_x = π2p_y), (π*2p_x = π*2p_y), σ*2p_z.
- For N₂ and lighter molecules: π2p lies below σ2p_z (s–p mixing).

Results: N₂ bond order 3 (diamagnetic); O₂ bond order 2 with **two unpaired electrons in π*** orbitals (paramagnetic—Srija's magnet!). O₂⁺ 2.5, O₂⁻ 1.5, O₂²⁻ 1. Higher bond order ⇒ shorter, stronger bond.

steps.title: Worked example: XeF₄
steps.body: Xe has 8 valence electrons; 4 bond to F, leaving 4 = 2 lone pairs. Steric number 6 ⇒ sp³d², octahedral arrangement; the two lone pairs sit opposite each other ⇒ **square planar** shape.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Naming the shape after the electron-pair geometry rather than the atom positions (NH₃ is pyramidal, not tetrahedral).
- Using the N₂ orbital ordering for O₂ (or vice versa).
- Thinking polar bonds always mean a polar molecule.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Bond order and magnetism of N₂⁺?

Answer: 13 electrons; bond order = ½(9 − 4) = 2.5; one unpaired electron ⇒ paramagnetic.

activity.prompt: Match each molecule with its shape.

quiz.q: Bond order of O₂
quiz.why: O₂ has 8 bonding and 4 antibonding electrons (counting from the σ2s onwards): bond order = (10 − 6)/2 = 2.

quiz.q: Which is paramagnetic?
quiz.why: O₂ is paramagnetic, because it has two unpaired electrons in its antibonding π* orbitals. N₂, F₂ and H₂ have all electrons paired.

quiz.q: Hybridisation of S in SF₆
quiz.why: SF₆ has six bond pairs around S in an octahedral arrangement, which needs sp³d² hybridisation.

quiz.q: Which is non-polar?
quiz.why: CCl₄ is a symmetric tetrahedron, so its bond dipoles cancel and it is non-polar. NH₃, H₂O and CHCl₃ are polar.

quiz.q: The bond angle in H₂O is less than in CH₄ because
options: two lone pairs repel the bond pairs more
quiz.why: Water has two lone pairs on oxygen, which repel the bond pairs more strongly than bond pairs repel each other, so the angle (about 104.5°) is smaller than the tetrahedral 109.5° in methane.

story.title: The colours of a chemistry set

scenes.text: In Jaipur, block-print artist Imran asks his chemist friend Neelam why copper sulphate is blue while some nickel compounds are green and some zinc compounds are colourless.
Neelam mentions cisplatin, a platinum complex used in cancer treatment, where one geometric isomer is the drug and the other is not.
Coordination chemistry links colour, magnetism and even medicine.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Central metal** + **ligands** (donor atoms) form the coordination sphere (written in [ ]); counter ions sit outside.
- **Coordination number**: number of donor atoms bonded (e.g., 6 in [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺).
- Ligands: monodentate (NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻, H₂O), bidentate (en, oxalate), hexadentate (EDTA⁴⁻). Ambidentate: NO₂⁻/ONO⁻, SCN⁻/NCS⁻.
- Chelates (ring-forming complexes) are extra stable.

steps.title: Naming (IUPAC)
steps.body:
Ligands alphabetically before the metal; anionic ligands end in -o (chlorido, cyanido); the metal's oxidation state in Roman numerals; anionic complexes end in -ate.
- [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃: hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride
- K₄[Fe(CN)₆]: potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II)
- [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]: diamminedichloridoplatinum(II)

steps.title: Crystal field theory
steps.body:
In an octahedral field, the d orbitals split into t₂g (lower) and e_g (higher), separated by Δₒ. Strong-field ligands (large Δₒ) cause pairing (low spin); weak-field ligands give high spin.

Spectrochemical series (simplified): I⁻ < Br⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO.

Spin-only magnetic moment **μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM** (n = unpaired electrons). Colour arises from d–d transitions absorbing visible light; we see the complementary colour. d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions are usually colourless (e.g., Sc³⁺, Zn²⁺).

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻: Fe²⁺ is d⁶; CN⁻ is strong field ⇒ t₂g⁶ e_g⁰, n = 0, **diamagnetic**.
2) [CoF₆]³⁻: Co³⁺ is d⁶; F⁻ is weak field ⇒ t₂g⁴ e_g², n = 4, μ = √24 ≈ 4.9 BM.
3) [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is square planar and diamagnetic; [NiCl₄]²⁻ is tetrahedral with 2 unpaired electrons.

steps.title: Isomerism
steps.body:
- Geometrical: cis/trans in square planar MA₂B₂ ([Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]: the cis isomer is the anticancer drug cisplatin) and octahedral MA₄B₂; fac/mer in MA₃B₃.
- Optical: e.g., [Co(en)₃]³⁺.
- Structural: ionisation ([Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ vs [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br), linkage (NO₂ vs ONO), hydrate and coordination isomerism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to find the metal's oxidation state first (count ligand charges).
- Counting a bidentate ligand as one donor for coordination number (en counts as 2).
- Assuming all four-coordinate Ni(II) complexes have the same geometry.

items.back: +3 (NH₃ is neutral; one Cl⁻ inside, two outside: x − 1 = +2)

items.front: Unpaired electrons in [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ (Fe³⁺, d⁵, strong field)

items.back: Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰ — no d–d transition is possible

items.front: Which isomer of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] is the anticancer drug?

quiz.q: IUPAC name of K₃[Fe(CN)₆]
quiz.why: In an anionic complex the name ends in '-ate'. With six CN⁻ ligands and Fe in +3 state, it is potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III).

quiz.q: Spin-only moment for 3 unpaired electrons
quiz.why: Spin-only magnetic moment = √(n(n + 2)) BM. For n = 3, that is √15 ≈ 3.87 BM.

quiz.q: Which is a strong-field ligand?
quiz.why: CN⁻ is a strong-field ligand, high in the spectrochemical series. The halides are weak-field ligands.

quiz.q: EDTA⁴⁻ is
quiz.why: EDTA⁴⁻ is hexadentate: it binds through 2 nitrogen atoms and 4 oxygen atoms.

quiz.q: [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ and [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br are
quiz.why: These two compounds have the same formula but give different ions in solution (SO₄²⁻ vs Br⁻), so they are ionisation isomers.

scenes.text: During Dev Deepawali in Varanasi, Aditi watches fireworks: crimson, yellow and green bursts. Her uncle, a chemistry lecturer, names the elements behind each colour.
Back home he shows her purple potassium permanganate and orange potassium dichromate—powerful oxidisers used in labs.
Each block of the periodic table has its own 'personality'.

steps.title: s-block
steps.body:
- Alkali metals: very reactive, +1 state, strong reducing agents; react with water to give hydroxide + H₂. Reactivity increases down the group.
- Flame colours: Li crimson red, Na golden yellow, K lilac/violet; Ca brick red, Sr crimson, Ba apple green.
- Washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O; baking soda NaHCO₃; plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O; quicklime CaO.

steps.title: p-block
steps.body:
- Group 15: N₂ is unreactive because of its strong triple bond; ammonia by the Haber process; HNO₃ by the Ostwald process.
- Group 16: O₃ in the stratosphere absorbs UV; H₂SO₄ is made by the contact process (V₂O₅ catalyst).
- Group 17: oxidising power F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂; HF is a weak acid because of its strong H–F bond (acid strength HI > HBr > HCl > HF).
- Group 18: xenon forms fluorides—XeF₂ linear, XeF₄ square planar, XeF₆ distorted octahedral.

steps.title: d- and f-block
steps.body:
- Transition metals: variable oxidation states, coloured ions, catalysis (Fe in the Haber process, Ni in hydrogenation, V₂O₅), complex formation, paramagnetism.
- **KMnO₄** in acidic medium: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (purple → almost colourless; it acts as its own indicator in titrations).
- **K₂Cr₂O₇**: Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) ⇌ CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) depending on pH; acidified dichromate is reduced to green Cr³⁺.
- **Lanthanoid contraction**: a steady decrease in size across the lanthanoids ⇒ Zr and Hf have almost identical radii.

steps.title: Worked example: titration equivalence
steps.body:
How many moles of Fe²⁺ are oxidised by 1 mol MnO₄⁻ in acid?

MnO₄⁻ gains 5 e⁻; each Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ loses 1 e⁻ ⇒ **5 mol Fe²⁺**. Similarly, 1 mol Cr₂O₇²⁻ (gains 6 e⁻) oxidises 6 mol Fe²⁺.

steps.title: Common mistakes and safety
steps.body:
- Writing HF as a strong acid.
- Forgetting that KMnO₄ gives MnO₂ (3 e⁻) in neutral or weakly basic medium, not Mn²⁺.
- Safety: fireworks contain oxidisers and metal salts—handle only under adult supervision; dichromates are toxic and carcinogenic—use gloves and proper disposal.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Why is Zn often not regarded as a typical transition element?

Answer: Zn and Zn²⁺ both have completely filled d¹⁰ orbitals, so zinc lacks partially filled d orbitals in its common state.

cards.front: Electrons gained by MnO₄⁻ in acid
Strongest hydrogen halide acid in water

cards.back: Zr and Hf have nearly identical sizes and properties

quiz.q: Catalyst in the contact process
quiz.why: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) is the catalyst in the contact process for making sulphuric acid.

quiz.q: Weakest acid
quiz.why: HF is the weakest of the hydrogen halides in water, because of the very strong H–F bond. HI is the strongest.

quiz.q: Colour change of acidified KMnO₄ in a titration with Fe²⁺
quiz.why: Purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺ by Fe²⁺ in acid, so the colour goes from purple to colourless.

quiz.q: Plaster of Paris is
quiz.why: Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO₄·½H₂O. Gypsum is CaSO₄·2H₂O.

quiz.q: Shape of XeF₄
quiz.why: XeF₄ has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs on Xe, and the two lone pairs sit opposite each other in an octahedral arrangement, so the shape is square planar.

questions.q: Element with the highest electronegativity
questions.why: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of all elements.

questions.q: Flame colour of potassium
questions.why: Potassium gives a lilac (pale violet) flame. Sodium is golden yellow and strontium is crimson.

questions.q: Shape of CO₂
questions.why: CO₂ has two bonding domains and no lone pairs on carbon, so its shape is linear.

questions.q: Coordination number of Fe in [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻
questions.why: Oxalate is a bidentate ligand, so three oxalates give a coordination number of 3 × 2 = 6.

questions.q: Bond order of O₂⁻ (superoxide)
questions.why: O₂⁻ has 17 electrons: 10 in bonding MOs and 7 in antibonding MOs (π* holds 3). Bond order = (10 − 7)/2 = 1.5.

questions.q: Which has the largest first ionisation enthalpy?
questions.why: First ionisation enthalpy generally rises across a period, with Al lower than Mg. Si has the highest among Na, Mg, Al and Si.

questions.q: Oxidation state of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇
questions.why: In K₂Cr₂O₇: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0, so 2x = 12 and x = +6.

questions.q: [Ni(CO)₄] is
questions.why: Ni(CO)₄ has Ni in the 0 state with sp³ hybridisation, so it is tetrahedral. All electrons are paired, so it is diamagnetic.

questions.q: Spin-only moment of [MnCl₆]⁴⁻ (Mn²⁺, weak field)
questions.why: Mn²⁺ is d⁵, and with weak-field Cl⁻ it is high spin with 5 unpaired electrons. μ = √(5 × 7) = √35 ≈ 5.92 BM.

questions.q: Moles of Fe²⁺ oxidised by 0.1 mol Cr₂O₇²⁻ in acid
questions.why: Cr₂O₇²⁻ takes 6 electrons, so each mole oxidises 6 mol of Fe²⁺. So 0.1 mol oxidises 0.6 mol.

questions.q: Which has zero dipole moment?
questions.why: BF₃ is planar and symmetric, so its bond dipoles cancel and its dipole moment is zero. NH₃, H₂O and NF₃ are polar.

questions.q: Number of geometrical isomers of [Co(NH₃)₃Cl₃]
questions.why: [Co(NH₃)₃Cl₃] has two geometrical isomers: fac (facial), where like ligands are on one face, and mer (meridional).

questions.q: Which has the shortest O–O bond?
questions.why: The O–O bond is shortest in O₂⁺, which has the highest bond order, 2.5. Higher bond order means a shorter bond.

questions.q: Correct order of atomic size
questions.why: Because of the lanthanoid contraction, Zr and Hf have almost the same size, and both are larger than Ti (a smaller 3d element).

school-senior-commerce.title: Senior Commerce (Class 11–12)
school-senior-commerce.description: Pathshala Senior commerce: accountancy from the accounting equation to final accounts, business studies from management principles to consumer rights, and micro and macro economics with worked numericals.

courses.title: Accountancy foundations
courses.summary: The accounting equation, double-entry rules, journal and ledger, trial balance, final accounts and depreciation — learned through a small business you follow from day one.
outcomes: Learners can apply the accounting equation to any transaction
Learners can record transactions with debit and credit rules
Learners can post a ledger and prepare a trial balance
Learners can prepare a trading and profit and loss account and a balance sheet
Learners can compute depreciation by straight-line and written-down-value methods

scenes.text: Neha, 19, in Nagpur, starts a home tiffin service with ₹1,00,000 of her savings.
Within a week she has bought groceries on credit, sold meals for cash and paid kitchen rent. Her notebook is a mess of numbers.
Her cousin, a CA student, shows her one line that never fails: Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

steps.title: Key terms
steps.body:
- **Assets**: resources the business owns or controls (cash, stock, equipment, debtors).
- **Liabilities**: amounts it owes outsiders (creditors, loans).
- **Capital**: the owner's claim (what the owner put in, plus profits, minus losses and drawings).
- **Revenue** (income) increases capital; **expenses** decrease it.
- **Business entity concept**: the business is separate from its owner—Neha's personal phone bill is not a business expense.

steps.title: The equation always balances
steps.body:
**Assets = Liabilities + Capital** (A = L + C).

Every transaction has two effects (dual aspect), so the equation stays balanced. Profit increases capital; expenses and drawings reduce it.

steps.title: Neha's first week
steps.body:
1) Starts with cash ₹1,00,000: Cash 1,00,000 = Capital 1,00,000.
2) Buys groceries (stock) ₹40,000 on credit from Ravi: Stock +40,000; Creditor +40,000.
3) Sells meals costing ₹20,000 for ₹30,000 cash: Cash +30,000; Stock −20,000; Capital +10,000 (profit).
4) Pays rent ₹5,000: Cash −5,000; Capital −5,000.

End: Cash 1,25,000 + Stock 20,000 = **₹1,45,000 assets** = Creditor 40,000 + Capital 1,05,000 ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating capital as an asset of the business (it is a liability to the owner from the business's view).
- Recording only one side of a transaction.
- Mixing personal and business transactions.
- Forgetting that drawings reduce capital.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Neha withdraws ₹3,000 cash for personal use. What changes?

Answer: Cash −3,000 (asset falls) and Capital −3,000 (drawings). The equation still balances.

activity.prompt: A business has assets of ₹2,50,000 and liabilities of ₹90,000. What is the owner's capital (₹)?

quiz.q: The accounting equation is
quiz.why: The accounting equation is Assets = Liabilities + Capital, since assets are funded by outsiders (liabilities) and the owner (capital).

quiz.q: Buying furniture for cash
quiz.why: Buying furniture for cash increases one asset (furniture) and decreases another (cash) by the same amount, so total assets stay the same.

quiz.q: Goods bought on credit increase
quiz.why: Goods bought on credit increase stock (an asset) and creditors (a liability), so both assets and liabilities rise.

quiz.q: Drawings
options: are an expense of the business
quiz.why: Drawings are what the owner takes out for personal use, so they decrease capital. They are not a business expense.

quiz.q: The business entity concept means
options: the business is treated as separate from the owner
the owner and the business are the same
quiz.why: The business entity concept treats the business as separate from its owner, so the owner's personal transactions are not mixed with the business.

lessons.title: Double entry: journal, ledger and trial balance

scenes.text: Imran runs a stationery shop in Lucknow. At month-end his total debits and credits differ by ₹900.
His accountant, Mrs Fernandes, traces the error to a sale posted to the wrong side of a customer's account.
'Get the debit–credit rules right,' she says, 'and the trial balance will tell you when something is off.'

steps.title: Debit and credit rules
steps.body:
**Modern (accounting-equation) approach**:
- Increase in **assets** or **expenses/losses** ⇒ **debit**.
- Increase in **liabilities**, **capital** or **revenues/gains** ⇒ **credit**.
- Decreases are the opposite.

**Traditional golden rules**:
- Personal accounts: debit the receiver, credit the giver.
- Real accounts: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.
- Nominal accounts: debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains.

steps.title: Journal entries
steps.body:
1) Started business with cash ₹50,000: Cash A/c Dr 50,000 To Capital A/c 50,000.
2) Bought goods on credit from Sohan ₹12,000: Purchases A/c Dr 12,000 To Sohan A/c 12,000.
3) Sold goods to Anita on credit ₹8,000: Anita A/c Dr 8,000 To Sales A/c 8,000.
4) Paid salary ₹5,000: Salary A/c Dr 5,000 To Cash A/c 5,000.
5) Received ₹8,000 from Anita: Cash A/c Dr 8,000 To Anita A/c 8,000.

steps.title: Ledger and trial balance
steps.body:
- The **journal** records transactions in date order; the **ledger** groups them by account. Each journal entry is posted to two ledger accounts.
- Balance each account: debit balance or credit balance.
- A **trial balance** lists all balances; total debits should equal total credits.

A balanced trial balance does **not** prove the books are error-free. Errors it cannot detect: complete omission, errors of principle (e.g., a machine purchase debited to Purchases), compensating errors, and posting the right amount to the wrong account on the correct side.

steps.title: Imran's ₹900 difference
steps.body: A credit sale of ₹450 to a customer was posted to the **credit** side of the customer's account instead of the debit side. The debit side is short by 450 and the credit side has an extra 450, so the totals differ by 2 × 450 = **₹900**. Halving the difference is a classic clue for a wrong-side posting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Debiting Sales for goods sold (Sales is credited).
- Recording goods bought for resale as an asset purchase (use Purchases).
- Forgetting that Capital is credited when the owner brings in money.

activity.prompt: For each transaction, which account is DEBITED?

items.text: Owner brings in cash as capital
Goods bought for resale on credit
Goods sold on credit to Anita

quiz.q: Salary paid in cash. The journal entry is
quiz.why: Salary is an expense, so it is debited. Cash goes out, so cash is credited: Salary A/c Dr, Cash A/c Cr.

quiz.q: Goods sold for cash: which account is credited?
quiz.why: Sales is revenue, and revenue increases are credited. So the Sales account is credited, and Cash is debited.

quiz.q: A trial balance mainly checks
options: that there are no errors at all
the arithmetical accuracy of ledger postings
quiz.why: A trial balance checks the arithmetical accuracy of ledger postings (total debits = total credits). It does not prove there are no errors.

quiz.q: Which error is NOT revealed by a trial balance?
quiz.why: If a transaction is completely omitted, both its debit and credit are missing, so the totals still agree and the error is not revealed.

quiz.q: Under the real-account rule, when furniture comes in
quiz.why: By the rule for real accounts, debit what comes in. So when furniture comes in, debit Furniture.

lessons.title: Final accounts: trading, profit and loss, balance sheet

scenes.text: Kavita runs a clothing boutique in Jaipur. Her sales were ₹90,000 this year, but her cash balance hardly grew.
'Did I make a profit or not?' she asks her nephew, a Class 12 commerce student.
He prepares her final accounts step by step.

steps.title: Trading account: gross profit
steps.body:
**Cost of goods sold (COGS)** = Opening stock + Purchases (net of returns) + Direct expenses (carriage inwards, wages, freight) − Closing stock.

**Gross profit** = Net sales − COGS.

steps.title: Profit and loss account: net profit
steps.body:
**Net profit** = Gross profit + Other incomes (interest received, commission) − Indirect expenses (salaries, rent, advertising, depreciation, office expenses, carriage outwards).

The **matching concept**: expenses are matched with the revenues of the same period (outstanding expenses are added; prepaid expenses are deducted).

steps.title: Kavita's accounts
steps.body:
Opening stock 10,000; purchases 60,000; carriage inwards 2,000; closing stock 12,000; sales 90,000.
- COGS = 10,000 + 60,000 + 2,000 − 12,000 = 60,000
- Gross profit = 90,000 − 60,000 = **₹30,000**

Indirect expenses: salaries 8,000, rent 4,000, advertising 2,000.
- Net profit = 30,000 − 14,000 = **₹16,000**

Her cash didn't grow much because she bought extra stock and some customers still owe her—profit is not the same as cash.

steps.title: Balance sheet
steps.body:
A statement of financial position on a date.
- **Assets**: non-current (land, machinery) and current (stock, debtors, cash, prepaid expenses).
- **Liabilities**: long-term loans and current liabilities (creditors, outstanding expenses).
- **Capital**: opening capital + net profit − drawings.

Total assets = total liabilities + capital.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting carriage outwards in the trading account (it is an indirect selling expense in P&L).
- Forgetting closing stock adjustments.
- Confusing profit with cash in hand.
- Treating capital expenditure (a new machine) as an expense.

activity.prompt: Complete the formulas.
activity.text: Gross profit = Net sales − ___. Net profit = Gross profit − indirect ___ + other incomes. Closing capital = Opening capital + net profit − ___.

quiz.q: Carriage inwards is shown in the
quiz.why: Carriage inwards (the cost of bringing goods to the business) is a direct expense, shown in the trading account.

quiz.q: Opening stock 5,000; purchases 40,000; closing stock 8,000. COGS =
quiz.why: Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases − closing stock = 5,000 + 40,000 − 8,000 = 37,000.

quiz.q: Which is a current asset?
quiz.why: Debtors are a current asset, since they are expected to be converted into cash within a year. Land and machinery are fixed assets.

quiz.q: Outstanding salary is
quiz.why: Outstanding salary is due but not yet paid, so it is a current liability.

quiz.q: The matching concept means
options: expenses are matched with revenues of the same period
quiz.why: The matching concept says expenses of a period should be matched with the revenues of the same period, to show a fair profit.

scenes.text: Ramesh buys a delivery van for his dairy in Anand for ₹6,00,000. He expects to use it for 5 years and then sell it for about ₹1,00,000.
'The van is wearing out every year,' his accountant says. 'That cost must be spread over the years it helps you earn.'
Two common methods give different yearly figures.

steps.title: What depreciation is
steps.body:
A systematic allocation of the cost of a fixed asset over its useful life, due to wear and tear, passage of time or obsolescence. It is a **non-cash expense** charged to the P&L account, and it reduces the asset's book value.

Cost includes the purchase price plus installation, freight and other costs to make the asset ready for use.

steps.title: Straight-line method (SLM)
steps.body:
**Annual depreciation = (Cost − Estimated scrap value) / Useful life**.

Ramesh's van: (6,00,000 − 1,00,000)/5 = **₹1,00,000 per year**. The same amount every year; simple; suits assets that give even service.

steps.title: Written-down-value method (WDV)
steps.body:
A fixed **percentage** of the book value at the start of each year. Higher in early years, lower later.

Example: machine ₹1,00,000 at 10% WDV:
- Year 1: 10,000 ⇒ book value 90,000
- Year 2: 9,000 ⇒ 81,000
- Year 3: 8,100 ⇒ 72,900
The book value never reaches zero.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body:
Machine costing ₹1,10,000 (including ₹10,000 installation), scrap value ₹10,000, life 5 years.
- SLM: (1,10,000 − 10,000)/5 = ₹20,000 each year.
- After 2 years, SLM book value = 1,10,000 − 40,000 = ₹70,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving installation costs out of the asset's cost.
- Applying the WDV rate to the original cost every year (it applies to the reducing balance).
- Thinking depreciation is cash set aside—it is an accounting allocation.

activity.prompt: A machine costs ₹50,000 and is depreciated at 20% per year on the written-down value. What is its book value at the end of year 2 (₹)?

quiz.q: Under SLM, depreciation each year is
quiz.why: Under the straight-line method (SLM), depreciation is the same amount every year.

quiz.q: Under WDV, the rate is applied to
options: book value at the start of the year
quiz.why: Under the written-down-value method, the depreciation rate is applied to the book value at the start of the year, so the charge decreases.

quiz.q: Asset cost ₹80,000, scrap ₹8,000, life 8 years. SLM depreciation per year
quiz.why: SLM depreciation = (cost − scrap) ÷ life = (80,000 − 8,000) ÷ 8 = ₹9,000 per year.

quiz.q: Depreciation is a
quiz.why: Depreciation is a non-cash expense, because no cash is paid out when it is charged. It only spreads the asset's cost over its life.

quiz.q: Which cost is included in an asset's cost for depreciation?
quiz.why: Installation charges are part of the asset's cost, as they bring it into working condition. Drawings, sales commission and office electricity are not.

questions.q: Assets = Liabilities + ?
questions.why: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. This is the accounting equation.

questions.q: Cash sales are credited to
questions.why: Cash sales are revenue, so they are credited to the Sales account.

questions.q: Goods returned by a customer are called
questions.why: Goods returned by a customer are sales returns (returns inwards), which reduce sales.

questions.q: Rent paid in advance is
questions.why: Rent paid in advance benefits a future period, so it is a prepaid expense and a current asset.

questions.q: Opening stock 20,000; purchases 80,000; wages 5,000; closing stock 25,000; sales 1,20,000. Gross profit
questions.why: COGS = 20,000 + 80,000 + 5,000 − 25,000 = 80,000 (wages are a direct expense). Gross profit = sales − COGS = 1,20,000 − 80,000 = 40,000.

questions.q: A trial balance differs by ₹600. A ₹300 item was probably
options: posted to the correct side of a wrong account
questions.why: An item posted on the wrong side moves the difference by twice its amount, so ₹300 on the wrong side gives a ₹600 difference.

questions.q: Machine ₹2,00,000 at 10% WDV. Depreciation in year 3
questions.why: Under WDV at 10%: year 1 = 20,000, year 2 = 18,000, so the book value at the start of year 3 = 1,62,000. Year 3 depreciation = 10% of 1,62,000 = ₹16,200.

questions.q: Capital at start ₹1,00,000; net profit ₹25,000; drawings ₹10,000; additional capital ₹15,000. Closing capital
questions.why: Closing capital = opening capital + additional capital + profit − drawings = 1,00,000 + 15,000 + 25,000 − 10,000 = ₹1,30,000.

questions.q: A machine purchase debited to the Purchases account is an error of
questions.why: Debiting a machine purchase to Purchases confuses a capital item with a revenue one. This is an error of principle.

questions.q: Closing capital ₹90,000, drawings ₹12,000, no additional capital, opening capital ₹80,000. Profit for the year
questions.why: Closing capital = opening capital + profit − drawings. So profit = 90,000 + 12,000 − 80,000 = ₹22,000.

questions.q: Asset cost ₹1,00,000, scrap ₹10,000, life 6 years, bought on 1 October; books close 31 March. First-year SLM depreciation
questions.why: Annual depreciation = (1,00,000 − 10,000) ÷ 6 = ₹15,000. From 1 October to 31 March is 6 months, so 15,000 × 6/12 = ₹7,500.

questions.q: Which error would make a trial balance still agree?
options: A balance left out of the trial balance
Cash discount omitted from one side only
A ₹500 purchase from Raj credited to Ravi's account
questions.why: Right side, wrong personal account: an error of commission that does not affect totals.

courses.title: Business studies: management, marketing & consumers
courses.summary: Management principles (Fayol and Taylor), the functions of management, marketing and the marketing mix, financial markets and consumer protection — with Indian business cases.
outcomes: Learners can explain and apply Fayol's and Taylor's principles
Learners can describe planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling
Learners can design a marketing mix for a product
Learners can explain financial markets and SEBI's role
Learners can use consumer rights and the complaint process in India

lessons.title: Principles of management: Fayol and Taylor

scenes.text: At a garment factory in Tiruppur, workers get orders from three supervisors at once. Deadlines slip; tempers rise.
New manager Lakshmi notices: no clear chain of command, no standard methods, no fair pay for faster work.
She reaches for two classic toolkits—Fayol's principles and Taylor's scientific management.

steps.title: Fayol's 14 principles (general management)
steps.body: Division of work · Authority and responsibility · Discipline · **Unity of command** (one boss per worker) · **Unity of direction** (one plan for one objective) · Subordination of individual interest to general interest · Remuneration · Centralisation and decentralisation · **Scalar chain** (formal line of authority; 'gang plank' for quick horizontal communication in emergencies) · Order · Equity · Stability of tenure · Initiative · Esprit de corps (team spirit).

steps.title: Taylor's scientific management (shop floor)
steps.body:
Principles: science, not rule of thumb; harmony, not discord; cooperation, not individualism; development of each person to their greatest efficiency.

Techniques: **functional foremanship** (specialist supervisors), standardisation of work, method study, motion study, time study, fatigue study, and the **differential piece wage system** (higher rate for workers who meet the standard).

steps.title: Lakshmi's fixes
steps.body:
- Three supervisors giving orders violates **unity of command** ⇒ each worker reports to one line supervisor.
- She runs **time and motion studies** to set a fair standard output.
- She introduces a **differential piece rate**: ₹X per piece below standard, a higher rate above it.
- She adds a monthly team recognition to build **esprit de corps**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing unity of command (one boss) with unity of direction (one plan).
- Thinking principles are rigid laws—they are flexible guidelines adapted to situations.
- Saying functional foremanship follows unity of command (it actually conflicts with it—a classic exam point).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A company has separate marketing teams for two products, each with its own head and plan. Which principle is followed?

Answer: unity of direction.

activity.prompt: Match each situation with the principle it reflects.
pairs: A worker reports to only one supervisor
One plan and one head for each product division
Workers are not shifted around too often
Studying the best way to do a task
Higher pay rate for workers who meet the standard

quiz.q: 'One subordinate should receive orders from only one superior' is
quiz.why: 'One subordinate should receive orders from one superior only' is Fayol's principle of unity of command.

quiz.q: Functional foremanship was proposed by
quiz.why: Functional foremanship was proposed by F.W. Taylor as part of scientific management. It uses specialist supervisors.

quiz.q: The 'gang plank' relates to
quiz.why: The 'gang plank' is a direct link between people at the same level, which allows quick communication without going through the scalar chain.

quiz.q: Fatigue study aims to
options: determine rest intervals to restore efficiency
quiz.why: A fatigue study finds how long and how often workers need rest, so they can restore their efficiency.

quiz.q: Management principles are
quiz.why: Management principles are flexible guidelines, adapted to circumstances. They are not rigid like scientific laws or legal rules.

scenes.text: Aditya's café in Shillong is a hit. He decides to open a second outlet in Guwahati within six months.
He needs a plan, a team structure, the right people, motivation and a way to check progress.
That's planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling.

steps.title: Planning
steps.body:
Deciding in advance what to do and how. Steps: set objectives → develop premises (assumptions) → identify alternatives → evaluate → select → implement → follow up.

Types of plans: objectives, strategies, policies, procedures, methods, rules, programmes and budgets. Planning is the primary function; all other functions follow it.

steps.title: Organising and staffing
steps.body:
- **Organising**: identify activities, group them into departments, assign duties, establish authority relationships. Structures: **functional** (by function—finance, marketing) and **divisional** (by product or region).
- **Delegation** passes authority, but **accountability cannot be delegated**.
- **Staffing**: manpower planning → recruitment → selection → placement → training and development → performance appraisal → compensation.

steps.title: Directing and controlling
steps.body:
- **Directing**: supervision, motivation, leadership and communication. **Maslow's hierarchy**: physiological → safety → social (belonging) → esteem → self-actualisation. Leadership styles: autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire.
- **Controlling**: set standards → measure performance → compare → analyse deviations → take corrective action. 'Management by exception': focus on significant deviations only.

steps.title: Aditya's plan in action
steps.body: Objective: break even at the new outlet within 6 months. Standard: 300 customers a day by month 3. Actual: 220. Deviation analysis: poor visibility from the road. Corrective action: signage and a launch offer. That is controlling feeding back into planning.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking controlling happens only at the end—it is continuous.
- Saying responsibility and accountability can be fully delegated.
- Mixing up recruitment (attracting applicants) and selection (choosing among them).

activity.prompt: Put the steps of the controlling process in order.

quiz.q: The primary function of management
quiz.why: Planning is the primary function of management, because the other functions depend on it.

quiz.q: Which cannot be delegated?
quiz.why: Authority and the task can be delegated, but accountability cannot. The delegator remains answerable for the result.

quiz.q: In Maslow's hierarchy, the need just above safety is
quiz.why: Maslow's order is physiological, safety, social (belonging), esteem and self-actualisation. So social comes just above safety.

quiz.q: A structure based on products or regions is
quiz.why: A divisional structure groups activities by product or region, and each division is a semi-independent unit.

quiz.q: Recruitment means
options: searching for and attracting prospective employees
quiz.why: Recruitment means searching for and attracting prospective employees. Selection, choosing the best, comes after it.

scenes.text: Leela buys a new mixer-grinder online in Madurai. The ad promised 'two-year warranty, 750 W'. It stops working after three weeks.
The seller ignores her emails. She feels helpless—until her son, a commerce student, explains her rights as a consumer.
Meanwhile, the company's marketing team is learning why broken promises cost more than they save.

steps.title: Marketing and the marketing mix
steps.body:
Marketing is about identifying customer needs and satisfying them profitably. The **marketing concept** puts customer satisfaction at the centre.

The **4 Ps**:
- **Product**: features, quality, branding, packaging, labelling, warranty.
- **Price**: cost, competition, demand, value to the customer.
- **Place**: channels of distribution, logistics.
- **Promotion**: advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public relations.

steps.title: Consumer rights in India
steps.body:
The **Consumer Protection Act, 2019** recognises rights including: the right to **safety**, to be **informed**, to **choose**, to be **heard**, to **seek redressal** and to **consumer education**. It covers online and offline purchases, unfair trade practices and misleading advertisements, and created the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA).

Complaints go to **Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions** at the district, state and national levels (which level depends on the value of goods or services; the limits are set by government rules).

steps.title: How to complain effectively
steps.body:
1. Keep the invoice, warranty card, screenshots and emails.
2. Write to the seller and manufacturer with dates and a clear request (repair, replacement or refund).
3. Contact the **National Consumer Helpline (1915)** for mediation.
4. If unresolved, file a complaint with the appropriate District Commission—online filing is available through the government's e-Daakhil portal.

This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Look for standard marks
steps.body:
- **ISI** mark (BIS) on many electrical goods; **BIS hallmark** on gold jewellery.
- **Agmark** on agricultural products.
- **FSSAI** licence number on packaged food.
These marks indicate certification against standards.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Throwing away the bill—the most important evidence.
- Thinking only very expensive items qualify for complaints.
- Confusing marketing with selling (selling pushes products; marketing begins with customer needs).

a.text: Leela's mixer-grinder stopped working within the warranty. The seller ignores her. What should she do first?

choices.label: Collect the invoice, warranty card and screenshots of the ad
choices.feedback: Evidence is the foundation of any complaint.

choices.label: Post angry reviews and give up
choices.feedback: Reviews may warn others but won't get her a remedy.

c.text: A week later, she still has a broken mixer. Try again?

choices.label: Gather the evidence and write formally to the seller and brand
choices.feedback: Better.

b.text: She writes formally to the seller and manufacturer. No reply in 15 days. Next?

choices.label: Call the National Consumer Helpline (1915)
choices.feedback: The helpline can mediate with the company.

choices.label: Throw the product away
choices.feedback: She may need the product as evidence.

e.text: Luckily her son stops her. What now?

choices.label: Keep the product and call 1915
choices.feedback: Good.

choices.label: File a complaint with the District Consumer Commission (online via e-Daakhil)
choices.feedback: Right forum for a small-value claim.

f.text: The commission orders a replacement and compensation. Leela's rights to be heard and to seek redressal worked.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the 4 Ps?
quiz.why: The marketing mix has four Ps: product, price, place and promotion. 'People' is not one of them.

quiz.q: The Consumer Protection Act currently in force in India is from
quiz.why: The Consumer Protection Act 2019 is the one in force in India. It replaced the Act of 1986.

quiz.q: The national consumer helpline number
quiz.why: The National Consumer Helpline number is 1915.

quiz.q: The ISI mark is issued by
quiz.why: The ISI mark is issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), which certifies the quality of products.

quiz.q: The marketing concept focuses on
