quiz.why: The marketing concept focuses on customer needs and satisfaction, rather than just production or selling.

story.title: Should the startup borrow or sell shares?

scenes.text: Two friends, Zoya and Karthik, run an ed-tech startup in Bengaluru. They need ₹50 lakh to expand.
A bank offers a loan at interest; an investor offers money for a 20% stake.
Their mentor explains financial decisions, capital structure and how markets work.

steps.title: Three financial decisions
steps.body:
- **Investment decision**: where to invest (long-term: capital budgeting; short-term: working capital).
- **Financing decision**: how to raise funds—**equity** (owners' funds; no fixed obligation, but ownership is shared) vs **debt** (loans; interest is fixed and tax-deductible, but adds risk).
- **Dividend decision**: how much profit to distribute vs retain.

steps.title: Capital structure and working capital
steps.body:
- **Financial leverage**: using debt can raise returns to shareholders when the return on investment is higher than the interest rate—and magnify losses when it isn't.
- **Working capital** = current assets − current liabilities. Businesses with long operating cycles (manufacturing) need more working capital than service firms.

steps.title: Financial markets
steps.body:
- **Money market**: short-term funds (treasury bills, commercial paper, call money).
- **Capital market**: long-term funds—**primary market** (new issues, e.g., IPOs) and **secondary market** (stock exchanges such as BSE and NSE, where existing securities trade).
- **SEBI** (Securities and Exchange Board of India) regulates the securities market to protect investors and develop the market.
- Shares are held electronically in **demat** accounts.

steps.title: Zoya and Karthik's choice
steps.body: If expansion earns 18% and the loan costs 12%, debt raises the owners' return—but repayments are due even in bad months. Equity has no fixed repayment but they give up 20% ownership and future profits. Many firms use a mix.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking debt is always cheaper and always better.
- Confusing the primary market (new securities) with the secondary market (trading existing ones).
- Investing based on tips without understanding risk—always check whether an advisor is SEBI-registered.

cards.back: Where to put funds (long-term assets, working capital)
How to raise funds: equity vs debt
How much profit to distribute vs retain
Where new securities are issued (e.g., IPO)
Where existing securities are traded (stock exchanges)

quiz.q: An IPO happens in the
quiz.why: An IPO (initial public offering) issues new shares, which happens in the primary market.

quiz.q: Interest on debt is
quiz.why: Interest on debt is a fixed obligation that must be paid regardless of profit. It is also tax-deductible.

quiz.q: Working capital =
quiz.why: Working capital = current assets − current liabilities.

quiz.q: The regulator of India's securities market
quiz.why: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) regulates the securities market.

quiz.q: Treasury bills are instruments of the
quiz.why: Treasury bills are short-term government borrowing instruments, so they belong to the money market.

questions.q: Who gave the 14 principles of management?
questions.why: Henri Fayol gave the 14 principles of management. Taylor gave scientific management.

questions.q: Which is a P of the marketing mix?
questions.why: The marketing mix has four Ps: product, price, place and promotion. So 'place' is one of them.

questions.q: Unity of direction means
options: one plan and one head for a group of activities with the same objective
questions.why: Unity of direction means one plan and one head for a group of activities with the same objective. Unity of command is about one boss per worker.

questions.q: Choosing the best candidate from applicants is
questions.why: Choosing the best candidate from the applicants is selection. Recruitment is attracting applicants.

questions.q: A worker receives orders from a production foreman and a quality foreman. This follows
questions.why: A worker taking orders from specialist foremen, such as production and quality foremen, follows Taylor's functional foremanship, which breaks unity of command.

questions.q: The right to be heard means a consumer
options: can have complaints considered at appropriate forums
questions.why: The right to be heard means a consumer can have complaints considered at appropriate forums.

questions.q: Under financial leverage, debt raises return on equity when
questions.why: Financial leverage helps when the return on investment is greater than the interest rate, so that debt raises the return on equity.

questions.q: 'Management by exception' in controlling means
questions.why: Management by exception means focusing on significant deviations from standards only, which saves managers' time.

questions.q: A manufacturer with a long production cycle will usually need
questions.why: A longer production cycle ties up funds for longer, so the firm needs more working capital.

questions.q: Which statement about delegation is correct?
options: Authority is delegated; accountability stays with the delegator
questions.why: Authority can be delegated, but accountability remains with the delegator. Delegation does not remove the manager's role.

questions.q: A misleading advertisement complaint at the national level can be investigated by the
questions.why: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the Central Consumer Protection Authority can investigate misleading advertisements at the national level.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: Fatigue study sets rest; time study sets standard time; method study finds the best way.

courses.title: Economics: micro and macro
courses.summary: Demand, supply and elasticity; costs and market equilibrium; national income accounting; money, banking and the RBI; and the government budget and multiplier — with numericals and Indian examples.
outcomes: Learners can compute price elasticity and find market equilibrium
Learners can explain cost curves and firm equilibrium under perfect competition
Learners can calculate GDP, NDP and national income
Learners can explain credit creation and RBI's monetary tools
Learners can compute fiscal, revenue and primary deficits and the investment multiplier

scenes.text: At Lasalgaon, near Nashik, onion prices double after unseasonal rain damages crops.
Homemaker Sushma in Pune buys fewer onions but still buys some—she can't cook without them.
Meanwhile, a café owner cuts back sharply on onion rings. Same price rise, different reactions: that's elasticity.

steps.title: Demand
steps.body:
**Law of demand**: other things equal, quantity demanded falls when price rises (inverse relationship).

Determinants (shift the curve): income, prices of related goods (substitutes, complements), tastes, expectations, population.
- **Movement along** the curve: due to the good's own price.
- **Shift** of the curve: due to other factors.
- Normal goods: demand rises with income; inferior goods: demand falls with income.

steps.title: Price elasticity of demand
steps.body:
**Ed = (% change in quantity demanded)/(% change in price)** (taken as a positive number).
- Ed > 1: elastic; Ed < 1: inelastic; Ed = 1: unitary.
- Necessities (salt, onions, medicines) tend to be inelastic; luxuries and goods with close substitutes tend to be elastic.
- **Total expenditure test**: if price falls and spending rises ⇒ elastic; spending falls ⇒ inelastic; unchanged ⇒ unitary.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) Price falls from ₹10 to ₹8 (−20%); quantity rises from 100 to 130 (+30%). Ed = 30/20 = **1.5** (elastic). Spending: 1000 → 1040, rises ✔.

2) **Market equilibrium**: Qd = 100 − 2P, Qs = 20 + 2P. Set equal: 100 − 2P = 20 + 2P ⇒ P = 20, Q = 60.

If demand rises (curve shifts right) with supply unchanged, both price and quantity rise.

steps.title: Supply
steps.body:
**Law of supply**: quantity supplied rises with price (other things equal). Determinants: input prices, technology, number of firms, taxes and subsidies, prices of other goods.

Government interventions: a **price ceiling** (maximum price, below equilibrium) can create shortages; a **price floor** (minimum support price, above equilibrium) can create surpluses.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a rise in demand due to a price fall a 'shift' (it's a movement along the curve).
- Forgetting the negative sign convention of Ed.
- Assuming elastic means 'more than zero' (it means greater than 1).

activity.prompt: Price of a good rises from ₹50 to ₹55 and quantity demanded falls from 200 to 190. What is the price elasticity of demand (positive value)?

quiz.q: A fall in the price of tea increases demand for
quiz.why: Tea and sugar are complements, so a fall in tea's price increases demand for tea and so for sugar. Coffee is a substitute.

quiz.q: Ed = 0.4 means demand is
quiz.why: Elasticity of 0.4 is less than 1, so demand is inelastic. A given percentage price change changes quantity by less.

quiz.q: A change in consumer income causes
options: a shift of the demand curve
quiz.why: A change in consumer income shifts the whole demand curve. A movement along the curve is due to the price of the good itself.

quiz.q: Price falls and total expenditure stays the same. Ed =
quiz.why: If a price change leaves total expenditure unchanged, the price elasticity of demand equals 1 (unitary).

quiz.q: A price ceiling below equilibrium tends to cause
quiz.why: A price ceiling set below the equilibrium price makes the quantity demanded exceed the quantity supplied, causing a shortage.

scenes.text: Raju sells samosas near a college in Kanpur. One extra helper doubles output; a third helper adds less, a fifth just gets in the way.
His rent is the same whether he sells 100 or 500 samosas; oil and potatoes rise with every batch.
Economics names these patterns: diminishing returns, fixed and variable costs, and marginal decisions.

steps.title: Production and returns
steps.body:
- **Short run**: at least one input fixed. **Law of variable proportions**: as more of a variable input is added to fixed inputs, marginal product first rises, then falls, and may become negative.
- **Long run**: all inputs variable; **returns to scale** (increasing, constant, decreasing).

steps.title: Costs
steps.body:
- **TC = TFC + TVC**; AFC = TFC/Q (falls continuously); AVC = TVC/Q; ATC = AFC + AVC.
- **Marginal cost** MC = ΔTC/ΔQ.
- MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minimum points; AVC, ATC and MC curves are U-shaped in the short run.

steps.title: Perfect competition
steps.body:
Many buyers and sellers, homogeneous product, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge ⇒ each firm is a **price taker**: P = AR = MR.

**Profit-maximising output**: MR = MC with MC rising. In the long run, free entry and exit drive economic profit to zero: P = minimum ATC.

Shut-down rule (short run): produce only if P ≥ minimum AVC.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
TFC = ₹100. TVC for 1, 2, 3 units = 40, 70, 110.
- TC = 140, 170, 210; MC = 40 (first), 30, 40.
- ATC = 140, 85, 70; AFC = 100, 50, 33.3.
If the market price is ₹40, Raju should produce up to the unit where MC = 40 and is rising: the 3rd unit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking fixed cost changes with output in the short run.
- Setting P = ATC instead of MR = MC for profit maximisation.
- Confusing diminishing returns (short run) with decreasing returns to scale (long run).

statements.s: Average fixed cost falls continuously as output rises.
statements.why: A constant TFC is spread over more units.

statements.s: MC cuts ATC at the minimum point of ATC.
statements.why: When MC < ATC, ATC falls; when MC > ATC, ATC rises.

statements.s: Under perfect competition, a firm can set its own price.
statements.why: It is a price taker.

statements.s: A firm should shut down in the short run if price is below minimum AVC.
statements.why: It cannot even cover variable costs.

statements.s: The law of variable proportions applies to the long run.
statements.why: It applies to the short run, with some inputs fixed.

quiz.q: TC = 500 when output is 10 and TFC = 200. AVC =
quiz.why: TVC = TC − TFC = 500 − 200 = 300. AVC = TVC ÷ output = 300 ÷ 10 = 30.

quiz.q: Under perfect competition, MR equals
quiz.why: Under perfect competition, the firm is a price taker, so price = AR = MR.

quiz.q: Profit is maximised where
quiz.why: A firm maximises profit where MR = MC, with MC rising (cutting MR from below).

quiz.q: Long-run profit under perfect competition is
quiz.why: With free entry and exit, firms in perfect competition earn only normal profit (zero economic profit) in the long run.

quiz.q: TC rises from 200 to 230 when output rises from 4 to 5. MC of the 5th unit
quiz.why: MC of the 5th unit = change in TC ÷ change in output = (230 − 200) ÷ 1 = 30.

scenes.text: Farmer Gopal in Punjab sells wheat to a flour mill; the mill sells flour to a bakery; the bakery sells bread to families in Delhi.
If we add all three sales, we count the wheat three times. Economists count only value added.
Student Ananya wants to compute India's national income the way statisticians do—carefully.

steps.title: Key aggregates
steps.body:
- **GDP at market price**: market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's domestic territory in a year.
- **NDP** = GDP − depreciation.
- **GNP** = GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA).
- **Net indirect taxes** = indirect taxes − subsidies.
- **National income (NNP at factor cost)** = GDP_MP − depreciation + NFIA − net indirect taxes.

steps.title: Three methods
steps.body:
1. **Value added (product) method**: sum of value added by all producers (output − intermediate consumption).
2. **Income method**: compensation of employees + rent + interest + profit + mixed income of the self-employed.
3. **Expenditure method**: C + I + G + (X − M).

All three give the same total (circular flow).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Wheat ₹100 (no inputs) → flour ₹150 → bread ₹220.
- Value added: 100 + 50 + 70 = **₹220** = value of the final good ✔.

GDP_MP = 1000; depreciation 100; NFIA −20; indirect taxes 80; subsidies 30.
- National income = 1000 − 100 − 20 − (80 − 30) = **₹830**.

steps.title: Real vs nominal GDP
steps.body:
**Nominal GDP** uses current prices; **real GDP** uses base-year prices and shows actual output growth. **GDP deflator** = (nominal GDP/real GDP) × 100.

GDP is not a perfect welfare measure: it ignores unpaid household work, income distribution, environmental damage and non-market activities.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting intermediate goods (double counting).
- Including transfer payments (pensions, scholarships) or sale of second-hand goods (only the dealer's commission counts).
- Forgetting NFIA when moving from domestic to national.

activity.prompt: Is each item included in India's GDP for this year?

items.text: A new car produced this year
Salary of a teacher in a government school
Commission earned by a second-hand car dealer
Purchase of shares on the stock market
Flour bought by a bakery to make bread

quiz.q: NDP equals
quiz.why: NDP = GDP − depreciation (consumption of fixed capital).

quiz.q: Which is a transfer payment?
quiz.why: A scholarship is a transfer payment, since the receiver provides no productive service in return. Wages, rent and profit are factor incomes.

quiz.q: GNP = GDP +
quiz.why: GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA).

quiz.q: Expenditure method: GDP =
quiz.why: By the expenditure method, GDP = C + I + G + (X − M).

quiz.q: Real GDP uses
quiz.why: Real GDP is measured at base-year prices, which removes the effect of price changes (inflation).

story.title: Where does the bank's money come from?

scenes.text: Rekha deposits ₹10,000 in her bank in Kochi. The bank lends most of it to a local tailor.
The tailor pays a cloth supplier, who deposits it in another bank, which lends again…
The Reserve Bank of India sets the rules that decide how far this chain can go.

steps.title: Money and its functions
steps.body:
Money solves the problems of barter (double coincidence of wants). Functions: **medium of exchange**, **measure of value (unit of account)**, **store of value**, **standard of deferred payment**.

Money supply measures include currency held by the public plus deposits; M1 is narrow money; M3 is broad money.

steps.title: Credit creation
steps.body:
Banks keep a fraction of deposits as reserves (legal reserve ratio, LRR) and lend the rest. **Money multiplier = 1/LRR**.

Rekha's ₹10,000 with LRR 10%: total deposits can grow to 10,000 × (1/0.1) = **₹1,00,000** (in theory, assuming all loans return as deposits).

steps.title: RBI's monetary policy tools
steps.body:
The RBI is India's central bank: it issues currency (except one-rupee notes and coins, which are issued by the Government of India), is banker to the government and to banks, lender of last resort and controller of credit.
- **Repo rate**: rate at which RBI lends to banks; raising it makes borrowing costlier ⇒ reduces credit and inflation.
- **Reverse repo** and the standing deposit facility: absorb liquidity.
- **CRR** (cash reserve ratio) and **SLR** (statutory liquidity ratio): reserve requirements.
- **Open market operations**: buying or selling government securities.
In India, a Monetary Policy Committee decides the policy repo rate with an inflation target.

steps.title: Fighting inflation
steps.body: Prices rise fast. The RBI can raise the repo rate, raise CRR or sell government securities ⇒ banks have less to lend and loans cost more ⇒ spending slows ⇒ inflation eases. To boost a slow economy, it does the opposite.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a higher CRR increases lending (it reduces it).
- Confusing repo (RBI lends to banks) with reverse repo (banks park funds with RBI).
- Thinking the multiplier is unlimited—real banks hold extra reserves and people hold cash.

activity.label: Legal reserve ratio (LRR) for a ₹10,000 initial deposit

bands.text: LRR 5%: multiplier 20 ⇒ deposits up to ₹2,00,000. Very loose credit.
LRR 20% or less: multiplier 5 or more ⇒ up to ₹50,000 at 20%.
LRR 25–30%: multiplier about 3.3–4. Credit is tighter.
LRR 50%: multiplier 2 ⇒ deposits up to ₹20,000. Very tight credit.

quiz.q: If LRR = 20%, the money multiplier is
quiz.why: The money multiplier = 1 ÷ LRR = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5.

quiz.q: To control inflation, the RBI would typically
quiz.why: To control inflation, the RBI raises the repo rate, which makes borrowing costlier and reduces demand and money supply.

quiz.q: 'Lender of last resort' refers to
quiz.why: The RBI is the lender of last resort, since it supports banks facing a liquidity crisis.

quiz.q: One-rupee notes in India are issued by
quiz.why: In India, one-rupee notes (and coins) are issued by the Government of India, while the RBI issues all other notes.

quiz.q: Money's function as a 'store of value' means
options: it can be saved to buy things later
quiz.why: As a store of value, money can be saved and used to buy things later, since it holds purchasing power over time.

lessons.title: Government budget, multiplier and the open economy

scenes.text: On 1 February, the Finance Minister presents the Union Budget. Siddharth's family in Ahmedabad watches: his father cares about income tax, his mother about LPG subsidies.
News anchors repeat 'fiscal deficit' a dozen times. Siddharth wants to know what it actually means.
His economics teacher shows him the formulas—and why spending can multiply income.

steps.title: Budget structure
steps.body:
- **Revenue receipts**: tax (income tax, GST, etc.) and non-tax (dividends, fees). Do not create liabilities or reduce assets.
- **Capital receipts**: borrowing, recovery of loans, disinvestment.
- **Revenue expenditure**: salaries, interest, subsidies (no asset creation).
- **Capital expenditure**: building roads, buying machinery, giving loans.

steps.title: The deficits
steps.body:
- **Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
- **Fiscal deficit** = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) = total borrowing requirement.
- **Primary deficit** = fiscal deficit − interest payments.

Example: total expenditure 100, revenue receipts 70, non-debt capital receipts 5, interest 15, revenue expenditure 80 ⇒ revenue deficit 10, fiscal deficit 25, primary deficit 10.

steps.title: The investment multiplier
steps.body:
When investment rises, income rises by more: **k = ΔY/ΔI = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS**.

MPC = 0.8 ⇒ k = 5. An extra ₹100 crore of investment can raise income by ₹500 crore (in this simple model), because each round of spending becomes someone else's income.

steps.title: Balance of payments and exchange rates
steps.body:
- **Current account**: trade in goods and services, income, transfers (e.g., remittances—India is among the world's largest recipients).
- **Capital account**: foreign investment, loans, banking capital.
- A flexible exchange rate is set by demand and supply of foreign currency; if the rupee depreciates, exports become cheaper for foreigners and imports costlier for Indians.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating borrowing as a revenue receipt (it is a capital receipt).
- Forgetting that subsidies and interest are revenue expenditure.
- Using MPC in place of MPS in the multiplier formula.

activity.prompt: Match each term with its formula or meaning.
pairs: Total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts)
Trade in goods and services, income and transfers

quiz.q: MPC = 0.75. Multiplier =
Which is a capital receipt?
quiz.why: Borrowing from the public creates a liability for the government, so it is a capital receipt. GST, fees and dividends are revenue receipts.

quiz.q: Fiscal deficit indicates
quiz.why: The fiscal deficit shows the government's total borrowing requirement: total expenditure minus total receipts other than borrowing.

quiz.q: If the rupee depreciates, Indian exports tend to
quiz.why: When the rupee depreciates, foreign buyers need fewer units of their currency to buy Indian goods, so exports become cheaper for them.

quiz.q: Subsidies are
quiz.why: Subsidies are revenue expenditure, because they do not create any asset for the government.

questions.q: The law of demand states that, other things equal, when price rises quantity demanded
questions.why: The law of demand says that, other things equal, when price rises, the quantity demanded falls.

questions.q: Who issues currency notes (other than ₹1) in India?
questions.why: The RBI issues currency notes in India, except ₹1 notes, which are issued by the Government of India.

questions.q: GDP − depreciation =
questions.why: GDP minus depreciation gives the net domestic product (NDP).

questions.q: Salt typically has demand that is
questions.why: Salt is a necessity with a very small share of the budget, so its demand is inelastic.

questions.q: Qd = 50 − P and Qs = 10 + P. Equilibrium price
questions.why: At equilibrium Qd = Qs: 50 − P = 10 + P, so 2P = 40 and P = 20.

questions.q: MPS = 0.2. Change in income from a ₹200 crore rise in investment
questions.why: Multiplier = 1 ÷ MPS = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5. Change in income = 5 × 200 = ₹1,000 crore.

questions.q: A firm in perfect competition shuts down in the short run when
questions.why: In the short run a firm shuts down when the price is below the minimum AVC, since it cannot even cover its variable costs.

questions.q: GDP_MP 2000, depreciation 200, NFIA 50, indirect taxes 150, subsidies 50. National income
questions.why: National income = NNP at factor cost = GDP − depreciation + NFIA − (indirect taxes − subsidies) = 2000 − 200 + 50 − (150 − 50) = 1750.

questions.q: Fiscal deficit 300, interest 120. Primary deficit
questions.why: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments = 300 − 120 = 180.

questions.q: Price rises 10% and total expenditure on the good rises. Demand is
questions.why: If price rises and total expenditure also rises, the quantity fell by less than 10%, so demand is inelastic.

questions.q: With LRR 12.5% and an initial deposit of ₹8,000, the maximum total deposits are
questions.why: The deposit multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.125 = 8, so the maximum total deposits = 8 × 8,000 = ₹64,000.

questions.q: Nominal GDP is ₹1,200 crore and the GDP deflator is 120. Real GDP
questions.why: Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ deflator × 100 = 1,200 ÷ 120 × 100 = ₹1,000 crore.

questions.q: Which open market operation increases money supply?
questions.why: When the RBI buys government securities, it pays money into the banking system, which increases the money supply.

school-senior-maths.description: Pathshala Senior maths: calculus, vectors and 3-D geometry, matrices and probability — with derivations, worked examples, common mistakes and exam-style drills.

Learners can differentiate using product, quotient, chain, implicit and logarithmic methods
Learners can solve rate-of-change and optimisation problems

story.title: Riya zooms in on a speedometer

scenes.text: Riya, 16, sits beside her father on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway. The speedometer reads 80 km/h. 'But speed at one instant—how can you divide distance by zero time?' she asks.
Her father, a civil engineer, smiles: 'You don't divide by zero. You see what the average speed approaches as the time interval shrinks.'
That 'approaching' idea is a limit—the foundation of all calculus.

steps.title: What a limit means
steps.body:
lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means f(x) gets as close to L as we like when x is close enough to a (x ≠ a). The value f(a) itself does not matter—it may not even exist.

The limit exists only if the **left-hand limit = right-hand limit**.

Algebra of limits: limits of sums, products and quotients are the sums, products and quotients of the limits (provided the denominator's limit ≠ 0).

steps.title: Standard limits to know by heart
steps.body:
- lim_{x→0} (sin x)/x = 1 (x in radians)
- lim_{x→0} (1 − cos x)/x² = ½
- lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1)/x = 1; lim_{x→0} (aˣ − 1)/x = ln a
- lim_{x→0} ln(1 + x)/x = 1
- lim_{x→0} (1 + x)^{1/x} = e
- lim_{x→a} (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹

steps.title: Continuity
steps.body:
f is continuous at a if **lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a)** (the limit exists, the value exists, and they match).

Example: f(x) = kx + 1 for x ≤ 2, and 3x − 1 for x > 2. Continuity at 2: 2k + 1 = 5 ⇒ **k = 2**.

Polynomials, sin, cos and eˣ are continuous everywhere; rational functions wherever the denominator ≠ 0. A differentiable function is continuous, but |x| at 0 is continuous yet not differentiable (a corner).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using degrees in sin x/x (the limit 1 holds only in radians).
- 'Cancelling' to get a value without checking the 0/0 form.
- Concluding a limit exists from one side only.
- Writing ∞/∞ = 1 or 0/0 = 1. They are indeterminate forms.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Evaluate lim_{x→0} (1 − cos 2x)/x².

Answer: 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin² x ⇒ 2(sin x/x)² → **2**.

activity.prompt: Match each limit with its value.

quiz.why: Factor x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3). Cancel (x − 3) to get x + 3, which tends to 6 as x → 3.

quiz.q: lim_{x→0} tan x / x
quiz.why: tan x/x = (sin x/x) × (1/cos x). As x → 0 the first factor → 1 and the second → 1, so the limit is 1.
Divide numerator and denominator by x: (2 + 1/x)/(1 − 7/x) → 2/1 = 2 as x → ∞.

quiz.q: f(x) = |x| at x = 0 is
quiz.why: |x| is continuous at 0 but has a corner, with left derivative −1 and right derivative +1, so it is not differentiable there.

quiz.q: A limit exists at a point when
quiz.why: A limit exists at a point when the left-hand and right-hand limits are equal and finite. The value f(a) need not be defined.

scenes.text: Ammi pours chai at 90 °C in a Hyderabad kitchen. Faisal notices it cools fast at first, then slowly.
'How fast is it cooling right now?' he asks. The answer is a derivative—the instantaneous rate of change.
He learns a small toolkit of rules that can differentiate almost anything.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h — the slope of the tangent, the instantaneous rate.

From first principles, f(x) = x²: [(x + h)² − x²]/h = 2x + h → **2x**.

steps.title: Standard derivatives and rules
steps.body:
- d/dx xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹; d/dx eˣ = eˣ; d/dx ln x = 1/x; d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a
- sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec² x; sec x → sec x tan x
- sin⁻¹x → 1/√(1 − x²); tan⁻¹x → 1/(1 + x²)
- **Product**: (uv)' = u'v + uv'; **Quotient**: (u/v)' = (u'v − uv')/v²
- **Chain**: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))·g'(x)

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) y = x² sin x ⇒ y' = 2x sin x + x² cos x.
2) y = sin(3x² + 1) ⇒ y' = cos(3x² + 1)·6x.
3) y = e^{2x}/(1 + x) ⇒ y' = [2e^{2x}(1 + x) − e^{2x}]/(1 + x)² = e^{2x}(1 + 2x)/(1 + x)².
4) **Implicit**: x² + y² = 25 ⇒ 2x + 2yy' = 0 ⇒ y' = −x/y. At (3, 4): slope −3/4.
5) **Logarithmic**: y = xˣ ⇒ ln y = x ln x ⇒ y'/y = ln x + 1 ⇒ y' = xˣ(1 + ln x).
6) **Parametric**: x = at², y = 2at ⇒ dy/dx = (2a)/(2at) = 1/t.

steps.title: Higher derivatives
steps.body: y'' = d²y/dx². For y = e^{3x}: y' = 3e^{3x}, y'' = 9e^{3x}. In physics, if x(t) is position, x' is velocity and x'' is acceleration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the chain-rule factor (d/dx sin 2x = 2 cos 2x, not cos 2x).
- Writing (uv)' = u'v'.
- Reversing the order in the quotient-rule numerator (it is u'v − uv').
- Applying the power rule to xˣ or 2ˣ (a variable exponent needs logs).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Differentiate y = ln(sin x).

Answer: (1/sin x)·cos x = **cot x**.

activity.prompt: Fill in the derivatives.

quiz.q: d/dx (tan x)
quiz.why: The derivative of tan x is sec² x, a standard result.

quiz.q: If y = (2x + 1)³, dy/dx =
quiz.why: By the chain rule, d/dx (2x + 1)³ = 3(2x + 1)² × 2 = 6(2x + 1)².

quiz.q: For x² + y² = 1, dy/dx =
quiz.why: Differentiating implicitly: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y.

quiz.q: d/dx (xˣ)
quiz.why: Let y = xˣ, so ln y = x ln x. Then y'/y = ln x + 1, so dy/dx = xˣ(1 + ln x).

quiz.q: d/dx (sin⁻¹ x)
quiz.why: The derivative of sin⁻¹ x is 1/√(1 − x²), a standard result.

lessons.title: Applications of derivatives: rates, maxima and minima

scenes.text: Kiran runs a small packaging business in Surat. From an 18 cm square of card, she cuts equal squares from each corner and folds up a box.
Cut too little: a flat tray. Cut too much: a tall thin box. Which cut gives the biggest volume?
Her nephew Varun, in Class 12, sets the derivative to zero and finds the answer in two lines.

steps.title: Rates of change
steps.body: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt). Example: a balloon's radius grows at 0.5 cm/s. When r = 10 cm, V = (4/3)πr³ ⇒ dV/dt = 4πr²(dr/dt) = 4π(100)(0.5) = **200π cm³/s**.

steps.title: Increasing/decreasing and extrema
steps.body:
- f' > 0 on an interval ⇒ increasing; f' < 0 ⇒ decreasing.
- Critical points: f'(c) = 0 or f' undefined.
- **First-derivative test**: f' changes + to − ⇒ local max; − to + ⇒ local min.
- **Second-derivative test**: f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) < 0 ⇒ max; > 0 ⇒ min; = 0 ⇒ the test fails.
- On a closed interval [a, b], the absolute max/min occur at critical points or endpoints—check them all.

steps.title: Kiran's box solved
steps.body:
Cut squares of side x. Box: base (18 − 2x)², height x. V = x(18 − 2x)², 0 < x < 9.

V' = (18 − 2x)² − 4x(18 − 2x) = (18 − 2x)(18 − 6x). V' = 0 ⇒ x = 3 (x = 9 gives zero volume).

Sign change: V' > 0 for x < 3 and V' < 0 for 3 < x < 9 ⇒ maximum.

**Maximum volume = 3 × 12² = 432 cm³.**

steps.title: Tangents and approximation
steps.body:
Tangent to y = x³ at (1, 1): slope 3 ⇒ y − 1 = 3(x − 1). Normal: slope −1/3.

Approximation: f(x + Δx) ≈ f(x) + f'(x)Δx. √25.1 ≈ 5 + (1/(2·5))(0.1) = 5.01.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stopping at f'(c) = 0 without checking whether it is a max or a min.
- Forgetting endpoints in closed-interval problems.
- Ignoring the domain (x must keep all dimensions positive).
- Confusing local and absolute extrema.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Find two positive numbers with sum 20 and maximum product.

Answer: P = x(20 − x), P' = 20 − 2x = 0 ⇒ x = 10; the numbers are 10 and 10, product 100.

activity.prompt: A rectangle has perimeter 40 m. What is the maximum possible area (m²)?

quiz.q: f(x) = x³ − 3x has a local maximum at
quiz.why: f'(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = ±1. f''(x) = 6x, and f''(−1) = −6 < 0, so x = −1 is a local maximum.

quiz.q: f(x) = eˣ is
quiz.why: f'(x) = eˣ, which is positive for all x, so eˣ is increasing everywhere.

quiz.q: Slope of the normal to y = x² at (2, 4)
quiz.why: dy/dx = 2x = 4 at (2, 4), so the tangent slope is 4. The normal is perpendicular, so its slope is −1/4.

quiz.q: A circle's area increases at 2π cm²/s. Rate of change of radius when r = 5 cm
quiz.why: A = πr², so dA/dt = 2πr (dr/dt). With r = 5: 2π = 10π (dr/dt), so dr/dt = 0.2 cm/s.

quiz.q: If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) = 0, then
quiz.why: If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) = 0, the second-derivative test is inconclusive. Use the first-derivative test, as for x³ at 0.

scenes.text: Farmer Baldev in Haryana owns a plot bounded by a straight road and a curved canal. The land record office needs its exact area.
His granddaughter Simran, a Class 12 student, models the canal as a curve and adds up thin vertical strips.
Adding infinitely many thin strips is integration—the reverse of differentiation.

steps.title: Antiderivatives
steps.body:
∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C where F' = f.
- ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C (n ≠ −1); ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C
- ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C; ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C; ∫cos x dx = sin x + C; ∫sec² x dx = tan x + C
- ∫dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹ x + C; ∫dx/√(1 − x²) = sin⁻¹ x + C

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body:
- **Substitution**: ∫2x cos(x²) dx, put t = x² ⇒ ∫cos t dt = sin(x²) + C.
- **By parts**: ∫u v dx = u∫v dx − ∫(u'∫v dx)dx; choose u by ILATE (Inverse trig, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential). ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C.
- **Partial fractions**: ∫dx/(x² − 1) = ½ ln|(x − 1)/(x + 1)| + C.
- Special: ∫eˣ[f(x) + f'(x)]dx = eˣ f(x) + C.

steps.title: Definite integrals and properties
steps.body:
**Fundamental theorem**: ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a).
- ∫₀^π sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^π = 2
- ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x)dx. Example: I = ∫₀^{π/2} sin x/(sin x + cos x)dx; adding it to the replaced form gives 2I = π/2 ⇒ **I = π/4**.
- ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 0 if f is odd; = 2∫₀ᵃ f if f is even.

steps.title: Area between curves
steps.body:
Area between y = x and y = x² (they meet at x = 0 and 1; x ≥ x² there):

A = ∫₀¹ (x − x²)dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]₀¹ = ½ − ⅓ = **1/6 square units**.

Area of the circle x² + y² = a²: 4∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²)dx = πa² ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting + C in indefinite integrals.
- Not changing the limits after substitution in definite integrals.
- Area below the x-axis: the definite integral is negative, but area must use |f|.
- ∫(1/x)dx is ln|x|, not x⁰/0.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Evaluate ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx.

Answer: [x eˣ − eˣ]₀¹ = (e − e) − (0 − 1) = **1**.

cards.back: Choosing the first function u in integration by parts

cards.front: Area between y = x and y = x²

quiz.q: ∫ cos x dx
quiz.why: The integral of cos x is sin x + C, since d/dx (sin x) = cos x.

quiz.q: ∫₀² x dx
∫₋₁¹ x³ dx
quiz.why: x³ is an odd function, so its integral over limits symmetric about 0 is 0.

quiz.q: Best choice of u for ∫x ln x dx by ILATE
quiz.why: By ILATE, the Logarithmic function comes before Algebraic, so choose u = ln x.

quiz.q: ∫ dx/(1 + x²)
quiz.why: ∫ dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹ x + C, a standard integral.

story.title: The bacteria and the hot car

scenes.text: Microbiology student Tara in Pune notes that a bacterial culture doubles every 3 hours.
Her friend Omar, in Dubai, wonders how quickly a hot car's interior cools after it is parked in the shade.
Both are described by equations involving rates—differential equations.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Order**: the highest derivative present. **Degree**: the power of the highest derivative when the equation is a polynomial in its derivatives.
- A general solution has as many arbitrary constants as the order; a particular solution uses given conditions.

Example: (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx) = 0 has order 2, degree 3.

steps.title: Variable separable
steps.body:
dy/dx = g(x)h(y) ⇒ ∫dy/h(y) = ∫g(x)dx.

**Growth**: dN/dt = kN ⇒ N = N₀e^{kt}. Tara's culture: doubling time 3 h ⇒ k = ln 2/3 per hour. After 9 h: N = N₀·2³ = 8N₀.

**Newton's law of cooling**: dT/dt = −k(T − Tₛ) ⇒ T = Tₛ + (T₀ − Tₛ)e^{−kt}.

steps.title: Homogeneous and linear equations
steps.body:
- **Homogeneous** dy/dx = F(y/x): substitute y = vx ⇒ v + x dv/dx = F(v), then separate.
- **Linear first order**: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x). Integrating factor **IF = e^{∫P dx}**; solution y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C.

Example: dy/dx + y = eˣ. IF = eˣ ⇒ y eˣ = ∫e^{2x}dx = e^{2x}/2 + C ⇒ **y = eˣ/2 + Ce^{−x}**.

steps.title: Worked example: separable
steps.body:
Solve dy/dx = xy with y(0) = 2.

∫dy/y = ∫x dx ⇒ ln|y| = x²/2 + c ⇒ y = Ae^{x²/2}. y(0) = 2 ⇒ A = 2. **y = 2e^{x²/2}**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the constant of integration (or losing it while rearranging).
- Using IF = e^{∫P dx} before writing the equation in standard form (the coefficient of dy/dx must be 1).
- Stating a degree when the equation is not a polynomial in its derivatives (e.g., sin(y') has no defined degree).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Find the IF of x dy/dx + 2y = x² (x > 0).

Answer: standard form dy/dx + (2/x)y = x ⇒ IF = e^{2 ln x} = **x²**.

a.text: You meet dy/dx = (x + y)/x. Which method?

choices.label: Variable separable
choices.feedback: Not directly: (x + y)/x = 1 + y/x can't be split into g(x)h(y).

choices.label: Homogeneous (y = vx) or linear
choices.feedback: Yes—it's homogeneous, and also linear: dy/dx − y/x = 1.

choices.label: Treat it as linear: dy/dx − (1/x)y = 1
choices.feedback: Good.

c.text: Linear form dy/dx − (1/x)y = 1. What is the integrating factor (x > 0)?

choices.label: x
choices.feedback: Sign error: ∫P dx = −ln x.

e.text: Recheck the sign of P. The IF is?

choices.label: 1/x
choices.feedback: Correct now.

d.text: y/x = ∫(1/x)dx = ln x + C. Final solution?

choices.label: y = x ln x + Cx
choices.feedback: Correct.

choices.label: y = ln x + C
choices.feedback: You forgot to multiply both terms by x.

g.text: Multiply through by x. Which is right?

choices.label: y = x ln x + Cx
choices.feedback: Yes.

f.text: Solved! Recognise the form → standard form → IF → integrate → don't forget C.

quiz.q: Order and degree of y'' + (y')² + y = 0
quiz.why: The highest derivative is y'', so the order is 2. It appears to the first power, so the degree is 1.

quiz.q: Solution of dy/dx = y
quiz.why: dy/dx = y is separable: dy/y = dx, so ln y = x + c and y = Ceˣ.

quiz.q: IF of dy/dx + 3y = x
quiz.why: For dy/dx + Py = Q, the integrating factor is e^(∫P dx). Here P = 3, so IF = e^(3x).

quiz.q: Number of arbitrary constants in the general solution of a 3rd-order DE
quiz.why: The general solution of an nth-order differential equation has n arbitrary constants, so a 3rd-order one has 3.

quiz.q: A population grows as dN/dt = kN and doubles in 5 years. In 15 years it becomes
quiz.why: Doubling every 5 years: in 15 years there are 3 doublings, so the population is 2³ × N₀ = 8N₀.

questions.q: lim_{x→0} (sin 3x)/x
questions.why: lim (sin 3x)/x = 3 × lim (sin 3x)/(3x) = 3 × 1 = 3.

questions.q: d/dx (x⁴)
questions.why: By the power rule, d/dx (x⁴) = 4x³.

questions.q: ∫ 2x dx
questions.why: The antiderivative of 2x is x² + C.

questions.q: Slope of the tangent to y = x³ − x at x = 2
questions.why: The slope of the tangent is dy/dx = 3x² − 1. At x = 2: 3(4) − 1 = 11.

questions.q: ∫₀^{π/2} cos x dx
questions.why: ∫₀^{π/2} cos x dx = [sin x]₀^{π/2} = 1 − 0 = 1.

questions.q: Minimum value of x² − 6x + 10
questions.why: x² − 6x + 10 = (x − 3)² + 1 and (x − 3)² ≥ 0, so the minimum value is 1, at x = 3.

questions.q: If y = sin²x, dy/dx =
questions.why: By the chain rule, d/dx (sin²x) = 2 sin x cos x = sin 2x.

questions.q: ∫₀^{π/2} √(sin x)/(√(sin x) + √(cos x)) dx
questions.why: Using ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x)dx, I = ∫ √cos/(√cos + √sin). Adding the two forms gives 2I = ∫₀^{π/2} 1 dx = π/2, so I = π/4.

questions.q: Area bounded by y = x² and y = 4
questions.why: The curves meet at x = ±2. Area = ∫₋₂² (4 − x²)dx = [4x − x³/3]₋₂² = 16 − 16/3 = 32/3.

questions.q: Solution of dy/dx = e^{x − y}
questions.why: dy/dx = e^{x−y} = eˣ/eʸ. Separating, eʸ dy = eˣ dx, so eʸ = eˣ + C.

questions.q: f(x) = x eˣ has a minimum at
questions.why: f'(x) = eˣ(1 + x) = 0 gives x = −1. f''(x) = eˣ(2 + x), and f''(−1) = e⁻¹ > 0, so it is a minimum.

questions.q: ∫ eˣ (1/x − 1/x²) dx
questions.why: The integral of eˣ[f(x) + f'(x)] is eˣ f(x) + C. Here f = 1/x and f' = −1/x², so the result is eˣ/x + C.

questions.q: A 5 m ladder slides down a wall; its foot moves away at 2 m/s. How fast does the top slide down when the foot is 4 m from the wall?
questions.why: x² + y² = 25. At x = 4, y = 3. Differentiate: 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0, so 8 × 2 + 6(dy/dt) = 0, so dy/dt = −8/3. The top slides down at 8/3 m/s.

courses.title: Vectors & 3-D geometry
courses.summary: Vectors, dot and cross products, triple products, and the geometry of lines and planes in space — with real uses in drones, torque, flight paths and solar panels.
outcomes: Learners can compute magnitudes, dot and cross products and projections
Learners can find areas, volumes and test coplanarity
Learners can write line equations and find angles and shortest distances
Learners can write plane equations and compute point–plane distances and angles

scenes.text: Startup engineer Nikhil in Bengaluru programs a delivery drone: 3 km east, 4 km north and 1 km up to a rooftop.
He needs the straight-line distance and the angle between the drone's path and the wind direction.
Vectors handle both with a few lines of algebra.

steps.title: Vector basics
steps.body:
A vector has magnitude and direction: a = a₁i + a₂j + a₃k; |a| = √(a₁² + a₂² + a₃²). Unit vector â = a/|a|.

Nikhil's drone: d = 3i + 4j + k ⇒ |d| = √26 ≈ 5.10 km.

Position vector of the point dividing AB internally in ratio m:n: (mb + na)/(m + n).

Direction cosines of a: aᵢ/|a|, with l² + m² + n² = 1.

steps.title: Dot (scalar) product
steps.body:
a·b = |a||b|cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃.
- a·b = 0 ⇔ perpendicular (non-zero vectors).
- Projection of a on b = (a·b)/|b|.
- Work done W = F·d.
- i·i = 1, i·j = 0.

steps.title: Work done
steps.body: A force F = 2i + 3j (N) moves a box by d = 4i (m). W = F·d = 8 J. Only the component along the motion does work—pulling a suitcase at a steep angle wastes the vertical component.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a·b as a vector (it is a scalar).
- Forgetting the k-component in 3-D.
- Confusing the scalar projection (a·b)/|b| with the projection vector ((a·b)/|b|²)b.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Find λ so that 2i + λj + k is perpendicular to i − 2j + 3k.

Answer: 2 − 2λ + 3 = 0 ⇒ λ = 5/2.

activity.prompt: Find a·b for a = 3i − 2j + k and b = i + 4j − 2k.

quiz.q: Magnitude of 2i − 2j + k
If a·b = 0 (both non-zero), a and b are
quiz.why: If a·b = 0 for non-zero vectors, then cos θ = 0, so they are perpendicular.

quiz.q: i·k equals
quiz.why: i·k = 0, because i and k are perpendicular unit vectors.

quiz.q: Work done by F = 5i (N) over d = 3i + 4j (m)
quiz.why: Work = F·d = (5i)·(3i + 4j) = 5 × 3 + 0 = 15 J. Only the x-components multiply.

quiz.q: Sum of the squares of the direction cosines
quiz.why: The direction cosines l, m, n of a line satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1.

scenes.text: Mechanic Salim in Chandigarh tightens a bolt. Pushing at the end of the spanner at right angles is easy; pushing along the spanner turns nothing.
The turning effect is a cross product—largest at 90° and zero at 0°.
His daughter Zara uses the triple product for a geometry problem: the volume of a slanted box.

steps.title: Cross (vector) product
steps.body:
a × b = |a||b| sin θ n̂, where n̂ is perpendicular to both (right-hand rule).
- Determinant form: a × b = |i j k; a₁ a₂ a₃; b₁ b₂ b₃|
- a × b = −(b × a) (not commutative); a × a = 0
- i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j
- |a × b| = area of the parallelogram on a and b; triangle area = ½|a × b|
- a × b = 0 ⇔ parallel (non-zero vectors).

steps.title: Scalar triple product
steps.body:
[a b c] = a·(b × c) = the determinant of the three rows of components.
- |[a b c]| = volume of the parallelepiped.
- [a b c] = 0 ⇔ the vectors are **coplanar**.
- Cyclic swaps keep the value; swapping two vectors changes its sign.

Example: a = i, b = j, c = i + j + k: [a b c] = det[[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[1,1,1]] = 1 ⇒ volume 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The sign of the middle term in the determinant expansion (it is −j(…)).
- Writing a × b = b × a.
- Using |a × b| for a triangle's area without the ½.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Are a = i + j + k, b = 2i + 2j + 2k and c = i − j coplanar?

Answer: b = 2a, so [a b c] = 0 ⇒ coplanar (any set containing two parallel vectors is coplanar).

statements.s: a × b = b × a
|a × b| is the area of the parallelogram with sides a and b.
statements.why: |a||b| sin θ.

statements.s: j × k = i
statements.why: Cyclic order i → j → k → i.

statements.s: If [a b c] = 0, the three vectors are coplanar.
statements.why: Zero volume.

statements.s: a × b is parallel to a.
statements.why: It is perpendicular to both a and b.

quiz.q: i × i equals
quiz.why: i × i is the zero vector, since sin 0 = 0.

quiz.q: k × j equals
quiz.why: j × k = i, so k × j is the reverse: −i.

quiz.q: Area of the triangle with sides a = 2i and b = 3j
quiz.why: a × b = 2i × 3j = 6k, so |a × b| = 6. The triangle's area is ½ × 6 = 3.

quiz.q: [i j k] equals
quiz.why: [i j k] = i·(j × k) = i·i = 1, the volume of the unit cube.

quiz.q: If a × b = 0 for non-zero a and b, they are
quiz.why: If a × b = 0 for non-zero vectors, sin θ = 0, so they are parallel.

scenes.text: Air-traffic trainee Meenakshi studies two flight paths in 3-D space near Delhi. They aren't parallel, but do they intersect?
If not, how close do the planes come? That shortest distance is a safety number.
Vector equations of lines make the calculation systematic.

steps.title: Equations of a line
steps.body:
Through point a with direction b: **r = a + λb**.

Cartesian: (x − x₁)/l = (y − y₁)/m = (z − z₁)/n, where (l, m, n) are direction ratios.

Through two points A and B: direction b = B − A.

Angle between two lines: cos θ = |b₁·b₂|/(|b₁||b₂|).

steps.title: Relative positions
steps.body:
- **Parallel**: b₁ ∥ b₂.
- **Intersecting**: not parallel and shortest distance 0.
- **Skew**: neither parallel nor intersecting (possible only in 3-D).

**Shortest distance between skew lines**: d = |(a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂)| / |b₁ × b₂|.

Parallel lines: d = |b × (a₂ − a₁)|/|b|.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
L₁: r = (i + j) + λ(2i − j + k); L₂: r = (2i + j − k) + μ(3i − 5j + 2k).
- b₁ × b₂ = |i j k; 2 −1 1; 3 −5 2| = 3i − j − 7k; magnitude √59
- a₂ − a₁ = i − k
- (a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂) = 3 + 0 + 7 = 10
- **d = 10/√59 ≈ 1.30 units** (non-zero, so the lines are skew).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a point on the line as its direction.
- Forgetting the absolute value in the distance formula.
- Assuming non-parallel lines must intersect (true in 2-D, false in 3-D).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Find the angle between lines with direction ratios (1, 1, 0) and (0, 1, 1).

Answer: cos θ = 1/(√2·√2) = ½ ⇒ θ = 60°.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find the shortest distance between two skew lines.
items: Write each line as r = a + λb
Take the dot product (a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂)
Divide its absolute value by |b₁ × b₂|

quiz.q: Direction ratios of the line (x − 1)/2 = (y + 3)/(−1) = z/4
quiz.why: In (x − 1)/2 = (y + 3)/(−1) = z/4, the direction ratios are the denominators: (2, −1, 4).

quiz.q: Two lines in 3-D that are neither parallel nor intersecting are
quiz.why: Skew lines lie in different planes, so they never meet and are not parallel. Coplanar lines must either intersect or be parallel, which is why 'coplanar' cannot be right.

quiz.q: The line through (1, 2, 3) and (3, 5, 9) has direction
quiz.why: A direction vector of the line through A and B is B − A = (3−1, 5−2, 9−3) = (2, 3, 6). The other options are position vectors or sums, not differences of the points.

quiz.q: If the shortest distance between two non-parallel lines is 0, they
quiz.why: The shortest distance between two lines is 0 only if they share a point. Non-parallel lines with a common point intersect; skew lines always have a positive distance.

quiz.q: Lines with directions (1, 2, 2) and (2, −2, 1) are
quiz.why: Two lines are perpendicular when the dot product of their directions is 0. Here 1·2 + 2·(−2) + 2·1 = 2 − 4 + 2 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

scenes.text: Solar installer Revathi in Coimbatore mounts panels on a sloping roof. The roof is a plane; the sun's rays are lines.
She needs the angle between the panel's normal and the sun's direction, and the distance from a chimney top to the roof plane.
Equations of planes turn these into arithmetic.

steps.title: Equation of a plane
steps.body:
Normal vector n and point a: **(r − a)·n = 0**, i.e., r·n = d. Cartesian: ax + by + cz = d with normal (a, b, c).

Intercept form: x/a + y/b + z/c = 1.

Through three non-collinear points: normal n = (B − A) × (C − A).

steps.title: Angles and distances
steps.body:
- Angle between planes = angle between normals: cos θ = |n₁·n₂|/(|n₁||n₂|).
- Angle between a line (direction b) and a plane (normal n): sin φ = |b·n|/(|b||n|).
- **Distance of point (x₀, y₀, z₀) from ax + by + cz = d**: |ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ − d| / √(a² + b² + c²).
- Distance between parallel planes ax + by + cz = d₁ and ax + by + cz = d₂: |d₁ − d₂|/√(a² + b² + c²).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using cos instead of sin for the line–plane angle.
- Substituting before bringing the plane to the form ax + by + cz − d.
- Using a point on the plane as its normal.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Distance between the planes 2x + 2y − z = 3 and 2x + 2y − z = 9?

Answer: |9 − 3|/√9 = 2.

activity.prompt: Match each task with the right formula.
pairs: Distance from a point to a plane
Angle between a line and a plane

quiz.q: Normal to the plane 3x − 4y + 12z = 5
quiz.why: For a plane ax + by + cz = d, the vector (a, b, c) is a normal. So the normal here is (3, −4, 12); the sign of each coefficient must be kept.

quiz.q: Distance of the origin from 3x − 4y + 12z = 26
quiz.why: Distance from the origin = |d|/√(a²+b²+c²) = 26/√(9+16+144) = 26/√169 = 26/13 = 2.

quiz.q: The planes x + 2y + 3z = 1 and 2x + 4y + 6z = 7 are
quiz.why: The normals (1, 2, 3) and (2, 4, 6) are proportional, so the planes are parallel. They are not coincident because the second equation's constant 7 is not 2 times 1.

quiz.q: Line with direction (1, 1, 1) and the plane x + y + z = 5: angle
quiz.why: The line's direction (1, 1, 1) is the same as the plane's normal, so the line is perpendicular to the plane. sin φ = |b·n|/(|b||n|) = 1, so the angle is 90°.

quiz.q: Intercepts of 2x + 3y + 6z = 6 on the axes
quiz.why: Divide 2x + 3y + 6z = 6 by 6 to get x/3 + y/2 + z/1 = 1. The denominators are the intercepts: 3 on x, 2 on y, 1 on z.

questions.why: The magnitude is √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. Do not forget the square root, which is why 25 is wrong.

questions.q: i × j
questions.why: By the right-hand rule, i × j = k. Reversing the order gives j × i = −k, which is the tempting wrong option.
The dot product multiplies matching components and adds: 2·1 + 1·(−3) = 2 − 3 = −1.

questions.q: Unit vector along i + j + k
questions.why: A unit vector is the vector divided by its magnitude. |i + j + k| = √3, so the unit vector is (i + j + k)/√3.

questions.q: Distance of (1, 1, 1) from the plane x + y + z = 0
Area of the parallelogram with sides i + j and j + k
questions.why: The area equals the magnitude of the cross product. (i + j) × (j + k) = i − j + k, whose magnitude is √(1+1+1) = √3.

questions.q: Angle between i + j and j + k
For which λ are 2i − j + k, i + 2j − 3k and 3i + λj + 5k coplanar?
Equation of the plane through (1, 2, 3) perpendicular to (2, −1, 2)
questions.why: A plane with normal (2, −1, 2) is 2x − y + 2z = d. Putting in (1, 2, 3) gives d = 2 − 2 + 6 = 6.

questions.q: Foot of the perpendicular from the origin to x + y + z = 3
questions.why: The foot lies along the normal direction (1, 1, 1), so take (t, t, t). It must satisfy x + y + z = 3, so 3t = 3, t = 1, giving (1, 1, 1).

questions.q: If |a| = 3, |b| = 4 and |a × b| = 6, then a·b could be
questions.why: |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ gives 6 = 12 sin θ, so sin θ = 1/2. Then cos θ = ±√3/2 (θ may be 30° or 150°), so a·b = 12 cos θ = ±6√3.

questions.q: Shortest distance between r = λ(i + j + k) and r = i + μ(i + j + k)
Volume of the tetrahedron with edges a = i, b = j, c = k from one vertex
questions.why: A tetrahedron's volume is one-sixth of the scalar triple product. [i j k] = 1, so the volume is 1/6, not 1 (that is the cube's volume).

courses.title: Matrices, determinants & probability
courses.summary: Matrix algebra, determinants and inverses for solving systems, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem, and the binomial distribution — with real decisions like reading a medical test.
outcomes: Learners can multiply matrices and use transpose and symmetry properties
Learners can compute determinants and inverses and solve linear systems
Learners can apply conditional probability, total probability and Bayes' theorem
Learners can compute means, variances and binomial probabilities

scenes.text: Fatima runs two bakery outlets in Lucknow. Each day she records how many breads, cakes and cookies each outlet sells.
Multiplying her quantity table by a price list gives each outlet's revenue in one step.
That one-step multiplication is matrix multiplication—the language of spreadsheets, graphics and AI.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
An m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. Types: square, diagonal, identity I, zero, symmetric (Aᵀ = A), skew-symmetric (Aᵀ = −A; diagonal entries 0).

Addition: same order, entry by entry. Scalar multiple: multiply every entry.

Any square matrix = ½(A + Aᵀ) [symmetric] + ½(A − Aᵀ) [skew-symmetric].

steps.title: Multiplication
steps.body:
(AB)ᵢⱼ = row i of A · column j of B. Defined only if the columns of A = the rows of B; (m × n)(n × p) = m × p.
- **AB ≠ BA in general.**
- AB = 0 does not imply A = 0 or B = 0.
- (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ; (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying entry by entry (that is not matrix multiplication).
- Writing (AB)ᵀ = AᵀBᵀ.
- Expanding (A + B)² as A² + 2AB + B² (correct: A² + AB + BA + B²).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
If A = [[0, 1], [−1, 0]], find A².

Answer: [[−1, 0], [0, −1]] = −I (A rotates vectors by 90°; applying it twice rotates by 180°).

statements.s: For all square matrices, AB = BA.
statements.why: Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative.

statements.s: (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ.
statements.why: Reversal law for the transpose.

statements.s: The diagonal entries of a skew-symmetric matrix are all zero.
statements.why: aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ ⇒ 0.

statements.s: A 2 × 3 matrix can be multiplied by a 2 × 3 matrix.
statements.why: Columns of the first (3) must equal rows of the second (2).

statements.s: AB = 0 implies A = 0 or B = 0.
statements.why: Non-zero matrices can multiply to zero.

quiz.q: Order of AB if A is 3 × 2 and B is 2 × 4
quiz.why: A product of a 3 × 2 and a 2 × 4 matrix is defined because the inner numbers match (2 and 2). The result takes the outer numbers: 3 × 4.

quiz.q: A matrix with Aᵀ = A is
quiz.why: By definition, a matrix equal to its own transpose is symmetric. A skew-symmetric matrix satisfies Aᵀ = −A instead.

quiz.q: (A + B)² equals
quiz.why: (A + B)² = (A + B)(A + B) = A² + AB + BA + B². Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so AB and BA cannot be combined into 2AB.
The trace is the sum of the main-diagonal entries: 2 + (−3) = −1.

quiz.q: For a scalar k, the matrix kA is
options: A with one row multiplied by k
A with every entry multiplied by k
quiz.why: Multiplying a matrix by a scalar k multiplies every entry by k, not only one row.

scenes.text: Agronomist Harish in Nashik needs to mix three fertilisers to hit exact amounts of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
That gives three equations in three unknowns. 'Write it as AX = B,' says his colleague Dr Leena, 'then X = A⁻¹B if |A| ≠ 0.'
Determinants tell whether a unique mix even exists.

steps.title: Determinants
steps.body:
2 × 2: |a b; c d| = ad − bc. 3 × 3: expand along any row or column with signs + − +.

Example: |1 2 3; 0 1 4; 5 6 0| = 1(0 − 24) − 2(0 − 20) + 3(0 − 5) = −24 + 40 − 15 = **1**.

Properties: swapping two rows changes the sign; two identical rows ⇒ 0; |Aᵀ| = |A|; |AB| = |A||B|; |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n × n matrix.

Area of the triangle with vertices (xᵢ, yᵢ) = ½|det[[x₁, y₁, 1], [x₂, y₂, 1], [x₃, y₃, 1]]|; zero ⇒ collinear.

steps.title: Inverse
steps.body:
A⁻¹ exists iff |A| ≠ 0 (non-singular). **A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A|**, where adj A = the transpose of the cofactor matrix.

2 × 2 shortcut: [[a, b], [c, d]]⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc))[[d, −b], [−c, a]]. Example: [[2, 1], [1, 1]]⁻¹ = [[1, −1], [−1, 2]].

Useful: A·adj A = |A|I; |adj A| = |A|ⁿ⁻¹.

steps.title: Solving AX = B
steps.body:
x + y = 5, 2x − y = 1. A = [[1, 1], [2, −1]], |A| = −3 ≠ 0.

A⁻¹ = (1/−3)[[−1, −1], [−2, 1]]. X = A⁻¹B = (1/−3)[[−5 − 1], [−10 + 1]] = (1/−3)[[−6], [−9]] = [[2], [3]] ⇒ **x = 2, y = 3**.

Consistency: |A| ≠ 0 ⇒ unique solution. |A| = 0 ⇒ compute (adj A)B: if it is non-zero, there is no solution; if it is zero, the system has either infinitely many solutions or none (investigate further).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the sign pattern in cofactors.
- Forgetting to transpose the cofactor matrix to get adj A.
- Using |kA| = k|A| for a 3 × 3 matrix (it's k³|A|).
- Writing X = BA⁻¹ instead of A⁻¹B.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
If |A| = 4 for a 3 × 3 matrix, find |2A| and |adj A|.

Answer: |2A| = 8 × 4 = 32; |adj A| = 4² = 16.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to solve a 3 × 3 system by the matrix method.
items: Write the system as AX = B
Compute |A| and check it is non-zero
Transpose the cofactor matrix to get adj A
Compute X = A⁻¹B and check in the original equations

quiz.why: For a 2 × 2 determinant |a b; c d| = ad − bc. Here 3·4 − 2·1 = 12 − 2 = 10.

quiz.q: A matrix with |A| = 0 is called
quiz.why: If |A| = 0 the matrix has no inverse, and such a matrix is called singular. A non-singular matrix has a non-zero determinant.

quiz.q: If two rows of a determinant are identical, its value is
quiz.why: If two rows are identical, subtracting one from the other leaves a row of zeros without changing the value. So the determinant is 0.

quiz.q: Inverse of [[3, 0], [0, 2]]
quiz.why: The inverse of a diagonal matrix with non-zero entries has the reciprocals on the diagonal: 1/3 and 1/2. Check: 3 × 1/3 = 1 and 2 × 1/2 = 1.

quiz.q: If A is 3 × 3 with |A| = 5, then |3A| =
quiz.why: For an n × n matrix, |kA| = kⁿ|A|. Here n = 3, so |3A| = 3³ × 5 = 27 × 5 = 135.

scenes.text: Ramesh, 45, in Mysuru gets a positive result on a screening test for a rare condition that affects 1 in 100 people. He panics.
His daughter Divya, who loves probability, asks the doctor two numbers: the test catches 99% of true cases but also flags 5% of healthy people.
Using Bayes' theorem, she finds the chance he actually has the condition is only about 1 in 6—so a confirmatory test is needed, not panic.

steps.title: Conditional probability
steps.body:
**P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B)**, P(B) > 0 — the probability of A given that B has happened.

Multiplication rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(B)·P(A|B).

**Independent** events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) (equivalently P(A|B) = P(A)). Independent ≠ mutually exclusive: mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are always dependent.

steps.title: Total probability and Bayes
steps.body:
If E₁, E₂, …, Eₙ partition the sample space:
- **Total probability**: P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ)
- **Bayes' theorem**: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) / Σ P(Eⱼ)P(A|Eⱼ)

It reverses the condition: from P(test positive | disease) to P(disease | test positive).

steps.title: Divya's calculation
steps.body:
D = has the condition, + = positive test. P(D) = 0.01, P(+|D) = 0.99, P(+|not D) = 0.05.
- P(+) = 0.01 × 0.99 + 0.99 × 0.05 = 0.0099 + 0.0495 = 0.0594
- P(D|+) = 0.0099/0.0594 = **1/6 ≈ 16.7%**

Intuition with 10 000 people: 100 have it, 99 test positive; 9 900 don't, 495 test positive. Of 594 positives, only 99 are true.

steps.title: Classic: bags and balls
steps.body:
Bag I: 3 red, 4 black. Bag II: 5 red, 6 black. A bag is chosen at random and a red ball is drawn. P(Bag I | red)?

P(red) = ½·3/7 + ½·5/11 = (33 + 35)/154 = 68/154. P(I|red) = (3/14)/(68/154) = (3/14)(154/68) = 33/68.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A) (the 'prosecutor's fallacy').
- Ignoring the base rate (prior) when interpreting tests.
- Treating mutually exclusive events as independent.
- Health note: screening results should always be interpreted by a doctor; this lesson is about mathematics, not medical advice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Two dice are thrown. Given that the sum is 8, find the probability that one die shows 3.

Answer: sum-8 outcomes are (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) — 5 outcomes; 2 contain a 3 ⇒ 2/5.

a.text: Ramesh's test is positive. The condition affects 1% of people; the test has 99% sensitivity and a 5% false-positive rate. What does Divya say first?

choices.label: 'You almost certainly have it—99% accurate!'
choices.feedback: That confuses P(+|D) with P(D|+).

choices.label: 'Let's use the base rate: what fraction of positives are true?'
choices.feedback: Exactly the Bayesian question.

b.text: The doctor gently asks: of 10 000 people, how many positives are true? Recalculate?

choices.label: Yes, count it out
choices.feedback: Good.

c.text: Out of 10 000: 99 true positives and 495 false positives. P(D|+) ≈ ?

choices.label: About 95%
choices.feedback: That ignores the 495 false positives.

e.text: Recount: 99 true positives among 594 positives. So?

choices.label: About 17%
choices.feedback: Yes.

choices.label: Take the confirmatory test the doctor advises
choices.feedback: Right: a second, independent test sharply changes the probability.

choices.label: Ignore it completely
choices.feedback: 17% is still far above the 1% base rate—follow up.

g.text: The doctor explains that 17% is still important. Reconsider?

choices.label: Book the confirmatory test
choices.feedback: Wise.

f.text: Calm and correct: Bayes' theorem turns panic into a plan. (If a second independent test is also positive, recompute with 17% as the new prior.)

quiz.why: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5. Dividing by P(A) instead would give 0.4, which is P(B|A).

quiz.q: If A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5, P(A ∩ B) =
quiz.why: For independent events P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15. Adding would give 0.8, which is wrong.

quiz.q: Mutually exclusive events with P(A), P(B) > 0 are
quiz.why: If A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A ∩ B) = 0. But independence needs P(A)P(B) > 0, so they are not independent; they are dependent.

quiz.q: A family has two children and at least one is a boy. P(both boys) =
quiz.why: With at least one boy, the equally likely cases are BB, BG and GB. Only one of these three is both boys, so the probability is 1/3, not 1/2.

quiz.q: Bayes' theorem computes
quiz.why: Bayes' theorem reverses conditioning. It finds the probability of a cause given an observed effect using prior probabilities and likelihoods.

lessons.title: Random variables and the binomial distribution

scenes.text: Neha, captain of her school basketball team in Shillong, makes 70% of her free throws. In a match she takes 5.
Coach Lyngdoh asks: what's the chance she makes at least 4? And how many should we expect on average?
The binomial distribution answers both.

steps.title: Random variables
steps.body:
A random variable X assigns numbers to outcomes. A probability distribution lists values xᵢ with P(xᵢ) ≥ 0 and ΣP = 1.
- **Mean** E(X) = Σ xᵢpᵢ
- **Variance** Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]²; SD = √Var

Example: a fair die: E(X) = 3.5, E(X²) = 91/6, Var = 91/6 − 12.25 = 35/12.

steps.title: Bernoulli trials and the binomial
steps.body:
Conditions: a fixed number n of independent trials, each a success with the same probability p (q = 1 − p).

**P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ**, r = 0, 1, …, n. **Mean = np, variance = npq.**

steps.title: Coins
steps.body: 10 fair coins. P(exactly 6 heads) = ¹⁰C₆/2¹⁰ = 210/1024 ≈ 0.205. P(at least one head) = 1 − (½)¹⁰ = 1023/1024. Use the complement for 'at least one'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the binomial when trials are not independent (drawing cards without replacement).
- Forgetting the ⁿCᵣ factor.
- Adding standard deviations instead of variances.
- Computing 'at least one' directly instead of 1 − P(none).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A binomial variable has mean 4 and variance 3. Find n and p.

Answer: q = 3/4 ⇒ p = 1/4 ⇒ n = 16.

activity.prompt: Complete the binomial facts.
activity.text: For a binomial distribution the mean is ___ and the variance is ___. The probabilities of all values must add up to ___.

quiz.q: Mean of B(20, 0.25)
quiz.why: The mean of a binomial distribution B(n, p) is np = 20 × 0.25 = 5.

quiz.q: Variance of B(20, 0.25)
quiz.why: The variance of B(n, p) is npq. With q = 0.75 this is 20 × 0.25 × 0.75 = 3.75. The value 5 is the mean, not the variance.

quiz.q: P(no six in 3 throws of a fair die)
quiz.why: Each throw has probability 5/6 of not showing a six. The throws are independent, so the probability is (5/6)³ = 125/216.

quiz.q: Which is NOT binomial?
options: Number of aces in 5 cards drawn without replacement
Number of correct guesses on 10 true/false questions
Number of defectives among 20 independent items with a fixed defect rate
quiz.why: Binomial trials must be independent with a fixed probability. Drawing cards without replacement changes the chance of an ace each time, so it is not binomial.

quiz.q: If P(X = 0) for B(n, ½) is 1/32, then n =

questions.q: Order of the product of a 2 × 3 and a 3 × 1 matrix
questions.why: For a (2 × 3) times a (3 × 1) matrix, the inner 3s match and the result is 2 × 1 (outer numbers).

questions.q: Probability of a head on a fair coin
questions.why: A fair coin has two equally likely outcomes, and one of them is a head, so the probability is 1/2.
The determinant is ad − bc = 1·4 − 2·3 = 4 − 6 = −2.
By the multiplication rule P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B|A) = 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3.

questions.q: If A is skew-symmetric of order 3, |A| =
questions.why: For a skew-symmetric matrix Aᵀ = −A. So |A| = |Aᵀ| = |−A| = (−1)³|A| = −|A| for order 3, which forces |A| = 0.

questions.q: A die is rolled twice. P(sum = 7)
questions.why: There are 36 equally likely outcomes. The sum 7 comes from (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1): 6 outcomes, so 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.q: Mean number of heads in 6 tosses of a fair coin
questions.why: The mean of a binomial distribution is np = 6 × 1/2 = 3.

questions.q: If A² = A (idempotent), then (I + A)² equals
questions.why: Expand (I + A)² = I + 2A + A². Since A² = A, this becomes I + 2A + A = I + 3A.

questions.q: Bag A: 2 white, 3 black; Bag B: 4 white, 1 black. A bag is picked at random and a white ball drawn. P(it came from B)
questions.why: By Bayes' theorem, P(B | white) = (½·4/5)/(½·2/5 + ½·4/5) = (2/5)/(3/5) = 2/3. Bag B has more white balls, so it is more likely.

questions.q: For which k does the system x + y = 2, 2x + 2y = k have infinitely many solutions?
questions.why: The system has infinitely many solutions when both equations are the same line. The second equation 2x + 2y = k is twice the first only when k = 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.q: If |A| = 3 for a 3 × 3 matrix A, |adj(adj A)| equals
questions.why: For an n × n matrix |adj A| = |A|ⁿ⁻¹. For n = 3, |adj A| = 3² = 9, and |adj(adj A)| = 9² = 81.

questions.q: Probability that at least one of two independent events with probabilities 0.3 and 0.4 occurs
questions.why: P(at least one) = 1 − P(neither). For independent events, P(neither) = 0.7 × 0.6 = 0.42, so the answer is 1 − 0.42 = 0.58. Adding 0.3 + 0.4 ignores the overlap.

questions.q: A biased coin with P(head) = p is tossed 4 times and P(exactly 2 heads) = P(exactly 3 heads). Then p =
questions.why: Equate C(4,2)p²q² and C(4,3)p³q: 6p²q² = 4p³q, so 6q = 4p. With q = 1 − p, 6 − 6p = 4p, so p = 3/5.

school-senior-physics.title: Senior Physics (Class 11–12)
school-senior-physics.description: Pathshala Senior physics: mechanics, rotation, thermodynamics, electricity, magnetism, optics and modern physics with full derivations, worked numericals and exam-style practice.

courses.title: Mechanics I: motion, forces & circles
courses.summary: Kinematics in 1-D and 2-D, Newton's laws with free-body diagrams, friction and circular motion — every formula derived, every idea used in worked numericals.
outcomes: Learners can derive and apply the equations of motion for constant acceleration
Learners can solve projectile problems including horizontal launches
Learners can draw free-body diagrams and apply ΣF = ma to connected bodies
Learners can solve friction, banked-road and vertical-circle problems

scenes.text: Aarav, 16, stands near the driver's cabin of a Delhi Metro train. He starts a stopwatch as the train leaves Rajiv Chowk.
The train speeds up smoothly for 25 s, cruises, then brakes into the next station. He wonders: how far did we go while speeding up?
His teacher Ms Kapoor says: 'Draw the velocity–time graph. The area under it is the displacement. Everything else follows.'

steps.title: Words that must be precise
steps.body:
- **Distance**: total path length (scalar, never negative).
- **Displacement**: straight-line change in position with direction (vector). Walk 3 m east then 3 m west: distance 6 m, displacement 0.
- **Velocity** v = dx/dt (vector); **speed** = |v|.
- **Acceleration** a = dv/dt. Negative acceleration only means 'opposite to the positive direction you chose', not always 'slowing down'.

Always choose a positive direction first and stick to it for every quantity.

steps.title: Derivation for constant acceleration
steps.body:
If a is constant, a = (v − u)/t, so **v = u + at** … (1)

Displacement = area under the v–t graph = rectangle (u·t) + triangle (½·(v − u)·t) = ut + ½(at)t, so **s = ut + ½at²** … (2)

Eliminate t using t = (v − u)/a in s = (u + v)t/2: s = (v² − u²)/2a, so **v² = u² + 2as** … (3)

Distance in the nth second: sₙ = u + a(2n − 1)/2 (difference of s at t = n and t = n − 1).

These hold ONLY when acceleration is constant. If a changes with time, integrate: v = u + ∫a dt, x = x₀ + ∫v dt.

steps.title: Worked example: braking distance
steps.body:
A car moves at 72 km/h and brakes with a deceleration of 5 m/s². Find stopping time and distance.

- Convert: 72 km/h = 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s. Take motion direction positive, so a = −5 m/s², final v = 0.
- Time: 0 = 20 − 5t ⇒ t = 4 s.
- Distance: 0 = 20² − 2·5·s ⇒ s = 400/10 = 40 m.

Note: stopping distance ∝ u². Double the speed (144 km/h) and the braking distance becomes 4 × 40 = 160 m. This is why speed limits matter.

steps.title: Worked example: free fall
steps.body:
A stone is dropped from a 45 m tall building (take g = 10 m/s², downward positive, u = 0).

- Time: 45 = ½·10·t² ⇒ t² = 9 ⇒ t = 3 s.
- Speed on impact: v = 0 + 10·3 = 30 m/s.
- Distance in the 3rd second: s₃ = 0 + 10(2·3 − 1)/2 = 25 m (check: 45 − 20 = 25 ✔).

Thrown **up** at u: max height H = u²/2g, time to top u/g, total flight time 2u/g (same level), and it returns with the same speed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing km/h with m/s (multiply km/h by 5/18).
- Taking g as +10 when you chose upward as positive (it must be −10).
- Using v = u + at when acceleration is not constant.
- Reporting distance when the question asks displacement (or vice versa) after the body reverses direction.
- On a v–t graph, area **below** the time axis is negative displacement but positive distance.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A ball is thrown vertically up at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Find (a) maximum height, (b) time to return, (c) displacement after 3 s.

Answers: (a) 20²/(2·10) = 20 m; (b) 2·20/10 = 4 s; (c) s = 20·3 − 5·9 = 15 m above the launch point (it is on its way down).

activity.prompt: Aarav's train starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 0.5 m/s² for 40 s. How far (in metres) does it travel in that time?

quiz.q: A body starts from rest with a = 2 m/s². Distance covered in the 5th second?
quiz.why: Distance in the nth second is sₙ = u + a(2n−1)/2. With u = 0, a = 2, n = 5: 2 × 9/2 = 9 m. The 25 m option is the distance in 5 seconds, not in the 5th second.

quiz.q: On a velocity–time graph, the slope gives…
quiz.why: On a velocity–time graph, slope = Δv/Δt, which is acceleration. The area under the graph gives displacement.

quiz.q: A car's speed doubles. Its braking distance (same deceleration) becomes…
quiz.why: With the same deceleration, s = u²/2a, so braking distance is proportional to speed squared. Doubling the speed makes it 2² = 4 times as long.

quiz.q: A ball thrown up returns to the thrower after 6 s. Its initial speed was (g = 10 m/s²)
quiz.why: The ball takes equal time up and down, so total time is 2u/g. Then 6 = 2u/10 gives u = 30 m/s.

quiz.q: Velocity of a ball at the highest point of a vertical throw is…
quiz.why: At the top the velocity is momentarily zero as the ball reverses direction. Gravity still acts, so the acceleration is g downward, not zero.

lessons.title: Projectile motion: two motions at once

scenes.text: At a club match in Kolkata, Priya fields the ball at the boundary and throws it towards the keeper, 35 m away.
Her coach shouts, 'Throw flatter!' Her friend Lucas, visiting from Berlin where he does shot put, says, 'No—45° gives maximum range!'
Who is right? Both, partly. Physics tells us exactly when, and why a real throw differs from the ideal.

steps.title: The big idea: independence
steps.body:
Ignoring air resistance, gravity acts only vertically. So:
- **Horizontal**: constant velocity uₓ = u cos θ (aₓ = 0).
- **Vertical**: uniformly accelerated, u_y = u sin θ, a_y = −g.

Treat them as two separate 1-D problems joined by the same time t.

steps.title: Derivations (launch and landing at same height)
steps.body:
x = (u cos θ)t, y = (u sin θ)t − ½gt²

- **Time of flight**: y = 0 ⇒ T = 2u sin θ / g
- **Maximum height**: v_y = 0 ⇒ H = u² sin²θ / 2g
- **Range**: R = uₓ·T = u² sin 2θ / g, maximum u²/g at θ = 45°
- **Trajectory**: eliminate t ⇒ y = x tan θ − g x² / (2u² cos²θ), a parabola.

Angles θ and (90° − θ) give the same range (sin 2θ is the same), but different heights and times.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
u = 20 m/s at θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s².
- T = 2·20·0.5/10 = 2 s
- H = 400·0.25/20 = 5 m
- R = 400·sin 60°/10 = 40 × 0.866 ≈ 34.6 m
- Speed at the top = u cos θ = 20 × 0.866 ≈ 17.3 m/s (not zero!).

So Priya's 35 m throw at 20 m/s needs about 30° (or 60°). The flatter 30° throw arrives in 2 s; the 60° throw takes about 3.5 s. That is why her coach wants it flat.

steps.title: Horizontal launch from a height
steps.body:
A ball rolls off an 80 m cliff at 15 m/s horizontally (g = 10).
- Vertical: 80 = ½·10·t² ⇒ t = 4 s (same as if dropped!).
- Horizontal distance: 15 × 4 = 60 m.
- Impact velocity: vₓ = 15, v_y = 40 ⇒ v = √(225 + 1600) ≈ 42.7 m/s at tan⁻¹(40/15) ≈ 69° below horizontal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using R = u² sin 2θ/g when launch and landing heights differ (e.g., a shot put released at 2 m height—optimal angle is then a little below 45°).
- Saying velocity is zero at the top. Only the vertical component is.
- Forgetting that real air drag reduces range and makes the path asymmetric.
- Mixing degree and radian mode on your calculator.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Two balls are fired with the same speed at 15° and 75°. Which lands farther? Which stays in the air longer?

Answer: same range (sin 30° = sin 150°); the 75° ball stays longer because T ∝ sin θ.

activity.label: Launch angle θ (same speed, level ground)

bands.text: Very flat: short flight time, short range (R ∝ sin 2θ is small).
Flat-ish: range rising fast. Fielders' throws live here—quick arrival.
Near 45°: maximum range u²/g on level ground (no air).
Steep: same range as its complement (90° − θ) but higher and slower.
Nearly vertical: huge height, tiny range. At 90° the ball comes straight back.

quiz.q: At the highest point of a projectile, acceleration is…
quiz.why: Only gravity acts on a projectile, so its acceleration is g downward throughout, including at the top. Only the vertical velocity is zero there.

quiz.q: Range is maximum for θ = ? (level ground, no air)
quiz.why: R = u² sin 2θ/g is largest when sin 2θ = 1, so 2θ = 90° and θ = 45°. A 90° throw goes straight up and has zero range.

quiz.q: A ball is thrown horizontally from a table and another is dropped at the same instant. Which lands first?
quiz.why: Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration g, from the same height. So they take the same time to fall and land together; the horizontal motion does not matter.

quiz.q: For u = 10 m/s at 60°, maximum height (g = 10) is
The trajectory of a projectile (no air) is a
quiz.why: Eliminating time gives y = x tan θ − gx²/(2u² cos²θ), which is quadratic in x. A quadratic relation graphs as a parabola.

scenes.text: In a Pune supermarket, Sneha pushes a loaded trolley. It refuses to move at first, then suddenly rolls.
Later, in the lift, she stands on a weighing scale (an experiment for her school project). It reads 72 kg as the lift starts up—but she weighs 60 kg!
Her elder brother draws boxes and arrows: 'Every problem is just a free-body diagram and ΣF = ma.'

steps.title: The three laws, properly
steps.body:
- **First law (inertia)**: a body stays at rest or uniform velocity unless a net external force acts. It defines **inertial frames** (non-accelerating).
- **Second law**: F_net = dp/dt; for constant mass, **F_net = ma**. Vector law—apply along each axis.
- **Third law**: forces come in pairs, equal and opposite, **acting on different bodies** and of the same type (e.g., both gravitational, both contact).

Impulse = F·Δt = Δp. That is why airbags and bending your knees when landing reduce force: they increase Δt.

steps.title: The free-body diagram (FBD) method
steps.body:
1. Isolate one body. Draw it as a dot or box.
2. Draw every force ON it: weight mg (down), normal N (perpendicular to surface), tension T (along string, away from body), friction f (along surface), applied forces.
3. Choose axes (along and perpendicular to motion/incline).
4. Write ΣF = ma along each axis.
5. Add constraint equations (same string ⇒ same acceleration magnitude).
6. Solve; check units and limiting cases.

steps.title: Atwood machine
steps.body:
Masses m₁ = 3 kg and m₂ = 2 kg hang over a light frictionless pulley (g = 10).
- m₁: m₁g − T = m₁a; m₂: T − m₂g = m₂a.
- Add: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) = 10/5 = 2 m/s².
- T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 2·3·2·10/5 = 24 N.

Check: if m₁ = m₂, a = 0 and T = mg ✔.

steps.title: Sneha's lift and the smooth incline
steps.body:
**Lift**: the scale reads the normal force N. Lift accelerating up at a: N − mg = ma ⇒ N = m(g + a). For 60 kg, a = 2 m/s²: N = 720 N, so the scale (calibrated in kg with g = 10) shows 72 kg. Accelerating down: N = m(g − a). Free fall: N = 0 (weightlessness).

**Smooth incline** of angle θ: along the plane mg sin θ = ma ⇒ a = g sin θ; perpendicular N = mg cos θ.
