steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Action and reaction cancel.' They never cancel because they act on different bodies.
- Writing 'ma' as an extra force on the FBD (in an inertial frame it is the result, not a force).
- Assuming N = mg always. On inclines, in lifts, or with vertical pushes it is different.
- Forgetting that a massless string has the same tension throughout (only if the pulley is light and frictionless).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A 5 kg block is pulled on a smooth floor by a 20 N force at 37° above horizontal (cos 37° = 0.8, sin 37° = 0.6, g = 10). Find a and N.

Answers: a = 20·0.8/5 = 3.2 m/s²; N = 50 − 20·0.6 = 38 N.

activity.prompt: Put the free-body-diagram method in the correct order.
items: Draw every force acting ON that body
Write ΣF = ma along each axis

quiz.q: A horse pulls a cart. Why does the system move if the cart pulls back equally on the horse?
options: Pair forces act on different bodies; ground friction on the horse's hooves gives a net external force
quiz.why: Third-law pairs act on different bodies; motion depends on net external force on the system.

quiz.q: A 50 kg person in a lift accelerating down at 2 m/s² (g = 10) has apparent weight
quiz.why: In a lift accelerating downward, the normal force (apparent weight) is N = m(g − a) = 50 × (10 − 2) = 400 N. It is less than the true weight of 500 N.

quiz.q: Block on a smooth 30° incline (g = 10). Acceleration?
quiz.why: On a smooth incline only the component of gravity along the slope accelerates the block: a = g sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s².

quiz.q: Masses 4 kg and 1 kg in an Atwood machine (g = 10). Acceleration?
quiz.why: In an Atwood machine, a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) = (4 − 1) × 10/5 = 6 m/s².

quiz.q: Catching a fast ball by pulling hands back reduces force because
quiz.why: Force = change in momentum ÷ time of impact. Pulling the hands back lengthens the time, so the same momentum change needs a smaller force. The momentum change itself stays the same.

scenes.text: Rohan rides his scooter onto a curved flyover in Mumbai after rain. He feels the bike wanting to slide outward.
Engineer Farah explains that the road is banked—tilted inward—so part of the normal force provides the centripetal force.
'Wet roads lower friction,' she adds. 'That changes your safe speed. Let's calculate it.'

steps.title: Friction laws
steps.body:
- **Static friction** adjusts itself up to a maximum: f_s ≤ μ_s N. It opposes the *tendency* of relative motion.
- **Kinetic friction**: f_k = μ_k N, usually μ_k < μ_s (that's why the trolley 'jumps' once it starts).
- Friction is (approximately) independent of contact area.
- **Angle of repose**: a block just starts sliding on an incline when tan θ = μ_s.
- On a rough incline sliding down: a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ).

steps.title: Circular motion basics
steps.body:
Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing direction, so there is acceleration towards the centre: **a_c = v²/r = ω²r**. Net inward force needed: **F_c = mv²/r**.

'Centripetal force' is not a new force—it is the name for whatever net force points inward: friction (car on a flat road), tension (stone on a string), gravity (satellite), normal-force components (banked road).

steps.title: Flat and banked roads
steps.body:
**Flat road**: friction provides mv²/r ≤ μmg ⇒ **v_max = √(μrg)**. r = 50 m, μ = 0.4, g = 10: v_max = √200 ≈ 14.1 m/s ≈ 51 km/h.

**Banked, frictionless**: N sin θ = mv²/r, N cos θ = mg ⇒ **tan θ = v²/(rg)**. For v = 20 m/s, r = 100 m: tan θ = 0.4 ⇒ θ ≈ 21.8°.

**Banked with friction**: v_max = √[rg(μ + tan θ)/(1 − μ tan θ)].

steps.title: Vertical circle (string or loop)
steps.body:
A stone of mass m on a string of length r in a vertical circle:
- At the top: T + mg = mv²/r. Minimum speed (T = 0): **v_top = √(gr)**.
- Using energy conservation, minimum speed at the bottom: **v_bottom = √(5gr)**.
- Tension at the bottom in that case: T = mg + mv²/r = 6mg.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding 'centrifugal force' while working in the ground (inertial) frame. Use it only if you deliberately work in the rotating frame.
- Writing friction = μN when the body is not sliding—static friction may be less than its maximum.
- Saying friction always opposes motion. When you walk, friction on your foot points **forward**.
- Using diameter instead of radius.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A coin placed 10 cm from the centre of a turntable just starts slipping at ω = 5 rad/s (g = 10). Find μ_s.

Answer: μg = ω²r ⇒ μ = 25 × 0.1/10 = 0.25.

statements.s: Static friction always equals μ_s N.
statements.why: It is self-adjusting up to μ_s N; it equals μ_s N only at the point of slipping.

statements.s: Centripetal force is a separate force that appears in circular motion.
statements.why: It is the net inward resultant of real forces like friction, tension or gravity.

statements.s: Safe speed on a flat curve does not depend on the vehicle's mass.
statements.why: v_max = √(μrg): mass cancels.

statements.s: Minimum speed at the top of a vertical circle on a string is √(gr).
statements.why: At the limit T = 0, so mg = mv²/r.

statements.s: When you walk, friction on your shoe points backward.
statements.why: Your foot pushes the ground backward; ground friction pushes you forward.

quiz.q: A block just starts to slide on an incline of 30°. μ_s is
quiz.why: A block just starts to slide when friction is at its limit: μ_s = tan θ. So μ_s = tan 30° ≈ 0.577 ≈ 0.58.

quiz.q: A car takes a flat curve of radius 40 m with μ = 0.25 (g = 10). Maximum speed
quiz.why: On a flat curve, friction provides the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r. So v = √(μ r g) = √(0.25 × 40 × 10) = √100 = 10 m/s.

quiz.q: Centripetal acceleration of a body at 6 m/s on a 3 m radius circle
quiz.why: Centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r = 6²/3 = 36/3 = 12 m/s². Dividing by 2r or forgetting to divide gives the wrong values.

quiz.q: Roads are banked so that
options: a component of the normal force provides centripetal force
quiz.why: On a banked road the normal force is tilted, so its horizontal component N sin θ supplies the centripetal force. This reduces the need for friction at the design speed.

quiz.q: Minimum speed at the lowest point for a stone on a string to complete a vertical circle of radius r
quiz.why: At the top, the minimum speed is √(gr) (tension just zero). Energy conservation over a height of 2r gives v² = gr + 4gr = 5gr at the bottom, so v = √(5gr).

questions.q: Which quantity can be zero while the other is non-zero?
questions.why: Displacement is the straight-line change in position, while distance is the path length. A round trip returns to the start, so displacement is zero but distance is positive.

questions.q: Unit conversion: 54 km/h equals
questions.why: To convert km/h to m/s multiply by 5/18. So 54 × 5/18 = 15 m/s.

questions.q: A body starts from rest with a = 4 m/s². Velocity after 5 s?
questions.why: Using v = u + at with u = 0: v = 4 × 5 = 20 m/s.

questions.q: Newton's third-law pair forces
questions.why: Newton's third-law pairs are equal and opposite, and they act on different bodies. Because they act on different bodies they do not cancel each other.

questions.q: Projectiles at 60° and 30° with the same speed. Ratio of maximum heights H₆₀ : H₃₀
questions.why: Maximum height H = u² sin²θ/2g, so H ∝ sin²θ. sin²60° = 3/4 and sin²30° = 1/4, so the ratio is 3 : 1.

questions.q: A 2 kg block on a rough floor (μ_k = 0.3, g = 10) is pulled by 10 N horizontally. Acceleration
questions.why: Friction = μmg = 0.3 × 2 × 10 = 6 N. Net force = 10 − 6 = 4 N, so a = 4/2 = 2 m/s².

questions.q: A stone dropped from rest travels distances in successive equal seconds in the ratio
questions.why: For a body starting from rest, distances in successive equal seconds are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5, from sₙ ∝ (2n − 1). The ratio 1 : 4 : 9 is for total distances.

questions.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from a height of 20 m (g = 10). Horizontal distance travelled
questions.why: The fall time is t = √(2h/g) = √(2 × 20/10) = 2 s. Horizontal speed stays 10 m/s, so x = 10 × 2 = 20 m.

questions.q: Banked road: radius 90 m, design speed 30 m/s, no friction (g = 10). tan θ =
questions.why: With no friction, tan θ = v²/(rg) = 900/(90 × 10) = 1, so the banking angle is 45°.

questions.q: Blocks of 2 kg and 3 kg in contact on a smooth floor; 10 N pushes the 2 kg block. Contact force between them
questions.why: Both blocks accelerate together: a = 10/(2 + 3) = 2 m/s². The contact force is the only force on the 3 kg block, so it is 3 × 2 = 6 N.

questions.q: x(t) = 3t² − 2t (SI). Acceleration at t = 2 s
questions.why: Differentiate x = 3t² − 2t to get v = 6t − 2, and again to get a = 6 m/s². It is constant, so it is 6 at t = 2 s too.

questions.q: A particle of mass m is projected with speed u at angle θ. Change in momentum between launch and landing (same level)
questions.why: The horizontal momentum is unchanged, but the vertical component goes from +mu sin θ to −mu sin θ. The change is 2mu sin θ downward.

questions.q: A block slides down a rough incline (θ = 37°, μ_k = 0.5, g = 10, sin 37° = 0.6). Acceleration
questions.why: Along the slope a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ). With cos 37° = 0.8: 10 × (0.6 − 0.5 × 0.8) = 10 × 0.2 = 2 m/s².

questions.q: A bob on a 1 m string just completes a vertical circle (g = 10). Ratio of tension at the bottom to weight
questions.why: To just complete the circle, v² at the bottom is 5gr. At the bottom T − mg = mv²/r = 5mg, so T = 6mg, giving a ratio of 6.

courses.title: Mechanics II & heat: rotation and thermodynamics
courses.summary: Torque, moment of inertia, angular momentum and rolling; then the first and second laws of thermodynamics with engines and refrigerators — derived and practised.
outcomes: Learners can compute torque and moments of inertia using parallel/perpendicular axis theorems
Learners can apply conservation of angular momentum and rolling energy
Learners can analyse isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isochoric processes
Learners can compute Carnot efficiency and refrigerator COP

scenes.text: Kavya, in Class 11 in Jaipur, tries to open the heavy wooden door of her grandmother's haveli by pushing near the hinges. It barely moves.
She pushes at the handle instead—same effort, and the door swings easily.
Her grandmother laughs: 'The carpenter knew physics. Distance from the hinge matters.' Kavya decides to find out exactly how much.

steps.title: Torque: the turning effect
steps.body:
**Torque τ = r × F**, magnitude τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the axis to the point of application and θ the angle between r and F. Unit N·m.

Equivalent: τ = F × (perpendicular distance from axis to the line of force) — the 'lever arm'.

Push at the handle (r = 0.9 m) instead of near the hinge (r = 0.1 m): nine times the torque for the same force.

Rotational analogue of Newton's second law: **τ_net = Iα** (α = angular acceleration).

steps.title: Moment of inertia I
steps.body:
I = Σ mᵢrᵢ² (or ∫r² dm). It measures how mass is distributed about the axis, not just how much there is.

Standard results (mass M, radius R, length L):
- Ring about its axis: MR²
- Disc / solid cylinder about its axis: ½MR²
- Solid sphere about a diameter: (2/5)MR²
- Thin hollow sphere: (2/3)MR²
- Thin rod about its centre (perpendicular): ML²/12; about one end: ML²/3

Radius of gyration k: I = Mk².

steps.title: Two theorems
steps.body:
- **Parallel axis**: I = I_cm + Md² (d = distance between the parallel axes). Rod about its end: ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3 ✔.
- **Perpendicular axis** (flat laminas only): I_z = I_x + I_y. For a disc, I about a diameter = ½ × ½MR² = ¼MR².

steps.title: Worked example: pulling a string on a disc
steps.body:
A disc (M = 2 kg, R = 0.5 m) pivoted at its centre has a string wound on its rim, pulled with F = 10 N.
- I = ½ × 2 × 0.25 = 0.25 kg·m²
- τ = FR = 10 × 0.5 = 5 N·m
- α = τ/I = 20 rad/s²
- After 2 s from rest: ω = αt = 40 rad/s; angle θ = ½αt² = 40 rad.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the length of r instead of the perpendicular lever arm.
- Applying the perpendicular axis theorem to 3-D bodies (it is only for planar laminas).
- Forgetting that I depends on the axis—'the moment of inertia of a rod' has no meaning without an axis.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Find I of a ring (M, R) about a tangent in its plane.

Answer: about a diameter = ½MR² (perpendicular-axis theorem); parallel shift by R: ½MR² + MR² = (3/2)MR².

activity.prompt: Match each body (about the stated axis) with its moment of inertia.

quiz.q: Torque of a 20 N force applied 0.5 m from the axis at 30° to the radius
quiz.why: Torque τ = rF sin θ = 0.5 × 20 × sin 30° = 0.5 × 20 × 0.5 = 5 N·m. Using the full 20 N would ignore the angle.

quiz.q: For the same mass and radius, which has the largest moment of inertia about its axis?
quiz.why: For equal mass and radius, a ring has all its mass at distance R, so its I = MR² is the largest. Solid shapes have mass closer to the axis, so their I is smaller.

quiz.q: I of a disc about a diameter is
quiz.why: For a disc, I about the central perpendicular axis is ½MR². By the perpendicular-axis theorem, the two diameters share it equally, so each gives ¼MR².

quiz.q: A torque of 4 N·m acts on a body with I = 2 kg·m². α =
quiz.why: Angular acceleration α = τ/I = 4/2 = 2 rad/s².

quiz.q: The parallel-axis theorem needs one axis to pass through
quiz.why: The parallel-axis theorem I = I_cm + Md² only works when I_cm is about an axis through the centre of mass. The new axis must be parallel to it, a distance d away.

scenes.text: Ananya practises figure skating at an indoor rink in Gurugram. When she pulls her arms in, she spins much faster.
Her friend Yuki, on a video call from Sapporo, races a ball and a ring down a slope for a science fair. The ball wins every time.
Same slope, same mass. Why do shape and arm position matter? Angular momentum and rotational energy answer both.

steps.title: Angular momentum and its conservation
steps.body:
For a rigid body about a fixed axis, **L = Iω**. In general L = r × p, and τ_ext = dL/dt.

If the net external torque is zero, **L is conserved**: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂.

Ananya: arms out I₁ = 4 kg·m², ω₁ = 2 rad/s. Arms in I₂ = 1.6 kg·m² ⇒ ω₂ = 4 × 2/1.6 = 5 rad/s.

Note her kinetic energy rises: ½·4·4 = 8 J → ½·1.6·25 = 20 J. The extra comes from the work her muscles do pulling her arms in.

steps.title: Rolling without slipping
steps.body:
Condition: **v_cm = ωR** (the contact point is momentarily at rest).

Kinetic energy = translational + rotational = ½Mv² + ½Iω² = ½Mv²(1 + k²/R²).

Rolling down an incline of height h from rest: Mgh = ½Mv²(1 + k²/R²) ⇒ v = √[2gh/(1 + k²/R²)], and acceleration **a = g sin θ/(1 + k²/R²)**.

steps.title: The race down the slope
steps.body:
k²/R² values: solid sphere 2/5, disc 1/2, hollow sphere 2/3, ring 1.
- Solid sphere: a = (5/7) g sin θ
- Disc: a = (2/3) g sin θ
- Hollow sphere: a = (3/5) g sin θ
- Ring: a = (1/2) g sin θ

The solid sphere wins because less of its energy goes into rotation. Mass and radius do not matter—only shape (k/R).

steps.title: Energy split
steps.body:
A solid cylinder (disc) rolls at v. Translational KE = ½Mv²; rotational KE = ½ × ½MR² × (v/R)² = ¼Mv². So translational : rotational = 2 : 1, total = ¾Mv².

For a ring the split is 1 : 1; for a solid sphere 5 : 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using conservation of angular momentum when an external torque acts (e.g., friction from an axle).
- Assuming kinetic energy is conserved when L is conserved—it usually isn't.
- Forgetting rotational KE in rolling problems (then everything 'arrives' at √(2gh)).
- Applying v = ωR when the body slips.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A disc rolls down a 1.5 m high ramp from rest (g = 10). Find its speed at the bottom.

Answer: v = √[2gh/(1 + ½)] = √(30/1.5) = √20 ≈ 4.47 m/s.

activity.prompt: Same mass and radius, released together on the same incline, rolling without slipping. Order them from FIRST to reach the bottom to LAST.

quiz.q: A skater halves her moment of inertia. Her angular speed
quiz.why: With no external torque, angular momentum Iω is constant. If I halves, ω must double.

quiz.q: Condition for rolling without slipping
quiz.why: In rolling without slipping the contact point is momentarily at rest. This means the centre's speed equals the rim speed relative to the centre: v = ωR.

quiz.q: Fraction of total KE that is rotational for a rolling ring
quiz.why: For a ring I = MR², so rotational KE = ½Iω² = ½Mv², equal to translational KE. So the rotational part is half of the total.

quiz.q: A solid sphere rolls down a 30° incline. Acceleration (g = 10)
quiz.why: For a solid sphere rolling, a = g sin θ/(1 + 2/5) = (5/7) g sin θ = (5/7) × 10 × 0.5 ≈ 3.57 m/s². This is less than the frictionless 5 m/s² because some energy goes into rotation.

quiz.q: Angular momentum of a system is conserved when
quiz.why: τ_ext = dL/dt, so if the net external torque is zero, L stays constant. Zero net force or no friction does not guarantee this.

scenes.text: In her Chennai kitchen, Lakshmi's pressure cooker whistles. Her son Karthik asks where the energy from the flame goes.
Earlier he noticed his bicycle pump getting warm when he pumped hard. 'Is that the same physics?'
Yes—both are about how heat, work and internal energy trade with each other. That bookkeeping is the first law.

steps.title: The law and sign convention
steps.body:
**Q = ΔU + W**, where Q = heat given TO the system, W = work done BY the system, ΔU = change in internal energy. (Some books write ΔU = Q + W_on; same physics, different sign of W.)

Work by a gas: W = ∫P dV (area under the P–V curve). Expansion: W > 0; compression: W < 0.

For an ideal gas, U depends only on temperature: **ΔU = nC_vΔT** for ANY process.

Molar heats: C_p − C_v = R (Mayer's relation), γ = C_p/C_v. Monatomic: C_v = 3R/2, γ = 5/3. Diatomic (room temperature): C_v = 5R/2, γ = 7/5.

steps.title: The four standard processes
steps.body:
- **Isochoric** (V const): W = 0, Q = ΔU = nC_vΔT.
- **Isobaric** (P const): W = PΔV = nRΔT, Q = nC_pΔT.
- **Isothermal** (T const): ΔU = 0, Q = W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁).
- **Adiabatic** (Q = 0): PV^γ = constant, TV^(γ−1) = constant, W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1) = −ΔU.

On a P–V diagram, an adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal one through the same point (slope −γP/V vs −P/V).

steps.title: Worked example: isobaric heating
steps.body:
2 mol of a monatomic ideal gas is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 400 K (R = 8.314 J/mol·K).
- ΔU = nC_vΔT = 2 × 1.5 × 8.314 × 100 ≈ 2494 J
- W = nRΔT = 2 × 8.314 × 100 ≈ 1663 J
- Q = nC_pΔT = 2 × 2.5 × 8.314 × 100 ≈ 4157 J

Check: ΔU + W = 4157 ✔. Of the heat supplied, 60% raises internal energy, 40% does work.

steps.title: Why the pump gets hot
steps.body:
Quick compression is nearly adiabatic: Q ≈ 0, W < 0 (work done ON the gas), so ΔU = −W > 0: temperature rises. Diesel engines use this—compression alone heats air enough to ignite fuel.

Conversely, gas escaping fast from a spray can cools (expansion does work, ΔU < 0).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing sign conventions within one problem.
- Saying 'isothermal means no heat flow'. Isothermal: ΔT = 0; heat flows and equals work. Adiabatic: no heat flow.
- Using ΔU = nC_pΔT. Internal energy change always uses C_v.
- Using °C where kelvin is needed (PV = nRT, ratios of temperatures).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
In a cyclic process, a gas absorbs 500 J of heat and rejects 300 J. What is the net work done by the gas?

Answer: ΔU = 0 for a cycle, so W = Q_net = 200 J (= area enclosed by the loop on the P–V diagram).

activity.prompt: Sort each statement into the process it describes (ideal gas).

quiz.q: In an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas
quiz.why: In an isothermal process the temperature is constant, so the ideal gas's internal energy does not change (ΔU = 0). By the first law Q = ΔU + W, so Q = W.

quiz.q: For a diatomic gas at room temperature, γ is
quiz.why: A diatomic gas at room temperature has 5 degrees of freedom: C_v = 5R/2 and C_p = 7R/2. γ = C_p/C_v = 7/5 = 1.4.

quiz.q: 100 J of heat is given to a gas and it does 40 J of work. ΔU =
quiz.why: By the first law ΔU = Q − W = 100 − 40 = 60 J.

quiz.q: Net work done in a complete cycle equals
options: the area enclosed by the P–V loop
quiz.why: Over a complete cycle the gas returns to its start, so ΔU = 0 and net work equals net heat. On a P–V diagram, this work equals the area enclosed by the loop.

quiz.q: Rapid compression of air heats it because
options: work done on the gas raises U with little heat loss
quiz.why: Rapid compression leaves little time for heat to escape, so it is nearly adiabatic (Q ≈ 0). The work done on the gas raises its internal energy, so it gets hotter.

lessons.title: Second law, heat engines and refrigerators

story.title: The power plant and the fridge

scenes.text: Vikram, an engineering intern at a coal power station in Maharashtra, learns that only about a third of the fuel's energy becomes electricity.
At home his sister Isha asks why the back of their refrigerator is hot if it is supposed to make things cold.
Both answers come from the second law: heat flows naturally from hot to cold, and no engine converts heat entirely into work.

steps.title: Statements of the second law
steps.body:
- **Kelvin–Planck**: no cyclic engine can convert all absorbed heat into work; some must be rejected to a colder reservoir.
- **Clausius**: heat cannot flow by itself from a colder body to a hotter one; a refrigerator needs work input.

The two are equivalent. The law introduces **entropy**: for an isolated system it never decreases.

steps.title: Engines and refrigerators
steps.body:
A **heat engine** takes Q_h from a hot reservoir, does W, rejects Q_c: W = Q_h − Q_c, efficiency **η = W/Q_h = 1 − Q_c/Q_h**.

A **Carnot engine** (reversible: two isothermal + two adiabatic steps) is the most efficient between two temperatures: **η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h** (kelvin!).

**Refrigerator**: W in, extracts Q_c from inside, dumps Q_h = Q_c + W outside (that's the hot back coil). Coefficient of performance **COP = Q_c/W**; ideal (Carnot) COP = T_c/(T_h − T_c).

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) Carnot engine between 500 K and 300 K: η = 1 − 300/500 = 0.40 (40%). If Q_h = 1000 J per cycle, W = 400 J, Q_c = 600 J.

2) An ideal refrigerator keeps its inside at 273 K in a 303 K room: COP = 273/30 = 9.1. To remove 910 J it needs only 100 J of work and dumps 1010 J into the room.

steps.title: Why real plants are well below Carnot
steps.body: Friction, heat leaks and finite-time (irreversible) processes all waste energy. Real plants also cannot use arbitrarily high temperatures because of material limits. This is why combined-cycle plants and co-generation (using waste heat) improve overall efficiency.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in 1 − T_c/T_h (e.g., 1 − 27/227 is wrong; use 300/500).
- Thinking COP cannot exceed 1. COP is not an efficiency; values of 3–10 are normal.
- Believing an open fridge door cools a room. It heats the room overall because the motor's work also becomes heat.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
An engine claims 60% efficiency between 400 K and 200 K. Is it possible?

Answer: Carnot limit = 1 − 200/400 = 50%. The claim violates the second law.

activity.prompt: A Carnot engine works between 627 °C and 27 °C. What is its efficiency in percent? (Convert to kelvin first.)

quiz.q: Carnot efficiency between 400 K and 300 K
quiz.why: Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_c/T_h = 1 − 300/400 = 0.25 = 25%. Temperatures must be in kelvin.

quiz.q: The back of a refrigerator is warm because
options: it releases Q_c + W to the room
quiz.why: A refrigerator removes heat Q_c from inside and uses work W, so it must reject Q_c + W to the room through the back coils. This is why they feel warm.

quiz.q: Which statement is the Clausius form of the second law?
options: Heat cannot flow by itself from cold to hot
quiz.why: The Clausius statement says heat cannot flow by itself from a colder to a hotter body. The statement that all heat can become work is false (Kelvin–Planck forbids it).

quiz.q: An engine absorbs 800 J and rejects 600 J per cycle. Efficiency
quiz.why: Work done = 800 − 600 = 200 J. Efficiency = W/Q_in = 200/800 = 25%. It cannot exceed 100%.

quiz.q: To raise Carnot efficiency, you should
quiz.why: η = 1 − T_c/T_h. It rises when the ratio T_c/T_h gets smaller, which means a hotter source or a colder sink.

questions.q: Unit of torque
questions.why: Torque is force times perpendicular distance, so its SI unit is N·m. It has the same dimensions as energy, but torque is not measured in joules.

questions.q: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on
questions.why: An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so its internal energy is only the molecular kinetic energy: U = nC_vT. It depends only on temperature.

questions.q: Moment of inertia of a thin rod (M, L) about one end
questions.why: About the centre, I = ML²/12. Shifting the axis to one end (distance L/2) gives I = ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3.

questions.q: Work done in an isochoric process
questions.why: Isochoric means constant volume. Work = PΔV, and ΔV = 0, so the work done is zero.

questions.q: A flywheel with I = 5 kg·m² rotates at 10 rad/s. Its rotational KE
questions.why: Rotational KE = ½Iω² = ½ × 5 × 10² = ½ × 5 × 100 = 250 J.

questions.q: A disc of radius R rolls without slipping at speed v. Speed of its topmost point
questions.why: The top point moves with the centre's speed v plus the rotational speed ωR = v, so it moves at 2v. The bottom point is at rest.

questions.q: 1 mol monatomic gas: adiabatic compression raises its temperature by 100 K. Work done ON the gas (R = 8.3)
questions.why: In an adiabatic process Q = 0, so the work done on the gas equals its rise in internal energy. For a monatomic gas C_v = 3R/2, so W = 1.5 × 8.3 × 100 = 1245 J.

questions.q: An ideal refrigerator works between 250 K and 300 K. COP
questions.why: For an ideal refrigerator COP = T_c/(T_h − T_c) = 250/(300 − 250) = 5.

questions.q: A ring and a disc of the same mass and radius roll at the same speed. Ratio of total KE ring : disc
questions.why: Rolling KE = ½Mv² + ½Iω². For a ring that is Mv² (½ + ½); for a disc it is ¾Mv² (½ + ¼). The ratio ring : disc is 1 : ¾ = 4 : 3.

questions.q: A person on a rotating stool (total I = 6 kg·m², 2 rad/s) pulls dumbbells in, making I = 2 kg·m². New ω
questions.why: Angular momentum is conserved when there is no external torque: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂, so 6 × 2 = 2 × ω₂ and ω₂ = 6 rad/s.

questions.q: For a gas with γ = 1.4, if volume is halved adiabatically, pressure becomes about
questions.why: For an adiabatic change PVᵞ is constant, so P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)ᵞ = 2^1.4 ≈ 2.64. This is more than 2 because the gas also heats up when compressed.

questions.q: A solid sphere rolls without slipping. Fraction of its KE that is rotational
questions.why: For a solid sphere, I = (2/5)MR², so rotational KE is (2/5) of the translational KE (½Mv²). The fraction rotational is (2/5)/(1 + 2/5) = 2/7.

questions.q: A Carnot engine of efficiency 25% has its sink temperature lowered by 50 K, making efficiency 50%. Source temperature
questions.why: η = 1 − T_c/T_h, so T_c = 0.75T_h at first. After lowering the sink by 50 K: 1 − (T_c − 50)/T_h = 0.5, so T_c − 50 = 0.5T_h. Subtracting gives 0.25T_h = 50, so T_h = 200 K.

courses.title: Electricity & magnetism
courses.summary: From Coulomb's law and Gauss's law to capacitors, circuits, magnetic fields, electromagnetic induction and AC — with real devices (flash, MRI, transformers) and home electrical safety.
outcomes: Learners can use Coulomb's and Gauss's laws to find forces and fields
Learners can solve capacitor and DC circuit problems including Kirchhoff's laws
Learners can calculate magnetic fields of currents and forces on charges
Learners can apply Faraday's and Lenz's laws and analyse series LCR circuits

lessons.title: Electric charge, field and Gauss's law

scenes.text: On a dry January night in Delhi, Meera pulls off her woollen sweater and hears crackles. Her hair stands up.
Her little brother rubs a balloon on his hair and sticks it to the wall. 'Magic!' he declares.
Meera, preparing for her Class 12 boards, knows it is charge transfer—and decides to calculate how strong these forces really are.

steps.title: Charge and Coulomb's law
steps.body:
- Charge is **quantised** (q = ne, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) and **conserved**.
- Rubbing transfers electrons; it does not create charge.
- **Coulomb's law**: F = k q₁q₂/r², k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Like charges repel, unlike attract.
- **Superposition**: total force = vector sum of individual forces.

steps.title: Electric field
steps.body:
E = F/q₀ (force per unit positive test charge). Point charge: **E = kq/r²**, radially outward for +q.

**Electric dipole** (charges ±q separated by 2a, p = q·2a, pointing from − to +):
- Axial point (far): E = 2kp/r³
- Equatorial point (far): E = kp/r³, opposite to p
- In a uniform field: torque τ = pE sin θ, net force zero.

steps.title: Gauss's law and its power
steps.body:
Flux through any closed surface Φ = ∮E·dA = q_enclosed/ε₀.

Choose a symmetric 'Gaussian surface' to find E quickly:
- Infinite line charge λ: E = λ/(2πε₀r)
- Infinite plane sheet σ: E = σ/(2ε₀), independent of distance
- Uniformly charged thin spherical shell (Q, R): outside E = kQ/r²; inside **E = 0**
- Conductors: E = 0 inside; charge resides on the surface (electrostatic shielding—why a car body protects you in lightning).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Charges +2 μC and +3 μC are 30 cm apart.

F = 9×10⁹ × (2×10⁻⁶)(3×10⁻⁶)/(0.3)² = 9×10⁹ × 6×10⁻¹²/0.09 = 0.6 N (repulsive).

Where between them is the field zero? Let x be the distance from 2 μC: 2/x² = 3/(0.3 − x)² ⇒ (0.3 − x)/x = √1.5 ≈ 1.225 ⇒ x ≈ 0.135 m = 13.5 cm from the 2 μC charge (closer to the smaller charge).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to convert μC (×10⁻⁶) and cm (×10⁻²).
- Adding field magnitudes from different charges without considering direction.
- Thinking Gauss's law fails for asymmetric cases—it always holds; it is just not *useful* for finding E without symmetry.
- Net flux depends only on enclosed charge; outside charges change E on the surface but not the net flux.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A charge q sits at the centre of a cube. What is the flux through one face?

Answer: total q/ε₀ shared equally by 6 faces ⇒ q/(6ε₀).

activity.prompt: Complete the key results.
activity.text: Coulomb's constant k is about ___ × 10⁹ N·m²/C². The field inside a charged conducting shell is ___. Flux through a closed surface equals enclosed charge divided by ___.

quiz.q: If the distance between two charges is doubled, the force becomes
quiz.why: Coulomb's force is inversely proportional to r². Doubling the distance makes the force 1/2² = 1/4 of the original.

quiz.q: Field due to an infinite plane sheet of charge
quiz.why: An infinite uniformly charged sheet gives E = σ/(2ε₀), which has no r in it. The field lines are parallel and do not spread out, so the field is the same at any distance.

quiz.q: A dipole in a uniform field experiences
quiz.why: In a uniform field the forces on +q and −q are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero. They act at different points, so they produce a torque pE sin θ.

quiz.q: Charge on a body can be
quiz.why: Charge is quantised: it is an integer multiple of e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Only 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (2e) fits, while 2.4, 0.8 and 1.0 are not whole multiples.

quiz.q: Why is sitting inside a metal car relatively safe in lightning?
options: Charge stays on the outer metal surface; the field inside ≈ 0
quiz.why: Electrostatic shielding by the conducting body (the tyres are not the main reason).

scenes.text: Dev, a photography enthusiast in Kochi, hears a high-pitched whine before his old camera's flash fires.
A 1.5 V battery somehow produces a flash needing hundreds of volts. The secret: a capacitor charged slowly, discharged in a millisecond.
Dev wants to know how much energy that tiny capacitor stores.

steps.title: Electric potential
steps.body:
Potential V = work done per unit charge to bring a test charge from infinity: point charge **V = kq/r** (a scalar—just add with signs).

- Potential energy of two charges: U = kq₁q₂/r.
- E = −dV/dr: the field points from high to low potential.
- Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines; no work is done moving along them.
- 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (energy gained by an electron across 1 V).

steps.title: Capacitors
steps.body:
C = Q/V (farad). Parallel-plate: **C = ε₀A/d**; with a dielectric of constant K filling the gap: C = Kε₀A/d.

- **Series**: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + … (same charge on each)
- **Parallel**: C = C₁ + C₂ + … (same voltage on each)
- **Energy**: U = ½CV² = Q²/(2C) = ½QV; energy density u = ½ε₀E².

steps.title: Worked example: series pair
steps.body:
2 μF and 3 μF in series across 10 V.
- C_eq = (2 × 3)/(2 + 3) = 1.2 μF
- Q = C_eq V = 12 μC (same on both)
- V₁ = 12/2 = 6 V, V₂ = 12/3 = 4 V (the smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage)
- Energy stored = ½ × 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 = 60 μJ.

steps.title: Inserting a dielectric
steps.body:
A capacitor is charged and the battery is **disconnected** (Q fixed). Inserting a dielectric K: C → KC, V → V/K, U = Q²/2C → U/K (energy decreases; the slab is pulled in).

With the battery **connected** (V fixed): C → KC, Q → KQ, U → KU.

steps.title: Common mistakes and safety
steps.body:
- Using the resistor rules for capacitors (they're reversed: capacitors add in parallel).
- Treating potential as a vector.
- Forgetting whether the battery stays connected when geometry changes.
- Large capacitors (in TVs, inverters, flashes) can hold dangerous charge even after unplugging—never touch their terminals.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Three 6 μF capacitors: what are the equivalent capacitances in series and in parallel?

Answer: series 2 μF; parallel 18 μF.

activity.prompt: Dev's flash capacitor is 100 μF charged to 200 V. How much energy (in joules) does it store?

quiz.q: Potential 10 cm from a 1 nC charge (k = 9 × 10⁹)
quiz.why: V = kq/r = 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁹/0.1 = 9/0.1 = 90 V. Remember 1 nC = 10⁻⁹ C and 10 cm = 0.1 m.

quiz.q: Two 4 μF capacitors in series give
quiz.why: In series, 1/C = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, so C = 2 μF. Series capacitors combine to less than the smallest one.

quiz.q: A charged, isolated capacitor has its plate separation doubled. Its energy
quiz.why: The capacitor is isolated, so Q stays fixed. Doubling the separation halves C, so U = Q²/2C doubles. The extra energy comes from the work done pulling the plates apart.

quiz.q: Work done moving a charge along an equipotential surface
quiz.why: Along an equipotential surface ΔV = 0, so W = qΔV = 0. This does not depend on the path taken.

quiz.q: Electric field direction is from
quiz.why: Since E = −dV/dr, the field points in the direction in which the potential falls fastest, from high to low potential.

lessons.title: Current electricity: Ohm, Kirchhoff and home safety

scenes.text: In Lucknow's peak winter, Arjun plugs a room heater and an iron into the same cheap extension board.
The board's plug gets hot and smells of melting plastic. His mother switches everything off at once.
Arjun wants to understand: what current was flowing, and why did the wire heat up?

steps.title: Current, drift and resistance
steps.body:
- Current I = dQ/dt = nAev_d (n = free electrons per m³, v_d = drift speed, typically only a fraction of a mm/s; the *signal* travels close to light speed).
- **Ohm's law**: V = IR (for ohmic conductors at constant temperature).
- **R = ρL/A**; resistivity ρ depends on material and temperature (for metals ρ rises with T).
- Stretching a wire to n times its length (volume constant) makes R → n²R.

steps.title: Combinations, EMF and power
steps.body:
- Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + … (same current). Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … (same voltage).
- A cell has EMF ε and internal resistance r: **I = ε/(R + r)**, terminal voltage **V = ε − Ir**.
- **Power** P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Energy in kWh ('units' on your bill): 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

steps.title: Kirchhoff's laws and the Wheatstone bridge
steps.body:
- **Junction law** (charge conservation): ΣI in = ΣI out.
- **Loop law** (energy conservation): ΣΔV around any closed loop = 0. Through a resistor along the current: −IR; through a cell from − to +: +ε.
- **Wheatstone bridge** P, Q, R, S: the galvanometer shows no current when **P/Q = R/S**. The metre bridge uses this idea.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) Battery ε = 12 V, r = 1 Ω, external R = 5 Ω: I = 12/6 = 2 A, terminal V = 12 − 2 = 10 V, power in R = 4 × 5 = 20 W.

2) Arjun's board at 230 V: heater 2000 W draws 2000/230 ≈ 8.7 A; iron 1000 W draws ≈ 4.3 A. Total ≈ 13 A. A board rated 6 A heats up (P = I²R in its thin wires and loose contacts) and can catch fire.

steps.title: Common mistakes and safety
steps.body:
- Assuming ε equals terminal voltage when current flows.
- Wrong signs in loop equations—pick a direction and be consistent; a negative answer just means current flows the other way.
- Never overload sockets; use correctly rated boards and MCBs; never bypass a fuse with ordinary wire.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Resistors 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel, in series with 2 Ω, across 12 V. Find the total current.

Answer: parallel = 2 Ω; total 4 Ω; I = 3 A.

a.text: Arjun's mother has switched everything off. The extension board is rated 6 A. They still need the heater tonight. What should Arjun do?

choices.label: Plug the heater alone into a proper 16 A wall socket
choices.feedback: The heater (≈ 8.7 A) needs a heavy-duty (16 A) socket and wiring.

choices.label: Use the same board but wrap the hot plug in tape
choices.feedback: Tape does not reduce current; the board is still overloaded.

b.text: Now the iron. Should he run it at the same time on another socket on the same circuit?

choices.label: Check the MCB rating for that circuit first; if unsure, iron later
choices.feedback: Smart: total current on one circuit must stay below its breaker rating.

choices.label: Yes, more sockets means more capacity
choices.feedback: Sockets on one circuit share the same wiring and breaker.

c.text: The plug overheats again and the plastic softens. What now?

choices.label: Switch off at the mains, let it cool, replace the damaged board
choices.feedback: Damaged insulation is a shock and fire risk; replace it.

d.text: Safe! Arjun learned: P = VI tells you the current; wiring and boards have current limits; overheating means I²R losses are too high.

quiz.q: A cell of EMF 6 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to 2.5 Ω. Terminal voltage
quiz.why: Total resistance = 0.5 + 2.5 = 3 Ω, so I = 6/3 = 2 A. Terminal voltage = EMF − Ir = 6 − 2 × 0.5 = 5 V, which is also I × 2.5 = 5 V.

quiz.q: A wire is stretched to twice its length. Resistance becomes
quiz.why: Stretching keeps the volume constant, so doubling the length halves the area. R = ρL/A becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times the original, i.e. 4R.

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's junction law is based on conservation of
quiz.why: Kirchhoff's junction law says the current in equals the current out, because charge cannot accumulate at a junction. This is conservation of charge; the loop law is energy conservation.

quiz.q: A 100 W bulb at 220 V draws about
Wheatstone bridge balance condition
quiz.why: A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when the ratios of the resistances in the two arms are equal: P/Q = R/S. Then no current flows through the galvanometer.

scenes.text: Zoya, shadowing a radiographer at a hospital in Hyderabad, must remove her hairpins before entering the MRI room.
The radiographer explains that the scanner's superconducting coils create a field tens of thousands of times stronger than Earth's.
Zoya connects this to her Class 12 chapter: moving charges make magnetic fields—and fields push on moving charges.

steps.title: Force on moving charges and wires
steps.body:
- **Lorentz force**: F = q(E + v × B). Magnetic part: F = qvB sin θ, perpendicular to both v and B, so it does **no work** (speed stays constant).
- In a uniform B with v ⟂ B: circular path, **r = mv/(qB)**, period **T = 2πm/(qB)** — independent of speed (the cyclotron principle).
- **Wire**: F = I L × B, magnitude BIL sin θ. Direction: Fleming's left-hand rule or the right-hand rule for the cross product.

steps.title: Fields produced by currents
steps.body:
Biot–Savart: dB = (μ₀/4π) I dl × r̂ / r², μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A.
- Long straight wire: **B = μ₀I/(2πr)**
- Centre of a circular loop (radius R, N turns): **B = μ₀NI/(2R)**
- Long solenoid (n turns per metre): **B = μ₀nI** inside, ≈ 0 outside
- Ampère's law: ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enclosed (use for symmetric cases).
- Two parallel wires: force per length = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd); same-direction currents **attract**.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) Wire with 10 A; field 5 cm away: B = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 10)/(2π × 0.05) = 4 × 10⁻⁵ T (comparable to Earth's field, roughly 5 × 10⁻⁵ T—why a compass near a cable deflects).

2) A proton (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) at 10⁶ m/s in B = 0.1 T: r = (1.67×10⁻²⁷ × 10⁶)/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 0.1) ≈ 0.104 m.

steps.title: Current loop as a magnet; galvanometer
steps.body: A loop of area A carrying I has magnetic moment m = NIA; in field B it feels torque τ = mB sin θ. The moving-coil galvanometer uses this: deflection ∝ current. Convert it to an **ammeter** with a small shunt in parallel; to a **voltmeter** with a large resistance in series.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a magnetic field can speed up a charge. It only changes direction.
- Using the right-hand rule for electrons without reversing the direction (negative charge).
- Confusing turns per metre (n) with total turns (N) in the solenoid formula.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A solenoid 0.5 m long has 500 turns and carries 2 A. Find B inside.

Answer: n = 1000 per m; B = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 1000 × 2 ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻³ T.

activity.prompt: Match each situation with its formula.
pairs: Radius of a charged particle in B

quiz.q: Work done by a magnetic force on a moving charge
quiz.why: The magnetic force qv × B is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work. It changes the particle's direction, not its speed.

quiz.q: Two parallel wires carry current in the same direction. They
quiz.why: Parallel wires with currents in the same direction attract each other. Opposite currents would repel.

quiz.q: Doubling a charged particle's speed in a uniform B changes its period by
quiz.why: The period of circular motion is T = 2πm/(qB). It does not contain v, because a faster particle moves on a larger circle but takes the same time.

quiz.q: To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, connect
quiz.why: A voltmeter must have high resistance so it draws very little current from the circuit. A large resistance in series with the galvanometer does that and drops most of the voltage across itself.

quiz.q: Field at the centre of a 1-turn loop of radius 0.1 m carrying 1 A (μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷)
quiz.why: At the centre of a circular loop, B = μ₀I/(2R) = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1/(2 × 0.1) = 2π × 10⁻⁶ T.

scenes.text: Selvi's uncle works at a wind farm near Kanyakumari. Each giant turbine spins a generator that pushes electricity into the grid.
At home, her family cooks on an induction cooktop that stays fairly cool to the touch while the steel pan gets hot.
Both are Faraday's discovery at work: a changing magnetic flux induces an EMF.

steps.title: Faraday and Lenz
steps.body:
Magnetic flux Φ = B·A = BA cos θ (weber).
- **Faraday**: ε = −N dΦ/dt.
- **Lenz**: the induced current opposes the change that produces it (the minus sign; energy conservation).
- **Motional EMF**: a rod of length l moving at v perpendicular to B: ε = Blv.
- Rotating coil (generator): ε = NBAω sin ωt, peak ε₀ = NBAω.
- Eddy currents: induced currents in bulk metal—used in induction cooking and magnetic braking; reduced in transformers by laminated cores.

steps.title: Inductance
steps.body: Self-inductance: ε = −L dI/dt; long solenoid L = μ₀n²Al. Energy stored U = ½LI². Mutual inductance couples two coils (the basis of transformers).

steps.title: Alternating current essentials
steps.body:
- V = V₀ sin ωt; **V_rms = V₀/√2**. Indian mains: 230 V rms, 50 Hz ⇒ peak ≈ 325 V.
- Reactances: X_L = ωL, X_C = 1/(ωC).
- Series LCR impedance: **Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²]**, phase tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R.
- **Resonance** at ω₀ = 1/√(LC): Z = R (minimum), current maximum (radio tuning).
- Average power P = V_rms I_rms cos φ (cos φ = power factor). Pure L or C: average power zero.
- **Ideal transformer**: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p = I_p/I_s. Power is transmitted at high voltage to cut I²R losses.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) A 0.5 m rod moves at 4 m/s perpendicular to B = 0.2 T: ε = 0.2 × 0.5 × 4 = 0.4 V.

2) Series LCR: R = 30 Ω, X_L = 80 Ω, X_C = 40 Ω, V_rms = 100 V. Z = √(900 + 1600) = 50 Ω; I_rms = 2 A; cos φ = 30/50 = 0.6; P = 100 × 2 × 0.6 = 120 W (= I²R ✔).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting N in Faraday's law or cos θ in flux.
- Adding R and reactances directly (they combine as phasors).
- Thinking transformers work on steady DC—they need changing flux.
- Mixing peak and rms values in power calculations.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A transformer steps 230 V down to 11.5 V. If the primary has 2000 turns, how many turns does the secondary have?

Answer: N_s = 2000 × 11.5/230 = 100 turns.

statements.s: An induced current always flows to oppose the change in flux that caused it.
statements.why: That is Lenz's law, a consequence of energy conservation.

statements.s: A transformer can step up a steady DC voltage.
statements.why: Steady DC gives no changing flux, so no induced EMF.

statements.s: At resonance in a series LCR circuit, impedance equals R.
statements.why: X_L = X_C cancels the reactive part.

statements.s: The peak value of 230 V rms mains is about 325 V.
A pure inductor in an AC circuit consumes large average power.
statements.why: Phase difference 90°: cos φ = 0, average power zero.

quiz.q: Flux through a 10-turn coil changes from 0.5 Wb to 0.1 Wb in 0.2 s. Induced EMF magnitude
quiz.why: By Faraday's law, ε = N|ΔΦ|/Δt = 10 × (0.5 − 0.1)/0.2 = 10 × 2 = 20 V. The turns multiply the EMF.

quiz.q: Inductive reactance at 50 Hz for L = 0.1 H
quiz.why: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.1 ≈ 31.4 Ω. The 314 Ω value comes from forgetting the 0.1.

quiz.q: Resonant frequency of an LC circuit depends on
quiz.why: In an LC circuit the resonant angular frequency is ω₀ = 1/√(LC), so it depends only on L and C. Resistance affects damping, not the resonant frequency.

quiz.q: Laminated transformer cores reduce
quiz.why: A laminated core is built from thin insulated sheets, which cut the paths for circulating eddy currents. This reduces the eddy-current heating loss.

quiz.q: Power is transmitted at high voltage to
quiz.why: Power P = VI, so a higher voltage means a lower current for the same power. Line loss is I²R, so it falls sharply.

questions.q: SI unit of capacitance
questions.why: Capacitance is C = Q/V (coulomb per volt), and this unit is the farad. Henry is for inductance, tesla for magnetic field and weber for flux.

questions.q: Unit of magnetic flux
questions.why: Magnetic flux is measured in weber (1 Wb = 1 T·m²). Tesla is the unit of field strength, not flux.

questions.q: Three 2 Ω resistors in parallel give
questions.why: For parallel resistors 1/R = 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 3/2, so R = 2/3 Ω. Parallel combinations are always less than the smallest resistor.

questions.q: Field inside a uniformly charged spherical shell
questions.why: By Gauss's law, a Gaussian surface inside a uniformly charged shell encloses no charge, so the field inside is zero.

questions.q: A 2 kW heater runs 3 hours a day for 30 days. Energy used
questions.why: Energy = power × time = 2 kW × 3 h × 30 days = 180 kWh. One kWh is one 'unit' of electricity.

questions.q: Equal charges +q at two corners of an equilateral triangle of side a. Potential at the third corner
questions.why: Potential is a scalar, so contributions simply add. Each charge gives kq/a at the third corner, so the total is 2kq/a. The √3 factor would apply to the field, not the potential.

questions.q: A proton and an α-particle enter a uniform B with the same speed. Ratio of radii r_p : r_α
questions.why: The radius is r = mv/(qB). A proton has m and q; an α-particle has 4m and 2q, so its m/q is twice as large. Hence r_p : r_α = 1 : 2.

questions.q: A charged capacitor (battery removed) has a dielectric K = 4 inserted. Its potential difference becomes
questions.why: With the battery removed, Q is fixed. A dielectric with K = 4 multiplies C by 4, and V = Q/C becomes V/4.

questions.q: Series LCR: R = 6 Ω, X_L = 12 Ω, X_C = 4 Ω. Power factor
questions.why: The impedance is Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²) = √(36 + 64) = 10 Ω. The power factor cos φ = R/Z = 6/10 = 0.6.

questions.q: Two cells (2 V, 1 Ω each) in parallel across a 1.5 Ω resistor. Current in the resistor
questions.why: Two identical cells in parallel give the same EMF 2 V but half the internal resistance, 0.5 Ω. The current is I = 2/(0.5 + 1.5) = 1 A.

questions.q: A 1 m rod rotates at ω = 20 rad/s about one end in B = 0.5 T perpendicular to the plane of rotation. EMF between its ends
questions.why: For a rod rotating about one end, ε = ½BωL² = ½ × 0.5 × 20 × 1² = 5 V.

questions.q: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 5 A and 10 A in opposite directions. Force per metre
questions.why: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 5 × 10/0.1 = 10⁻⁴ N per metre. Currents in opposite directions repel.

questions.q: A 10 μF capacitor charged to 100 V is connected across an identical uncharged capacitor. Energy lost
questions.why: Initial energy = ½ × 10⁻⁵ × 100² = 0.05 J. The common voltage is 50 V, so final energy = 2 × ½ × 10⁻⁵ × 50² = 0.025 J, and energy lost = 0.05 − 0.025 = 0.025 J.

questions.q: A metre bridge balances at 40 cm with R = 3 Ω in the left gap. Unknown resistance in the right gap
questions.why: A metre bridge balance gives R/X = l/(100 − l) = 40/60. So X = 3 × 60/40 = 4.5 Ω.

courses.title: Optics & modern physics
courses.summary: Mirrors, lenses and the eye; interference, diffraction and polarisation; photons and matter waves; Bohr's atom, nuclei and radioactivity — derived, explained and drilled.
outcomes: Learners can apply mirror, lens and lens-maker formulas with correct signs
Learners can analyse YDSE, single-slit diffraction and polarisation
Learners can solve photoelectric and de Broglie problems
Learners can use Bohr energies, binding energy and half-life calculations

lessons.title: Ray optics: mirrors, lenses and your eyes

scenes.text: Suresh Dadaji, 64, in Indore, can no longer read the newspaper without holding it at arm's length.
The optometrist prescribes +2.5 D reading glasses. His granddaughter Nisha asks, 'What does +2.5 even mean?'
It is the lens power in dioptres: P = 1/f with f in metres. Nisha sets out to master the lens formula.

steps.title: Reflection, refraction, TIR
steps.body:
- Mirrors: f = R/2. **Mirror formula** 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; magnification m = −v/u.
- **Snell's law**: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Light bends towards the normal entering a denser medium.
- **Total internal reflection** going dense → rare beyond the critical angle: sin C = n₂/n₁ (= 1/n into air). Glass n = 1.5: C ≈ 41.8°. Used in optical fibres; it also gives diamonds their sparkle.
- Apparent depth = real depth / n (a pool looks shallower).

steps.title: Thin lenses (Cartesian sign convention)
steps.body:
Distances are measured from the optical centre; along the incident light = positive. Object on the left ⇒ u negative.
- **Lens formula**: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f
- **Magnification**: m = v/u (negative ⇒ real, inverted)
- **Lens maker's formula**: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
- **Power** P = 1/f (f in m), unit dioptre (D). Convex +, concave −. Lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Object 30 cm in front of a convex lens of f = 20 cm: u = −30, f = +20.

1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60 ⇒ v = +60 cm. m = v/u = −2: real, inverted, twice the size, 60 cm behind the lens.

Move the object to 10 cm (inside f): 1/v = 1/20 − 1/10 = −1/20 ⇒ v = −20 cm: virtual, erect, magnified ×2 (a magnifying glass).

steps.title: Eye defects
steps.body:
- **Myopia** (near-sightedness): the image forms in front of the retina; corrected by a **concave** lens. Far point 2 m ⇒ P = −1/2 = −0.5 D.
- **Hypermetropia** (far-sightedness): corrected by a **convex** lens.
- **Presbyopia**: age-related loss of accommodation; reading glasses (convex), like Dadaji's +2.5 D (f = 40 cm).
- **Astigmatism**: corrected by cylindrical lenses.

See an optometrist or eye doctor for any vision change; this is general education.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing the mirror formula (1/v + 1/u) with the lens formula (1/v − 1/u).
- Forgetting u is negative for real objects.
- Using f in cm when computing power in dioptres.
- Thinking a glass lens has the same focal length in water—it increases because (n_lens/n_medium − 1) shrinks.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Two thin lenses of +5 D and −3 D are in contact. Find the focal length of the combination.

Answer: P = +2 D ⇒ f = 0.5 m = 50 cm (converging).

activity.prompt: An object is 15 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image (v in cm, Cartesian sign)?

quiz.q: Power of a lens with f = −25 cm
quiz.why: Power P = 1/f with f in metres. For f = −25 cm = −0.25 m, P = −4 D. The negative sign shows a diverging (concave) lens.

quiz.q: Critical angle for glass (n = 1.5) to air: sin C =
quiz.why: At the critical angle sin C = 1/n = 1/1.5 ≈ 0.67 for light going from glass to air.

quiz.q: Myopia is corrected using
quiz.why: A myopic eye focuses distant objects in front of the retina. A concave (diverging) lens spreads the rays slightly so the image falls back on the retina.

quiz.q: A concave mirror (f = −10 cm) and object at u = −20 cm. v =
quiz.why: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/10 + 1/20 = −1/20 ⇒ v = −20 cm (at C, same size, inverted).

quiz.q: Optical fibres work on
quiz.why: Optical fibres trap light inside the core by repeated total internal reflection, so it travels along the fibre with little loss.

scenes.text: At a Cape Town beach, Anika blows soap bubbles for her cousin. Swirls of colour drift across each bubble.
Her cousin's polarised sunglasses make the glare from the sea vanish—until he tilts his head.
Both effects only make sense if light is a wave. Anika's physics teacher, Mr Naidoo, sketches crests and troughs.

steps.title: Huygens and interference
steps.body:
Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets (Huygens). Two coherent sources superpose:
- **Constructive** (bright): path difference Δ = nλ
- **Destructive** (dark): Δ = (n + ½)λ

**Young's double slit**: slit separation d, screen distance D. Bright fringes at y = nλD/d. **Fringe width β = λD/d**. Intensity I = 4I₀cos²(φ/2) for equal sources.

steps.title: Worked example: YDSE
steps.body:
λ = 600 nm, D = 1 m, d = 0.5 mm. β = (600×10⁻⁹ × 1)/(0.5×10⁻³) = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m = 1.2 mm.

Immerse the setup in water (n ≈ 1.33): λ becomes λ/n, so β ≈ 0.9 mm. Increase d ⇒ the fringes crowd together.

steps.title: Diffraction and resolution
steps.body:
**Single slit** of width a: minima at a sin θ = nλ (n = ±1, ±2 …). The central maximum's angular width ≈ 2λ/a — a narrower slit gives a wider spread.

Diffraction limits how fine a detail telescopes and microscopes can resolve; larger apertures and shorter wavelengths resolve better.

Thin-film colours (bubbles, oil on wet roads) come from interference between reflections at the film's two surfaces.

steps.title: Polarisation
steps.body:
Light is a transverse wave, so it can be polarised.
- **Malus's law**: I = I₀ cos²θ after an analyser at angle θ.
- Unpolarised light through one polaroid: intensity halves.
- **Brewster's law**: reflected light is fully polarised when tan θ_B = n (glass: ≈ 56°). Polarised sunglasses block this mostly horizontally polarised glare.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to convert nm and mm.
- Mixing up the double-slit maxima condition (d sin θ = nλ) with single-slit minima (a sin θ = nλ)—same form, opposite meaning.
- Forgetting the ½ factor when unpolarised light meets the first polaroid.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through two polaroids at 60° to each other. Final intensity?

Answer: I₀/2 × cos²60° = I₀/2 × ¼ = I₀/8.

cards.back: Thin-film interference of reflections from the two surfaces

quiz.q: In YDSE, if the slit separation is doubled, the fringe width
quiz.why: Fringe width β = λD/d, so β is inversely proportional to the slit separation d. Doubling d halves β.

quiz.q: Polarisation shows that light is
quiz.why: Only transverse waves, whose vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of travel, can be polarised. So polarisation shows that light is transverse.

quiz.q: Unpolarised light (I₀) through one ideal polaroid gives
quiz.why: Unpolarised light has all vibration directions equally. An ideal polaroid passes the average of cos²θ, which is ½, so the intensity is I₀/2.

quiz.q: Brewster angle for n = √3
quiz.why: At the Brewster angle tan θ_B = n. With n = √3, tan θ_B = √3, so θ_B = 60°.

quiz.q: Narrowing a single slit makes the central maximum
quiz.why: The angular width of the central maximum is about 2λ/a. A narrower slit (smaller a) gives a wider central maximum, as the light spreads out more.

lessons.title: Dual nature: photoelectric effect and matter waves

scenes.text: In a Rajasthan village, Hemant watches solar street lights switch on by themselves at dusk.
In the city, his cousin Ritika notices that mall doors open as she approaches—another light sensor.
Their science teacher says these devices rely on light arriving in packets—photons. Einstein received the Nobel Prize for explaining the photoelectric effect this way.

steps.title: What the experiments showed
steps.body:
When light falls on a metal surface, electrons may be emitted. Observations that waves could not explain:
- Below a **threshold frequency** ν₀, no emission at all—however intense the light.
- The maximum kinetic energy of electrons depends on **frequency**, not intensity.
- Intensity changes only the **number** of electrons (photocurrent).
- Emission is practically instantaneous.

steps.title: Einstein's equation
steps.body:
Light consists of photons of energy **E = hν = hc/λ** (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s). Handy: E (eV) ≈ 1240/λ(nm).

**K_max = hν − φ**, where the work function φ = hν₀. Stopping potential: eV₀ = K_max.

The graph of V₀ versus ν is a straight line with slope h/e and intercept ν₀—the same slope for every metal.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Metal with φ = 2.0 eV, light of 400 nm.
- E = 1240/400 = 3.1 eV
- K_max = 3.1 − 2.0 = 1.1 eV
- Stopping potential V₀ = 1.1 V
- Threshold wavelength λ₀ = 1240/2.0 = 620 nm (red light at 700 nm would emit nothing).

steps.title: Matter waves
steps.body: De Broglie: every particle has λ = h/p = h/(mv). For an electron accelerated through V volts: **λ ≈ 1.227/√V nm**. At 100 V, λ ≈ 0.123 nm—comparable to atomic spacings, which is why electron microscopes can resolve tiny structures. Confirmed by the Davisson–Germer experiment (electron diffraction from nickel).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying brighter light gives faster electrons (it gives more electrons).
- Forgetting to convert eV ↔ J (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).
- Using λ = h/mv for photons (use λ = h/p with p = E/c).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Photons of 3 eV fall on a metal with φ = 2 eV. If the frequency is doubled, what happens to K_max?

Answer: new photon energy 6 eV ⇒ K_max = 4 eV (it was 1 eV)—it more than doubles.

activity.prompt: Above threshold, what does each change do?
buckets: Changes only the number of electrons (current)

items.text: Use a metal with a lower work function
Very bright light below the threshold frequency

quiz.q: Photon energy of 620 nm light
Stopping potential depends on
quiz.why: From eV₀ = hν − φ, the stopping potential depends on the frequency of the light (and the metal). Intensity only changes how many electrons are emitted.

quiz.q: Slope of the V₀ vs ν graph
quiz.why: V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ/e is a straight line in V₀ versus ν. Its slope is h/e.

quiz.q: De Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V
quiz.why: For an electron accelerated through V volts, λ = 1.227/√V nm. With V = 100: 1.227/10 = 0.1227 nm.

quiz.q: Threshold wavelength for φ = 3.1 eV
quiz.why: Threshold wavelength λ₀ = 1240/φ (eV) nm = 1240/3.1 = 400 nm. Light of a longer wavelength will not eject electrons.

scenes.text: At a museum lab in Lucknow, archaeologist Dr Fatima Khan measures the carbon-14 left in a charcoal sample from an ancient hearth.
'Half-life is our clock,' she tells visiting student Leo from Toronto. 'After about 5,730 years, half the carbon-14 is gone.'
Next door, a spectroscope splits hydrogen light into sharp coloured lines. Leo learns that quantum rules govern both.

steps.title: Bohr model of hydrogen
steps.body:
Postulates: electrons move in stationary orbits with angular momentum L = nh/2π; they emit or absorb a photon only when jumping between orbits: hν = E_i − E_f.

For hydrogen-like atoms (atomic number Z):
- Radius rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å
- Energy **Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV**
- Wavelengths: 1/λ = R Z²(1/n_f² − 1/n_i²), R ≈ 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹.

Series: **Lyman** (to n = 1, ultraviolet), **Balmer** (to n = 2, visible), **Paschen** (to n = 3, infrared).

steps.title: Worked example: the red line
steps.body:
Hydrogen, n = 3 → n = 2: ΔE = 13.6(1/4 − 1/9) = 13.6 × 5/36 ≈ 1.89 eV. λ = 1240/1.89 ≈ 656 nm — the red Hα line of the Balmer series.

Ionisation energy from the ground state = 13.6 eV.

steps.title: Nucleus and binding energy
steps.body:
Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3) (R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm) ⇒ nuclear density is roughly the same for all nuclei.

**Mass defect** Δm = (mass of separate nucleons) − (mass of nucleus). Binding energy = Δm c²; 1 u ≈ 931.5 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron (about 8.8 MeV), so **fission** of heavy nuclei and **fusion** of light nuclei both release energy.

steps.title: Radioactive decay
steps.body:
- α (helium nucleus): A − 4, Z − 2. β⁻ (electron + antineutrino): Z + 1. γ: no change in A or Z.
- Law: **N = N₀e^(−λt)**; half-life **T½ = ln 2/λ ≈ 0.693/λ**; mean life τ = 1/λ.
- After n half-lives, the fraction left = (½)ⁿ.

Example: 160 g of an isotope with T½ = 2 days: after 6 days (3 half-lives) 20 g remains.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Z instead of Z² in hydrogen-like energies (He⁺ ground state is −54.4 eV).
- Thinking a sample vanishes after two half-lives (¼ remains).
- Getting the mass number change wrong in β decay (A is unchanged).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
²³⁸U (Z = 92) emits one α and then two β⁻ particles. Find the final A and Z.

Answer: α ⇒ A = 234, Z = 90; two β⁻ ⇒ Z = 92. Final: A = 234, Z = 92 (an isotope of uranium).

activity.prompt: Put these discoveries in chronological order.

events.text: Einstein explains the photoelectric effect with light quanta
Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom

quiz.q: Energy of the hydrogen electron in n = 2
quiz.why: The energy of level n in hydrogen is −13.6/n² eV. For n = 2 this is −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV.

quiz.q: The Balmer series lies mainly in the
quiz.why: The Balmer series is made of transitions ending at n = 2, and most of its lines lie in the visible region. Lyman is ultraviolet and Paschen is infrared.

quiz.q: After 4 half-lives, the fraction remaining
quiz.why: Each half-life halves the amount left. After 4 half-lives, the fraction is (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.

quiz.q: In β⁻ decay
quiz.why: In β⁻ decay a neutron changes into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino. The mass number A stays the same and the atomic number Z goes up by 1.

quiz.q: Binding energy per nucleon is highest near
quiz.why: Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron and nickel, at about 8.8 MeV, which makes these nuclei the most stable. Both fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei move towards this peak.

questions.q: SI unit of lens power
questions.why: Lens power is P = 1/f with f in metres, and its SI unit is the dioptre (D).

questions.q: The red line of hydrogen (656 nm) belongs to the
questions.why: The red 656 nm line is from the 3 → 2 transition, which ends at n = 2. That makes it part of the Balmer series.

questions.q: Light enters glass from air. It bends
questions.why: When light enters a denser medium such as glass, it slows down and bends towards the normal. The angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence.

questions.q: Increasing light intensity (above threshold) increases
questions.why: Above the threshold frequency, higher intensity means more photons per second and so more electrons emitted: a larger photocurrent. Stopping potential and K_max depend on frequency, not intensity.

questions.q: Convex lens f = 10 cm, object at 20 cm. The image is
options: real, inverted, same size at 20 cm
questions.why: For an object at 2f (20 cm) a convex lens forms a real, inverted image also at 2f, of the same size (m = −1). The image is at 20 cm, not at infinity.

questions.q: A radioactive sample's activity falls to 1/8 in 15 days. Half-life
questions.why: Activity falls to 1/8 = (1/2)³, which takes 3 half-lives. So 3 half-lives = 15 days, and one half-life is 5 days.

questions.q: In YDSE, λ = 500 nm, d = 1 mm, D = 2 m. Fringe width
questions.why: The fringe width is β = λD/d = (500 × 10⁻⁹ × 2)/(1 × 10⁻³) = 10⁻³ m = 1 mm.

questions.q: Ionisation energy of He⁺ from the ground state
questions.why: For a hydrogen-like ion, ionisation energy = 13.6Z² eV. For He⁺, Z = 2, so it is 13.6 × 4 = 54.4 eV.

questions.q: 5 eV photons eject electrons with K_max = 2 eV. If the photon energy becomes 8 eV, the stopping potential becomes
questions.why: From K_max = E − φ: φ = 5 − 2 = 3 eV. With 8 eV photons K_max = 8 − 3 = 5 eV, so the stopping potential is 5 V.

questions.q: A glass lens (n = 1.5) has f = 20 cm in air. In water (n = 4/3) its focal length becomes
questions.why: 1/f ∝ (n_lens/n_medium − 1). In air this is 1.5 − 1 = 0.5; in water 1.5/(4/3) − 1 = 1.125 − 1 = 0.125. The power falls to 1/4, so f becomes 4 × 20 = 80 cm.

questions.q: An electron and a proton have the same de Broglie wavelength. Which has more kinetic energy?
questions.why: With the same wavelength λ, both have the same momentum p = h/λ. Then KE = p²/2m is larger for the particle with the smaller mass, the electron.

questions.q: Two polaroids are crossed. A third is inserted between them at 45° to both. Fraction of unpolarised I₀ transmitted
questions.why: The first polaroid passes I₀/2. The middle one at 45° passes cos²45° = 1/2 of that, and the last, also at 45° to the middle, passes another 1/2. Total = I₀/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = I₀/8.

questions.q: Ratio of the longest wavelength of the Lyman series to that of the Balmer series (hydrogen)
questions.why: Longest wavelengths: Lyman 2 → 1 gives 1/λ ∝ 1 − 1/4 = 3/4; Balmer 3 → 2 gives 1/λ ∝ 1/4 − 1/9 = 5/36. So λ_L/λ_B = (5/36)/(3/4) = 5/27.
